books.title: Living in Deserts
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing for this desert-life book.

pages.text: A Tuareg woman prepares a meal outside her home in the Sahara in Mali. Demanding Deserts Dictionary definitions of the word desert typically describe barren lands that can support little to no life. While that definition describes some desert regions, other desert landscapes are very different. They include trees, shrubs, and cacti growing on mountainsides. Many kinds of creatures call these areas home. Other deserts appear to be endless seas of sand with waves of rolling sand dunes. Streams and rivers even pass through some desert regions, although the waterways can remain empty for long periods of time.
pages.brief: A Tuareg woman in Mali prepares a meal outside her home in the Sahara, surrounded by desert. Nearby, desert landscapes show trees, shrubs and cacti on mountainsides, rolling sand dunes, and streams or rivers that can stay empty for long periods.

pages.text: All desert areas have some aspects in common. Compared with the rest of the world, deserts are arid places. They usually receive less than 25.4 centimeters (10 in.) of rain or snow each year. Deserts tend to have dry soil and not much vegetation. Although some deserts can get very cold, most deserts are sunny and hot. Palm trees near an oasis in the Sahara in Egypt (top left); flowers in sand dunes in Australia (bottom left); running water in the Sonoran Desert (top right); the world’s largest salt flat, in Bolivia (bottom right)
pages.brief: Palm trees stand near an oasis in Egypt’s Sahara; flowers grow in sand dunes in Australia; running water flows in the Sonoran Desert; and the world’s largest salt flat stretches across Bolivia. The scenes show dry soil, sparse vegetation, and sunny, hot desert conditions.

pages.text: Children run together in India’s Thar Desert. Nearly one-fifth of Earth’s land is deserts. Five of the seven continents have hot deserts (Europe and Antarctica do not). Deserts also vary in size. Some deserts are small, but others are huge. Let’s travel around the world and learn more about some of the world’s deserts and the Indigenous peoples who have called them home for thousands of years. People who live in the desert survive just like everyone else—by adapting to their surroundings. They locate food, water, and shelter as in any other demanding location on Earth. For inhabitants of desert regions, though, the desert isn’t just about survival. It is so much more than that—it is home and a way of life.
pages.brief: Children run together in India’s Thar Desert. The scene shows a desert home and way of life, with people locating food, water and shelter by adapting to their surroundings. The desert is more than survival—it is home.

pages.text: The Tohono O’odham and the Sonoran Desert The hot, dry Sonoran Desert stretches for 310,800 square kilometers (120,000 sq. mi.) across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Months may pass without any rain, and summer days can reach 49º Celsius (120ºF). On the other hand, winter nights can dip below freezing. It rains more in the Sonoran Desert than in any other desert in the world. Summer monsoons often drench the entire desert. Shade trees, large cacti such as the saguaro (suh-WAR-oh), and even summer flowers all grow there. The Tohono O’odham (toe-HOE-noh OH-eh- dom) are Indigenous people who live in the Sonoran Desert. Tohono O’odham means “desert people.” The Sonoran Desert California Arizona New Mexico PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico NORTH NORTH AMERICA AMERICA More than 2,500 native plants grow in the Sonoran Desert. No other desert in the world has more.
pages.brief: The hot, dry Sonoran Desert stretches across the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Large saguaro cacti, shade trees and summer flowers grow there after monsoons. The Tohono O’odham, whose name means 'desert people,' live in this desert.

pages.text: For the past few hundred years, people from Europe and the United States have moved onto and slowly taken land that the O’odham lived on for thousands of years. Today, the land where many O’odham live is divided among four tribes, one of which is the Tohono O’odham Nation. O’odham people at the Gila River Indian Community, the Ak-Chin Indian Community, and the Salt River (Pima Maricopa) Indian Community speak the O’odham language, although there are differences from tribe to tribe. The largest community, and the capital of the Tohono O’odham Nation, is in Sells, Arizona. Today, O’odham people live on reservations and off reservations in towns and cities. Francine Jose shows baskets made by her relatives long ago.
pages.brief: Francine Jose shows baskets made by her relatives long ago. O’odham people at the Gila River, Ak-Chin and Salt River Indian Communities speak the O’odham language, and the Tohono O’odham Nation’s capital is in Sells, Arizona. O’odham people live on and off reservations.

pages.text: For thousands of years, the desert has provided the O’odham with water, food, and shelter. Using floodwater irrigation techniques, such as water diversion, and carefully selecting planting sites, O’odham became masters at dryland agriculture, growing crops such as corn, squash, and beans. Over time, more of their land was taken and they were pressured by the U.S. government to adapt to the ways of the United States. Still, the O’odham people have fought to keep their traditions over the years. Many O’odham include their traditions in their modern lives, including farming, cooking, and basketmaking. Saguaro Fruit Harvesting The saguaro cactus is an important part of Tohono O’odham culture. Each spring, beautiful flowers bloom on the cactus. Large red fruit then ripens in mid-June. The Tohono O’odham use special tools to harvest the fruit from the tops of the giant cacti, which can reach upwards of 22 meters (75 ft.). They turn the fruit into wine that is important to their New Year celebration in early July.
pages.brief: O’odham people use floodwater irrigation and careful planting sites to grow corn, squash and beans. They harvest ripe red saguaro fruit from tall cacti with special tools and turn it into wine for their New Year celebration. Farming, cooking and basketmaking remain part of their traditions.

pages.text: Bedouin children prepare to race their camels. The Bedouin and the Sahara The Sahara stretches across northern Africa for 8.6 million square kilometers (3.3 million sq. mi.). It is very hot and dry in the Sahara. Because so little rain falls there, few plants and animals flourish there. Bedouin (BED-oo-in) are people who live in the Sahara. Bedouin comes from the Arabic word Badw, which means “people of the desert.” The Sahara Desert Morocco Tunisia Western Sahara Algeria Libya Egypt Mauritania Mali Sudan EUROPE EUROPE Niger Chad ATLANTIC OCEAN AFRICA AFRICA AFRICA In some parts of the Sahara, it rains less than 25 millimeters (1 in.) per year!
pages.brief: Bedouin children prepare to race their camels in the Sahara, which stretches across northern Africa. The desert is hot and dry, with so little rain that few plants and animals flourish there. The Bedouin are people of the desert.

pages.text: Homes in this Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara are built with dry vegetation (top). The inside of this Bedouin tent in Oman is colorful (bottom). Traditionally, the Bedouin are animal herders who roamed the desert during the rainy winter, returning with their camels, sheep, and goats to farmland during the dry summer months. Sparse natural resources forced the Bedouin to be nomadic. They traveled from oasis to oasis and also dug wells to get water. Some Bedouin still live as their ancestors did, but nomadic Bedouin today can also get supplies from markets, sellers, or other places.
pages.brief: A Bedouin village in Egypt’s Sahara shows homes built with dry vegetation, while the inside of a Bedouin tent in Oman is colorful. Traditionally, Bedouin herders roamed with camels, sheep and goats, traveling from oasis to oasis and digging wells for water.

pages.text: Bedouin lived in low black tents, called bayts, made out of goat hair or sheep’s wool. Bayts protected them from the sun, wind, and blowing sand. Some Bedouin still live in them today. In a matter of hours, Bedouins can take down their bayts and pack up their camps. For the past hundred years or so, different countries have been taking over the land where Bedouins have traditionally lived. Many Bedouin are no longer nomadic. Instead, they lead seminomadic or even settled lives. Bedouins no longer only work herding animals. Today, they have many different types of jobs. Umm Sayhoun is a Bedouin village near Petra, in Jordan (left). A Bedouin mother smiles with her son inside their home in Oman (right).
pages.brief: A Bedouin mother smiles with her son inside their home in Oman. Nearby, Umm Sayhoun is a Bedouin village near Petra in Jordan. Bedouin once lived in low black bayts made of goat hair or sheep’s wool, which protected them from sun, wind and blowing sand; some still live in them today.

pages.text: ASIA ASIA The Gobi Desert INDIAN OCEAN Mongolia China The Gobi is a rain shadow desert. It formed because mountains blocked rainy weather that would have allowed plants to flourish there. Mongolian Nomads and the Gobi Stretching for 1.3 million square kilometers (500,000 sq. mi.) across southern Mongolia to northern China, the Gobi is a rocky landscape. In the language of the Indigenous Mongolian people, Gobi means “large and dry” or the “waterless place.” Mongolian nomads have been roaming the cold, windy Gobi herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle, and two-humped Bactrian camels for thousands of years. A Mongolian woman herds her animals in the Gobi.
pages.brief: A Mongolian woman herds her animals in the Gobi, a rocky, cold and windy desert stretching from southern Mongolia to northern China. Mongolian nomads have roamed the Gobi for thousands of years, herding horses, sheep, goats, cattle and two-humped Bactrian camels.

pages.text: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. Traditionally, home is a yurt—a round tent called a ger. Made of a wooden framework covered in felt, it is able to withstand harsh weather. Gers do a good job of protecting people from extreme heat and cold, but their animals can still suffer. Many families have left nomadic lives in the desert behind. Exceptionally harsh winters and dry summers have caused thousands of families to lose part or all of their herds. Changes in government have also affected herders, making it difficult for them to earn a living. In fact, since 1989, more than half a million Mongolian nomads have moved to Mongolia’s capital city in search of food and work. Most bring their gers with them, leading to districts of gers in the city.
pages.brief: A Mongolian boy runs outside his family’s ger in the Gobi. The round tent, made of a wooden framework covered in felt, withstands harsh weather and protects people from extreme heat and cold. Many families have left nomadic lives, and some bring their gers to the capital city.

pages.text: A Way of Life People have called deserts home for thousands of years. Each desert has different challenges. The Indigenous peoples who live there have always found solutions using local resources to build homes and find food and water. Today, much has changed, and many desert dwellers lead modern lives. However, some continue to live traditional lives, as their ancestors once did, and many continue to celebrate the traditions of their desert communities. Life in the desert is as demanding as it is rewarding. The people who make the desert their home have always had deep respect for their surroundings. They honor and use its offerings while also recognizing its great power and beauty. A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates.
pages.brief: A man walks a camel along a busy street in the United Arab Emirates. People have called deserts home for thousands of years, using local resources to build homes and find food and water. Some desert dwellers lead modern lives while continuing to celebrate their communities’ traditions.

books.title: The Great Hunger
books.art_why: The Great Hunger happened in the 1800s, so no real photograph of these events exists; period-style drawings suit the famine, workhouses and coffin ships.

pages.text: Liffey River Bridge, a popular tourist area of Dublin, Ireland The Emerald Isle Ireland, known as the Emerald Isle, is a beautiful island off northwestern Europe with rolling green hills, ancient castles, and windy shores. It has a colorful history and is famous for music, literature, and folklore. Some think of it as a magical land of elves, leprechauns, and faeries. Beyond its natural beauty, Ireland is a hardworking country whose economic health matches that of most of Western Europe. Tourism remains a prime industry. Over six million people travel to Ireland each year to see the beautiful countryside and places of historical interest. It hasn’t always been that way, however.
pages.brief: Sunlight on the Liffey River Bridge in Dublin, tourists strolling and taking in the city. Beyond the rooftops, rolling green hills, an old stone castle and a windy Atlantic shore show the island of Ireland, a green land of music, story and folklore that visitors travel far to see.

pages.text: Hard Times Between 1800 and 1840, Ireland’s population increased by over 50%, to 8.5 million people. There was little industry to support so many people. While the island had been ruled by Britain for over a century and was a part of the United Kingdom, the Irish people did not have equal rights with the people of Britain. Most could not vote or hold public office, and few owned land. Unlike Britain, Ireland did not have many factories where people could work. Most people farmed land that they leased from wealthy landlords who lived in Britain. Many farms were only the size of a few acres. Tenant farmers grew wheat or other grains to pay the rent, and they grew potatoes to feed their families.
pages.brief: A tenant farmer family on a few acres of leased ground, sowing wheat and setting potato ridges by hand. In the background a landlord's fine house stands apart. The fields are small, the tools simple, and the family works long hours to grow grain for rent and potatoes to eat.

pages.text: A Horrible Discovery Farmers made a horrible discovery as they went to their fields on a foggy, fall day in 1845. The smell of decay filled the air, and the leaves of the potato plants were black and wilted. The farmers dug desperately beneath the plants, only to discover that the potatoes were mushy. Something had happened during the night. Some thought it was the unusually wet, cool weather that had killed the potatoes. Others claimed it must have been tribes of warring faeries that had destroyed the crop. Some British people of the Protestant faith thought it was God’s punishment on the Irish people for their Catholic faith. Voyage of the Potato People often associate potatoes with Ireland, but the plant was originally grown in South America. The Spanish brought potatoes to Europe in the 1500s.
pages.brief: A foggy autumn morning in 1845. Farmers kneel in a potato field, faces stricken, holding blackened, wilted leaves and digging up mushy rotten potatoes. Mist drifts between the ridges. One man stares at the ruined crop in his hands while others gather behind him in dismay.

pages.text: People depended on the potato crop for food; three million Irish people ate almost nothing but potatoes. A farmer with an acre of land could grow enough potatoes to feed his family. Potatoes, which could be stored all winter, provided a nutritious diet when eaten with milk, cabbage, and fish. Now a third of the crop rotted in the ground, and struggling families worried about how they would survive until spring.
pages.brief: A family at a plain wooden table eating boiled potatoes with milk, cabbage and fish, a piled basket of potatoes beside them. Outside, the same field shows a third of the crop blackened and rotting in the ground while the family looks anxiously toward the bare storage pit.

pages.text: First Winter The landlords took the farmers’ grain as payment for rent. Without potatoes, families had little to eat. They sold their livestock, furniture, and clothes to buy food. The government opened large workhouses where desperate families could live in exchange for work. No one wanted to go to a workhouse for help. Families worked long hours for a ragged bed and a little food, and no one could leave without permission.
pages.brief: A grey stone workhouse with a high wall and a closed gate. Inside, families in rough clothes work at scrubbing and hauling for a ragged bed and thin food. Nearby, a farmer hands over sacks of grain to a landlord's agent while a household sells furniture and clothes.

pages.text: The government bought Indian corn from America to help feed the hungry population, but people did not have a way to grind the hard, dry kernels into cornmeal, and some got sick from eating poorly cooked corn. Food got more expensive, and people became desperate to find a way to earn money. The government started public works projects, such as building roads and bridges to provide jobs. The work was hard, and the pay was low. It took nearly five days of work to buy cornmeal to feed a family of six for three days. Still, men walked many miles and stood in long lines to get any work they could find.
pages.brief: Men in worn coats stand in a long line on a muddy road, shovels over their shoulders, waiting for work on a new road and bridge. Sacks of hard yellow Indian corn are stacked nearby, and a woman struggles to grind the dry kernels by hand at a stone.

pages.text: Hope, Disaster, and Relief Finally the long winter ended, and farmers eagerly waited for the new potato crop. Disaster struck again in August, when three-fourths of the crop failed. Desperate families had nothing left to sell, the workhouses were crowded, and a long winter with no food loomed ahead. Families like ten-year-old Michael O’Kane’s had no choice but to go to the workhouse because his father, a farm laborer, could find no work. Michael, his parents, two brothers, and three sisters walked hours to the workhouse from Killylea (kih-lee-LAY) Village in September of 1847. He had to live with the boys and men in a separate area away from his mother and sisters. He went to school in the morning and then whitewashed walls or cleaned pigpens all afternoon. His youngest sister, Bridget, died over the winter. Diseases spread easily, especially in the workhouses. Even more people died of typhus and cholera than died of starvation. Despite the obvious need, many officials and landowners in Britain ignored all pleas for help or relief plans. Grain was exported to other countries rather than kept to help Irish farmers.
pages.brief: Ten-year-old Michael O'Kane walks a country road with his parents, two brothers and three sisters toward the workhouse, leaving Killylea village in September 1847. Inside, he whitewashes a long wall while other boys and men are kept apart from the women and girls in a crowded, bare room.

pages.text: Other people wanted to help. The British Relief Association and the Society of Friends (Quakers) raised money for relief. Irish immigrants in America sent money to help family and friends. Soup kitchens opened, and each day up to three million men, women, and children stood outside in long lines for a bowl of soup and a piece of bread. It was not nearly enough.
pages.brief: A crowded street outside a soup kitchen, where a long line of men, women and children holds out bowls and tin cups. Volunteers ladle soup from steaming pots and cut bread. Quakers and relief workers hand out coins and food, but the line stretches far beyond the doorway.

pages.text: Going to America Every penny a family had was spent for food, so there was nothing left to pay the overdue rent on their farm. Some landlords gave money or grain to their starving tenants, but it was only a temporary help. Other landowners evicted families from their homes, then tore down or burned the empty houses to avoid paying taxes on them. Driven from their country by hopeless conditions, hundreds of thousands of Irish people crowded onto ships bound for the United States or Canada, leaving their Irish homeland forever.
pages.brief: An eviction on a hillside: a family carries bundles and furniture out of a small cottage while men tear down the roof and set the thatch alight. Down at the harbour, a dense crowd of people with sacks and trunks climbs aboard a ship bound for America.

pages.text: It was a difficult journey because a ship took forty days to cross the Atlantic Ocean, even when the weather was good. Many of the ships carrying the Irish emigrants were called “coffin” ships. Passengers were packed below deck, where disease spread in the overcrowded, filthy conditions. There often was not enough food, water, or blankets for the passengers. Many died, and many of those who survived arrived in America sick and weak. Ireland’s Potato Blight and Famine 1800 to 1840s - POPULATION INCREASE Ireland’s population soars by 50% between 1800 and 1840, but employment remains limited. Struggling rural families depend on potatoes as their main food source. 1845 - FIRST BLIGHT REPORTED IN AUGUST By September, the potato blight has spread from southern Britain, Scotland, Belgium, and Holland to Ireland. 1846 - RELIEF EFFORTS BEGIN Workhouses are expanded, and government work projects begin. Three-fourths of the year’s potato crop is lost that fall. 1847 - MASS EVICTIONS BEGIN Soup kitchens feed over 3 million people a day. Landlords begin to evict tenant farmers and burn homes to avoid paying taxes. 1848 to 1849 - WORKHOUSES ARE FULL - DISEASE SPREADS Reports of cholera increase, especially in overcrowded, filthy workhouses. Two-thirds of the 1849 potato crop is lost. 1852 - BLIGHT GRADUALLY ENDS By 1852, the potato blight has ended. Over one million people have died, and another million have emigrated.
pages.brief: Below deck on an emigrant ship crossing the Atlantic, passengers are packed tightly on wooden bunks in dim, filthy air between the timbers. On the open deck, a few weak and sick travellers huddle under thin blankets, staring at empty water barrels and the endless grey sea.

pages.text: Aftermath The potato blight was over by 1852, but Ireland was changed forever. A million people had died, and over a million had emigrated. Many people who stayed in Ireland were homeless and jobless. The landlords could not make money, so they sold the land for other purposes or simply abandoned it rather than pay high taxes. With no land and no jobs, many Irish people continued to emigrate over the next decades. By 1861, the population of Ireland had dropped from over 8.5 million to 5 million; more than one in three people were gone. Ten years later, the population had dropped even further to 4.5 million. Many Irish people blamed Britain, the most powerful country in the world at that time, for not helping more. This bitterness would help fuel the revolution that finally split Ireland into two countries in 1922. The Two Irelands Since 1922, the island of Ireland has been divided into two countries. The independent Republic of Ireland is in the south. Northern Ireland is still part of the United Kingdom.
pages.brief: A quiet abandoned countryside of roofless cottages, empty fields and an old landlord's house standing silent. At a harbour, another group of emigrants boards a ship. A map-like view of the island shows green land fading into two separate countries, north and south.

pages.text: Conclusion Scientists eventually discovered that the potato plants died of a disease called late potato blight, which was caused by the funguslike organism Phytophthora infestans. Spores from the organism were blown by wind and washed into the soil by rain. Even after the Great Hunger, as the famine was called in Ireland, Irish immigration to the United States continued. Over five million people arrived between 1850 and 1920. Some ran for political office, and others started businesses. Famous Americans, including President John F. Kennedy and inventor Henry Ford, had ancestors who came to America during the famine. Today, forty million Americans proudly claim Irish roots, celebrate its folk traditions and holidays, and continue to popularize Irish literature, music, and film as an established part of world culture. The statue of Annie Moore and her brothers at Cobh Harbor, Ireland, has come to represent all of the famine emigrants who left Ireland in search of a better life.
pages.brief: A scientist at a bench peers through a microscope at the fungus-like organism that killed the potatoes, spores drifting on wind and rain. At Cobh Harbour, a bronze statue of Annie Moore and her two brothers stands on the quay, watched by visitors remembering the emigrants who left Ireland.

books.title: Woods of Wonder
books.art_why: The text describes real, present-day forests, parks, trees and animals, so photographs are appropriate.

pages.text: Woods of Wonder.
pages.brief: A quiet woodland scene filled with trees and green undergrowth, shown as a place of wonder. The view is wide and peaceful, with layered branches and shaded forest floor. Tall trunks rise into a soft, dim canopy, and the whole woods feel mysterious and inviting, with no people or animals in sight.

pages.text: Oh, That’s Old! Imagine you’re in a dark, lovely forest. Trees with trunks wider than cars tower overhead and block almost all the sunlight. Small ferns and other plants soak up what little light they can find. Pine needles and other dead leaves cover the ground. Like something out of a fairy tale, an old- growth forest is a place of wonder and mystery.
pages.brief: Inside a dark, lovely old-growth forest, huge tree trunks wider than cars tower overhead and block almost all sunlight. Small ferns and other plants grow on the shaded ground among pine needles and dead leaves. The scene feels like a fairy-tale place of wonder and mystery.

pages.text: For some old-growth forests, this scene wouldn’t be far from the truth. Others might look quite different. Some old-growth forests have only one type of tree, while others have many. Some may have trees that seem to touch the sky, while others have trees shorter than a house. Because of this variety, scientists do not have one definition for old-growth forests. Still, they have found some features that many old-growth forests share. Many scientists agree that an old-growth forest must be at least 150 years old. The age of each tree in the forest may vary widely, however. The forest’s structure must also be complex. This means that the canopy must have varying layers with large trees, both living and dead (or dying). Fallen trees create holes in the canopy where young trees can find the sunlight to grow. Fallen trees and upright dead trees, called snags, provide food and shelter for many animals, plants, and fungi. Some of these species live nowhere else on Earth.
pages.brief: An old-growth forest with a complex canopy of tall living trees, dying trees and upright dead snags. A fallen tree has opened a gap where young trees reach for sunlight. Fallen wood and snags shelter animals, plants and fungi on the forest floor.

pages.text: Forest Levels Old-growth forests are some of the most beautiful and scientifically interesting places on Earth. Yet because of humans, many of them have shrunk or disappeared. By carefully studying and protecting the ones that remain, we can understand the complex and delicate ecosystems they create.
pages.brief: A broad view of a beautiful old-growth forest with layered levels of trees and plants, shown as a scientifically interesting ecosystem. Nearby, a smaller patch of forest suggests places that have shrunk or disappeared because of human actions. The scene focuses on the complex, delicate life that remains.

pages.text: United States Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California together cover more than 1,353 square miles (3,504 sq km). They hold more than 300 square miles (777 sq km) of old-growth forest. This forest includes a variety of tree species, mostly coniferous but deciduous as well. One of the most amazing of these is the giant sequoia. Found only in California, these huge trees are among the oldest on Earth. They can live for more than 3,000 years. A giant sequoia known as the General Sherman Tree is the largest tree in the world.
pages.brief: In Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks in California, an old-growth forest holds coniferous and deciduous trees across a vast protected landscape. A giant sequoia, found only in California, rises among them. The General Sherman Tree stands as the largest tree in the world, ancient and enormous.

pages.text: Thousands of creatures live in the park, including the Pacific fisher. This relative of the weasel lives under the thick canopy in old-growth forests. It hunts birds and small mammals—but its favorite meal is porcupine. Because its habitat is limited to old-growth forests, it is now rare in California, Oregon, and Washington. Sequoia vs. Redwood Giant redwoods and giant sequoias both grow in California. They have the same color bark. Both are huge, but they’re different. Giant redwoods are the tallest trees in the world. They can reach up to 378 feet (115 m)! Giant sequoias are the largest. At up to 40 feet (12 m) in diameter, they can grow almost twice as wide as redwoods. Redwoods grow best in fog. Sequoias need dry heat for their cones to open. Redwoods grow near sea level. Sequoias grow at 5,000 to 7,000 feet (1,524 to 2,134 m).
pages.brief: Under the thick canopy of an old-growth forest in the park, a Pacific fisher, a weasel relative, hunts birds and small mammals. Nearby, giant redwoods and giant sequoias show their different shapes: redwoods are tallest, sequoias widest, with redwoods in fog and sequoias in dry heat.

pages.text: Across the United States in the Appalachian Mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee, Great Smoky Mountains National Park covers more than 800 square miles (2,072 sq km). Almost all of the park is forest, with old-growth forests only making up about 25 percent. Deciduous trees make up most of the old-growth forests in this area. Species include dogwood, Carolina silverbell, magnolia, American beech, yellow bird, and maple, among others.
pages.brief: In Great Smoky Mountains National Park in North Carolina and Tennessee, forest covers almost the whole landscape. Within it, an old-growth deciduous forest holds dogwood, Carolina silverbell, magnolia, American beech, yellow bird and maple trees. The old-growth area is a smaller part of the larger forest.

pages.text: Northern flying squirrel The endangered Carolina northern flying squirrel makes its home among these trees. These small mammals don’t actually fly. They use skin attached at their front and back paws to glide. They mostly eat fungi and lichens but may also feed on fruits and nuts. Without the old-growth forest, these animals would vanish. Tough, Not Tall Not all old-growth forests feature towering trees. In some harsh places exposed to fierce and frigid winds, pines, spruces, and other coniferous trees become stunted and twisted. These trees are called Krummholz, a German word meaning “crooked wood.” They live near the Arctic and near timberline, the boundary on a mountain where the trees stop growing. They never grow much over 6 feet (1.8 m) tall, but don’t let their size fool you: Some are one thousand years old.
pages.brief: A small Carolina northern flying squirrel glides between trees using skin attached at its front and back paws. Nearby, stunted, twisted Krummholz pines and spruces grow in a harsh, windy place near timberline. The trees stay under six feet tall, though some are a thousand years old.

pages.text: A Seibold’s beech tree reaches for the sun in Shirakami-Sanchi, Japan. Japan In the northern part of Japan sits Shirakami- Sanchi. It’s one of the last untouched old-growth forests in East Asia. Made up mostly of Seibold’s beech trees, the area covers just 65 square miles (170 sq km) of the Shirakami Mountains. Forests like this one once covered most of northern Japan, but many have been cut down.
pages.brief: In Shirakami-Sanchi in northern Japan, a Seibold’s beech tree reaches toward the sun in an untouched old-growth forest. Seibold’s beech trees make up most of this 65-square-mile area in the Shirakami Mountains. Forests like this once covered most of northern Japan, but many were cut down.

pages.text: Almost completely untouched by humans, Shirakami-Sanchi has no trails or structures. Because of its steep slopes, no trees have been cut down. Wildlife within the area is protected, although hunters called Matagi are sometimes allowed to hunt bears as part of their religion. The forest is also home to the Japanese serow. This goatlike animal is only found here and in two other small areas in Japan. More than 2,100 insect species and 87 bird species live in the forests—including the black woodpecker, an endangered species in Japan. Japanese serow Black woodpeckers.
pages.brief: On steep slopes in untouched Shirakami-Sanchi, there are no trails or structures. A goatlike Japanese serow stands among the protected trees. A black woodpecker, endangered in Japan, clings to a trunk. The forest shelters more than 2,100 insect species and 87 bird species, while Matagi hunters are sometimes allowed to hunt bears.

pages.text: Fallen trees like this fir can nurse along other plants in this old-growth forest in the Caucasus region of Russia. Russia Russia’s Western Caucasus region stretches about 1,062 square miles (2,750 sq km) from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains. Protected within Caucasus State Biosphere Reserve and Sochi National Park, this area shows great diversity. Coniferous trees make up most of the forests. Different species, such as pine, cedar, fir, and spruce—as well as beech and oak (both deciduous)—grow in different areas and at different elevations.
pages.brief: In the Western Caucasus region of Russia, a fallen fir tree nurses other plants in an old-growth forest. The protected area stretches from the Black Sea to the Caucasus Mountains. Coniferous trees such as pine, cedar, fir and spruce grow at different elevations, with beech and oak in different areas.

pages.text: Snow leopards A variety of endangered animals make their home in these forests. Some scientists think that a very small number of endangered snow leopards survive there. No sightings have been reported for years, but scientists still find signs of the large cats, such as paw prints and scat. The endangered wisent, or European bison, has also been returned to the forest. The last wild wisent was killed in the Western Caucasus in 1927. People set captive wisents free in the area in 1940. Wisents.
pages.brief: In the Western Caucasus forests, a snow leopard is shown as an endangered large cat known only from signs such as paw prints and scat. A European bison, or wisent, stands nearby. The last wild wisent was killed in 1927, and captive wisents were set free in the area in 1940.

pages.text: The Future of Old-Growth Forests Old-growth forests often contain very complex ecosystems that have been supporting life for hundreds or even thousands of years. Governments, national parks, and organizations protect many of these places. However, other old-growth forests, both small and large, are in danger. Human actions can damage or destroy these delicate ecosystems. Once gone, the beauty and scientific information that these old- growth forests hold may be lost forever. Laws prevent logging in some old-growth forests but not others. People continue to debate how much protection is enough.
pages.brief: A view of a complex old-growth forest that has supported life for hundreds or thousands of years. Protected areas remain, but other old-growth forests are in danger from human actions. The scene suggests both beauty and loss, as people debate how much protection is enough and laws cover only some forests.

books.title: What Is Water Worth?
books.art_why: The book shows real places, people, water systems, and environmental scenes.

pages.text: Russia’s Lake Baikal is the deepest and oldest freshwater lake in the world. It is also the largest by volume but not by surface area. Lake Superior holds that record. Water, Water Everywhere Many of us around the world take water for granted. Why shouldn’t we, when water is all around? It comes out of our faucets and collects in puddles on the sidewalk when it rains. Lakes and rivers brim with water. We buy water in bottles and slurp it from drinking fountains. In fact, if we had a drinking glass as big as the United States and filled it with every drop of water on the planet, the glass would have to be 145 kilometers (90 mi.) tall to hold it all. With so much water, you’d think everyone would have enough to drink. Not so!
pages.brief: A wide view of Russia’s Lake Baikal, the deepest and oldest freshwater lake, with clear blue water. A smaller lake nearby shows Lake Superior’s larger surface area. People fill bottles at a drinking fountain, rain collects in a sidewalk puddle, and lakes and rivers brim with water, while a giant drinking glass rises 90 miles tall.

pages.text: A Drop in the Bucket Water is fast becoming more precious than gold or oil. The planet simply does not have enough usable water for everyone. For one thing, most of Earth’s water is salt water, which we can’t drink or use to water our crops. Only about 3 percent of Earth’s water is fresh. Most of that is locked away in polar ice caps, glaciers, or underground layers of rock called aquifers. Where’s the Water? Oceans (salt water) 97% Earth’s water Fresh water 3% Ice caps and glaciers 68.7% Fresh water Groundwater* 30.1% Surface water 0.3% Fresh surface water Lakes 87% Rivers 2% Swamps 11% *Groundwater provides 25% to 40% of the world's drinking water. It provides even more water for growing food. However, groundwater supplies are shrinking.
pages.brief: A single water drop falls toward a bucket beside a vast blue ocean, polar ice caps, and a glacier. Below the surface, layers of rock hold groundwater in an aquifer. A tiny fresh surface lake, river, and swamp show the small share of Earth’s water that is fresh and usable.

pages.text: Even though the region is water-starved, the people of Saudi Arabia can access water because it is a high-income country. Some countries have more fresh water than others, but most have enough water to meet people’s needs. What they don’t always have is the means to make that water available to people. High-income countries can tap into hard-to-get sources of water much more easily than low- income countries, where people often don’t have enough money to dig wells or build dams to create reservoirs. Today, we humans can only reach and use 1 percent of Earth’s freshwater. That 1 percent is under stress due to three underlying problems: pollution, increased demand driven by the world’s ever-growing population, and climate change.
pages.brief: In water-starved Saudi Arabia, people access water because it is a high-income country. In a low-income country, people lack money to dig a well or build a dam and reservoir. A small portion of Earth’s freshwater is visible, while pollution, growing population demand, and climate change put pressure on it.

pages.text: Pollution’s Impact Water pollution is a huge problem on many continents. South America’s Amazon rainforest spans 7 million square kilometers (2.7 million sq. mi.) and is home to about 30 million people and more than 30,000 plant species. For years, people have been dumping untreated human waste and toxic chemicals into the Amazon River. Drilling for oil and mining for gold have made some sections of the Amazon River toxic. In other low-income areas where fresh water often goes untreated, pollution makes people sick in other ways. Because people lack access to running water or indoor plumbing, human waste ends up outside.
pages.brief: Dense Amazon rainforest surrounds the Amazon River where people dump untreated human waste and toxic chemicals. Oil drilling and gold mining leave some river sections toxic. In a low-income area nearby homes without running water or indoor plumbing sit beside waste that ends up outside.

pages.text: Do You Know? Worldwide, more people have a mobile phone than a toilet. That waste, filled with bacteria, then flows into rivers and streams. People use the water in these toxic waterways for drinking, cooking, and bathing. According to the United Nations Development Program, half the world’s hospital beds contain patients sick from drinking unclean water. High-income countries such as the United States, where most people have access to clean drinking water, experience other challenges with pollution. The most common challenge comes from agriculture. Every time it rains, chemicals and animal waste from farming are washed into waterways. An aging sewage treatment system, oil, and other kinds of pollution all threaten U.S. waters as well.
pages.brief: A person holds a mobile phone near a simple outdoor toilet, showing that more people have phones than toilets. Bacteria-filled waste flows into a river where people scoop water for drinking, cooking, and bathing. In a U.S. farm setting, rain washes chemicals and animal waste toward a waterway, while an aging sewage system and oil threaten the water.

pages.text: Population’s Impact In 2011, the human species hit a milestone. On October 30, a baby girl was born in the Philippines: the world’s 7 billionth person. By 2050, experts say that 9.7 billion people will be walking the planet, each looking for food, energy, land, and water. Growing populations reduce the amount of water available for each person. In 1950, the 2.5 billion people on Earth only used a third of the fresh water that we use today. Now, research shows that 1 in 9 people lack safe water to drink. Many live on less than 8 liters (2 gal.) a day. By 2050, more than half of the world’s people will be living in areas where water is scarce. High-income countries are far less likely to face polluted drinking water than low-income countries, but some face surging populations. This can lead to water shortages, in part because people in high-income countries use more water. Average Daily Water Use: Americans vs. Others Compare daily water use between Americans (left) and many low-income people around the world (above).
pages.brief: A baby girl is born in the Philippines on October 30, 2011, marking the world’s 7 billionth person. Around her, a crowded city and a dry village show growing populations needing food, energy, land, and water. One family uses many containers of water while another uses only a few, comparing daily water use.

pages.text: In the United States, a four-person family, on average, uses 1,514 liters (400 gal.) of water a day, about 379 liters (100 gal.) per person. This level of use could last if only a few people were using the water. Instead, more and more people rely on limited water sources. For example, Los Angeles County’s population is expected to reach 13 million by 2050. Yet the area can only support 1 million people on its own water. Big Population = Big Water Demand.
pages.brief: A four-person family in the United States uses water at home, with many gallons flowing for daily needs. In Los Angeles County, a sprawling city grows crowded as its population climbs toward 13 million by 2050, while the area’s own water can support only 1 million people. More people mean greater water demand.

pages.text: The Impact of Climate Change Climate change is already affecting people around the world by producing extreme weather conditions such as storms and floods. Yet the threat that climate change presents to the global water supply may be the worst threat of all. Scientists predict that by 2050, more than 5 billion people may face severe water shortages as a result of climate change. Climate change results from too much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. These gases, produced in large part by the burning of fossil fuels, trap the Sun’s heat close to Earth’s surface, much like a greenhouse. The result is an overall increase in Earth’s temperature. That warming, in turn, leads to climate change. The warmer temperatures disrupt the water cycle, which is a delicate balance between evaporation and precipitation. Warmer temperatures increase the rate of surface water evaporation into the atmosphere. That, in turn, affects different parts of the world in different ways. Increased evaporation might dry out some areas while producing droughts in other areas. A drought is a long period of lower-than-normal precipitation that results in a shortage of water.
pages.brief: A storm and flood strike a community while a greenhouse-like layer of gases traps the Sun’s heat close to Earth. Warmer temperatures speed evaporation from lakes and soil, disrupting the balance between evaporation and precipitation. One area dries out while another suffers a long drought with lower-than-normal rain and a water shortage.

pages.text: Regions at the highest risk of drought include the Mediterranean and the Middle East. In the United States, most scientists say that climate change is responsible for an extreme drought in the Southwest and California. The drought in the Southwest has been causing problems in the region since 1999. The water level of Lake Mead, on the border between Nevada and Arizona, has plummeted. The lake, which is fed by the Colorado River, is a source of fresh water for 25 million people. If rains don’t increase soon, odds are good that desert residents will have to start rationing water. A River Runs Dry Nearly 40 million people depend on the Colorado River. It now trickles to an end before it can reach the sea.
pages.brief: A Mediterranean and Middle Eastern landscape shows drought risk. In the U.S. Southwest and California, parched ground surrounds Lake Mead on the Nevada-Arizona border, where the water level has plummeted; the lake is fed by the Colorado River and supplies 25 million people. Desert residents face water rationing as the Colorado River trickles to an end before reaching the sea.

pages.text: A boy fishes in the Daning River, one of many rivers fed by the Himalayas. Climate change is also responsible for the melting of glaciers high in the Himalaya mountains. The glaciers help provide fresh water for 1.5 billion people living in India, Pakistan, and six other Asian countries. In the past, the melting glaciers slowly released water into the rivers below. Now the glaciers are melting rapidly, and the long-term water supply is shrinking. At the same time, the increased melting has caused severe flooding along these rivers. As climate change worsens, less water is available for ranching, growing crops, and producing energy. Nature and wildlife suffer. Arguments break out between cities, states, and even countries over who has more right to the same source of water. For instance, Pakistan and India are in a race to build dams on the headwaters of the same river. Tensions between the two countries run high, and the growing water crisis hasn’t helped.
pages.brief: A boy fishes in the Daning River, fed by the Himalayas. High in the mountains, glaciers melt rapidly, causing flooding downstream and shrinking the long-term water supply for 1.5 billion people in India, Pakistan, and six other Asian countries. Farmers, ranchers, and wildlife suffer as cities and countries argue over the same water; Pakistan and India race to build dams.

pages.text: Solving the Problem So what can we do? Each person’s efforts to conserve water can help. States can conserve, too. The Colorado River supplies water to much of the American West. While cities are growing rapidly, farming and ranching still use more than 70 percent of the river’s water. Should some of that water go to cities instead? Countries need to find solutions, too. Workers in Saudi Arabia are converting salt water to fresh water in a process called desalination. The process is expensive, though, and many countries cannot afford to build desalination plants. What Can You Do? • Take shorter showers (or take baths if you like to linger). • When you can, buy used or recycled stuff instead of new stuff. • To help stop climate change, ride your bike, walk, or use public transit. • Turn off the water when brushing your teeth. • Buy a rain barrel to store water for plants. • Fix leaks and drips. • Eat less meat (on average, beef requires 125 times more water than the same amount of potatoes).
pages.brief: A person takes a shorter shower and turns off the water while brushing teeth. Outside, a rain barrel collects water for plants, and someone fixes a leaking pipe. A cyclist rides past instead of driving, and a meal with less meat sits beside potatoes. In Saudi Arabia, workers convert salt water to fresh water at a desalination plant.

pages.text: Competing Water Uses KEY 8% 8% 10% 11% 22% 30% 82% 70% 59% High-income countries World The island of Singapore has experimented with cleaning wastewater that comes from washing dishes, flushing toilets, and taking baths and showers. Some other countries do this, too, but Singapore obtains one-third of its water this way. While cities are growing rapidly, agriculture uses about 70 percent of the world’s water. Some farmers and ranchers are trying to use water in more efficient ways. The water saved could go to cities instead. Solving the planet’s water problem is hard. Still, we all need to find ways to conserve this valuable resource, not just for our generation, but for the ones yet to come.
pages.brief: In Singapore, wastewater from washing dishes, flushing toilets, and taking baths and showers is cleaned and reused, supplying one-third of the island’s water. Nearby, a farm uses water efficiently while a growing city waits for some of the saved supply. Agriculture takes about 70 percent of the world’s water, and people must conserve this valuable resource for future generations.

books.title: Ostriches: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Living ostriches exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Ostriches: Giant Birds.
pages.brief: An ostrich, a giant bird, stands alone with its long neck extended and strong legs planted. Its large body and height dominate the image. The bird looks powerful and imposing. No other animals or people are present.

pages.text: How Big Is It? Ostrich height: 9 feet (2.74 m) weight: 350 pounds (158.8 kg) Human height: 6 feet (1.8 m) weight: 175 pounds (79.4 kg) The Original Big Bird It’s huge, it’s powerful, and it means business! It’s an ostrich—the world’s largest living bird— and it’s a far cry from the delicate songbirds that come to mind when most people think of birds. Ostriches are marathon runners and heavyweight kickboxers rolled into one. Don’t ruffle their feathers or you’ll be in a heap of trouble!
pages.brief: A tall adult ostrich stands beside a grown human, the bird's head rising well above the person's head. Both are on flat ground, facing forward. The ostrich's powerful body and long legs are clear, showing it is much larger and heavier.

pages.text: No Ordinary Bird Ostriches are the giants of the bird world. Adult males can grow as tall as 9 feet (2.7 m) with their neck extended and weigh up to 350 pounds (160 kg). Females are slightly smaller but still enormous. Adult males and females are easy to tell apart by their coloring. The males are a striking black and white, while females and juveniles are grayish-brown. Some ostriches have pink necks and thighs. Male and female ostriches take turns watching their chicks until they are full grown.
pages.brief: An adult male ostrich, striking black and white, stands near a grayish-brown female and several juveniles. The group is on open ground, with the adults watching the young. One ostrich shows pinkish skin on its neck and thighs.

pages.text: An ostrich’s main toe, which enables it to run fast, has a sharp claw that measures 4 inches (10 cm) long. Ostriches are different from most birds in that they cannot fly. However, they’re the fastest birds on foot. They can run 30 miles per hour (48.2 kph) over a long distance and can sprint up to 45 miles per hour (72.4 kph). In spite of their large size, ostriches are agile and can turn on a dime using their wings for balance. As the only two-toed birds in the world, ostriches are adapted for running. They run on each foot’s longer toe and use the other toe for balance.
pages.brief: A close view of an ostrich's strong foot shows two toes and a long, sharp claw touching dry ground. Behind it, the bird runs fast with wings partly spread for balance, turning sharply on open land.

pages.text: What Makes an Ostrich a Bird? An ostrich’s eyes are five times bigger than a human’s eyes. An ostrich has nostrils on its bill to help it breathe. An ostrich can’t fly, but its feathers keep it warm. Its wings help it balance when running. Ostrich eggs are the largest and thickest of any bird’s. An ostrich only has two toes on each foot. All birds • have a backbone • have feathers • have wings.
pages.brief: A close-up of an ostrich's head fills the view, one huge eye and nostrils on its bill clearly visible. Its soft feathers and wing show behind. Nearby on the ground lie large, thick ostrich eggs, and one foot reveals two toes.

pages.text: Ostriches also have unusual feathers. Most birds have stiff feathers with a strong spine down the middle. In contrast, ostriches have soft, fluffy feathers. The feathers protect these giants from sunlight during the day and keep them warm at Most birds have a gland that spreads oil over their feathers when they clean themselves. The oil makes their feathers waterproof. Because ostriches don’t have this gland, they can get soaked to the skin when it rains. These birds have enormous eyes—the largest of any land animal. Each of their eyes measures almost 2 inches (5 cm) across. Their brain is about the same size as one of their eyes, which is quite small for such a huge animal. Ostrich veterinarian Dr. Carole Price says, “Ostriches are as dumb as a box of rocks. They run or fight—they don’t think.” They are, however, curious about everything and have to check it out, whether it’s a wrinkle in a person’s T-shirt or sparkly jewelry. One of these big birds earned the nickname “The $10,000 Ostrich” after plucking and swallowing one of its owner’s diamond earrings.
pages.brief: An ostrich leans in close, curious, inspecting a person's sparkly earring and the wrinkle in a T-shirt. Its huge eye is prominent, and its soft, fluffy feathers look different from stiff flight feathers. Rain clouds gather overhead, hinting that wet feathers offer little protection.

pages.text: Where Ostriches Live ATLANTIC OCEAN Ostrich range AFRICA Equator INDIAN OCEAN ATLANTIC OCEAN Ostrich range Bird Herd Ostriches live in African deserts and savannas. The areas where they live are dry, with extreme heat during the day and cold temperatures at night. Ostriches live in herds that usually have fewer than twelve birds, though a group of one hundred or more may occasionally gather near a watering hole. Hanging out in a herd, ostriches use teamwork to stay safe. Their good vision and long necks help them spot danger from far away.
pages.brief: A group of ostriches stands in a dry African savanna under a hot sky, long necks raised to scan for danger. Sparse plants and dusty ground show the desert edge. In the distance, a watering hole draws a larger gathering of ostriches, while a small herd stays close together.

pages.text: A rooster—the dominant male—is in charge of the herd. He makes a roaring “boo-boo-BOO- hoo” call to warn the flock about nearby danger. He also sounds off to intimidate other males and impress the females, or hens. The dominant male goes through an elaborate courtship dance to attract the main hen. He bows, shakes one wing at a time, and moves his tail up and down. Then he holds out his wings and approaches the female while stamping his feet. A male ostrich displays his feathers as part of his courtship dance.
pages.brief: A dominant male ostrich stands before several hens, wings held out and tail lifted in a courtship display. His neck is bowed, one wing shaken, feet stamping the ground. Nearby males keep their distance as he calls, showing he is in charge of the herd.

pages.text: Unlike the legs of humans and many other animals, an ostrich’s legs bend forward, producing a powerful kick. Kickboxing Champs Ostriches have no trouble holding their own against predators. That’s where the kickboxing comes in. Their kick is so strong that it can kill a full-grown lion with one blow. In the event that an ostrich can’t fight or flee, it lies down and places its long neck on the ground. By staying still in that position, it makes itself less visible. This defense has given rise to the myth that ostriches bury their heads in the sand.
pages.brief: An ostrich delivers a powerful forward kick toward a full-grown lion, its long leg extended and claw visible. The lion recoils on the open savanna. In the background, another ostrich lies low with its long neck stretched on the ground, making itself less visible.

pages.text: Ostriches don’t need to drink water; they get enough from the plants they eat. Eating like a Bird Ostriches are omnivores. Their typical food is leaves, seeds, and roots. They also eat lizards, snakes, rodents, insects, and any other food they can find if they’re hungry. Their diet varies throughout the year, and food is sometimes scarce. To make sure they get as many nutrients as possible from their food, their intestines have evolved to be extra long—46 feet (14 m)—that’s almost twice the length of human intestines! These giant birds swallow pebbles and sand to help them grind up food in their gizzard, a special digestive organ.
pages.brief: An ostrich bends to eat leaves, seeds, and roots from low plants on dry ground. Nearby, a small lizard and insects suggest its omnivore diet. Scattered pebbles and sand lie within reach, and the bird's long body hints at the extra-long digestive tract inside.

pages.text: The dominant male ostrich digs a shallow pit in the dirt for the main hen to lay her eggs. Egg-stra Large A female ostrich lays six or more eggs in a shallow depression in the sand. All females in the herd place their eggs in the main hen’s nest. The main hen sits on them during the day, and the dominant male takes night duty. The eggs hatch after about forty days. Few animals mess with adult ostriches, but their eggs can be stolen by predators such as vultures, jackals, and hyenas, which may also take young ostriches. Ostrich chicks are the size of full-grown chickens when they hatch. Males and females work together to care for the chicks. The dominant male protects them by distracting predators and also teaches the chicks what to eat. They grow about 1 foot (30 cm) each month. By the age of six months, they’re close to adult size. Ostriches can live to age fifty or older.
pages.brief: A shallow nest pit in the sand holds a clutch of huge ostrich eggs. A grayish-brown female sits on them in daylight while a black-and-white male stands guard nearby. Around the nest, several chicken-sized chicks follow the adults, and a jackal watches from a distance.

pages.text: Raising Giants Ostrich numbers dropped sharply in the 1700s and 1800s because they were hunted for their feathers, which were used in women’s fashion long ago. They were also hunted for food and leather as well as for making feather dusters. When ostrich farming began in 1838, some wild herds recovered. Wild ostriches are not at risk of becoming endangered. Ostriches are now farmed around the world for meat, leather, feathers, and eggs. • Ostriches lay the world’s biggest eggs. It would take two dozen chicken eggs to equal the weight of one ostrich egg. An ostrich egg measures about 6 inches (15 cm) long and weighs about 3 pounds (1.5 kg). • Ostriches are among Tyrannosaurus rex’s closest living relatives. A scientist found a Tyrannosaurus rex bone. He compared the cells to those of twenty-one modern animals. They most closely matched ostriches and chickens.
pages.brief: On an ostrich farm, several ostriches stand in fenced enclosures beside a collection of huge eggs. A person holds a feather duster and an old-fashioned feathered hat, showing why the birds were hunted and farmed. In the background, a scientist studies a fossil bone beside modern animal cells.

pages.text: A female ostrich chases away a rival. Awesome Birds Unlike most other birds, ostriches are not timid, delicate, or easily startled. These bold, sturdy creatures hold their ground when challenged. They’re agile runners and masterful fighters with a host of fascinating adaptations. Simply put, ostriches are the biggest, baddest birds in the world.
pages.brief: A female ostrich charges across open ground, wings spread and legs kicking up dust as she chases away a rival. Her bold posture shows she is not timid or delicate. Behind her, another ostrich retreats, while the strong, sturdy body of the chasing bird fills the scene.

books.title: Sacagawea and the Corps of Discovery
books.art_why: The story is set in the early 1800s, before photographs, so historical events must be illustrated.

pages.text: Sacagawea and the Corps of Discovery Sacagawea and the Corps of Discovery Written by Kira Freed and Charlie Alolkoy Illustrated by Elaine S. Verstraete.
pages.brief: A dignified historical portrait of Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman, standing outdoors with her infant son carried on her back in a cradleboard, calm and determined, with a wide western river landscape and distant boats behind her.

pages.text: Introduction In the first decade of the 1800s, a Lemhi Shoshone teenager went on one of the most difficult and dangerous trips in American history. As the only female in the group, she faced isolation. She also faced hunger, illness, severe weather, and challenging terrain—all with a baby to care for. This girl was Sacagawea (sah-kah- gah-WEE-ah), one of the most famous Native women in U.S. history. Sacagawea’s Name Sacagawea’s name is written with several different spellings. Her name is also pronounced in different ways, although (sah-kah-gah-WEE-ah) is common. Some people think that her name meant “Bird Woman.” In Shoshone, her name may have meant “Boat Launcher.” Sacagawea’s Name Sacagawea’s name is written with several different spellings. Her name is also pronounced in different ways, although (sah-kah-gah-WEE-ah) is common. Some people think that her name meant “Bird Woman.” In Shoshone, her name may have meant “Boat Launcher.”
pages.brief: Sacagawea, a Lemhi Shoshone teenager, walks through harsh country with her baby on her back, alone among the male explorers; she looks tired but steady as wind, snow, and rocky ground show the hunger, illness, and severe weather she faced.

pages.text: The Louisiana Territory Oregon Country The Louisiana Territory included all or part of fifteen present-day states. Louisiana Territory Growth of the United States In 1803, the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France. This huge area of land west of the Mississippi measured 820,000 square miles (2,123,800 sq km). Buying it doubled the country’s size. Many nations of Native people had been living in that area for thousands of years. However, like many European countries, the United States wished to claim their land as its own. President Thomas Jefferson sent a team of explorers to the area. Called the Corps (KOR) of Discovery, the troop was led by U.S. Army Captain Meriwether Lewis and Second Lieutenant William Clark. Jefferson instructed them to search for the Northwest Passage, a waterway believed to connect the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Their job also included learning about the new lands and establishing relations with the many Native nations that inhabited the territory. The Corps began their trip on May 14, 1804, heading up the Missouri River from St. Louis by boat.
pages.brief: President Thomas Jefferson stands with Captain Meriwether Lewis and Lieutenant William Clark beside a large table, while outside a boat waits on the Missouri River; beyond them stretch wide plains and Native villages of the Louisiana Territory.

pages.text: Sacagawea’s Roots Sacagawea was born in 1788 or 1789 in what is now Idaho. She was the daughter of a Lemhi (LEM-hy) Shoshone chief. Unlike other Native nations in the area, her people had no firearms, so they were at the mercy of their enemies. Fearful of the Blackfoot and Hidatsa nations, they had fled to the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. In the fall of 1800, when Sacagawea was about twelve, she was captured by a group of Hidatsa in present-day Montana and taken to live with them. Sacagawea never expected to see her own people again. Within a couple of years, the Hidatsa sold her to Toussaint Charbonneau (too-SAN shar- buh-NO), a French-Canadian trapper who made her his wife. They lived among the Mandan and Hidatsa in present-day North Dakota.
pages.brief: A young Sacagawea, about twelve, stands with her Lemhi Shoshone people in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains; Hidatsa warriors on horseback approach to capture her, and later she lives among the Mandan and Hidatsa with trapper Toussaint Charbonneau.

pages.text: Joining the Corps of Discovery After traveling up the Missouri River for six months, Lewis and Clark reached the area where Sacagawea lived. In November 1804, the Corps of Discovery built a fort near the Mandan village. Over the winter, they learned everything they could about the lands to the west from the Mandan and Hidatsa. Lewis and Clark needed horses to cross the Rocky Mountains. They also needed interpreters to help them communicate with Native nations they would meet on their trip. Lewis and Clark heard about the Shoshones— Sacagawea’s people. They lived at the base of the Rockies and owned many horses. Lewis and Clark hired Charbonneau and asked him to bring Sacagawea to serve as an interpreter. The arrangement was an amazing stroke of luck for both parties. Lewis and Clark were heading into an unknown region. Sacagawea knew both the area and the Shoshone language. For Sacagawea, this was an opportunity to return to her homeland. Sacagawea joined the expedition, becoming its only female member, even though she was pregnant at the time. Before the start of the journey, with Lewis’s help, Sacagawea gave birth to a son named Jean Baptiste.
pages.brief: Inside a log fort near a Mandan village in winter, Lewis and Clark meet with Toussaint Charbonneau and Sacagawea, who is pregnant; nearby, with Lewis’s help, Sacagawea holds her newborn son, Jean Baptiste, wrapped warmly.

pages.text: During the trip, Clark developed a special fondness for the boy and called him “Little Pomp” or “Pompey.” Sacagawea’s son became the youngest member of the Corps of Discovery. For most of the journey, Sacagawea carried her infant son in a cradleboard on her back. She endured the same hardships as the men of the Corps while keeping her son alive and healthy. The expedition left the Mandan village on April 7, 1805, after the spring thaw. Thirty-three people, including Sacagawea and her baby, traveled in two large rowboats with sails and six canoes. They set out to explore territory that none of them, including Sacagawea, had ever seen before. On May 14, Charbonneau was steering one of the large rowboats when a high wind caused the boat to tip. The expedition’s most valuable items, including journals, navigational instruments, and medicines, started to float away. Pompeys Pillar National Monument On the return trip, Clark climbed a rock formation in what is present-day Montana. Alongside people’s animal carvings, he carved his name and the date in the sandstone. Today, the formation is known as Pompeys Pillar. Clark’s carving is the only physical evidence of the journey that remains. Pompeys Pillar National Monument On the return trip, Clark climbed a rock formation in what is present-day Montana. Alongside people’s animal carvings, he carved his name and the date in the sandstone. Today, the formation is known as Pompeys Pillar. Clark’s carving is the only physical evidence of the journey that remains.
pages.brief: The expedition’s two large rowboats and six canoes travel upriver; on May 14 a high wind tips Charbonneau’s rowboat, and journals, navigational instruments, and medicines begin floating away while Sacagawea holds baby Jean Baptiste in a cradleboard.

pages.text: Losing those items would have meant disaster for the group. With Jean Baptiste on her back, Sacagawea reached out an arm. She rescued almost all the items before the current carried them away. “The Indian woman, to whom I ascribe equal fortitude and resolution with any person on board at the time of the [accident], caught and preserved most of the light articles which were washed overboard,” wrote Lewis in his journal. Sacagawea was also helpful to the expedition in other ways. She found plants that added important nutrients to their diet of deer and buffalo meat. Lewis was less impressed with Charbonneau, whom he dismissed as “a man of no particular merit.”
pages.brief: With Jean Baptiste on her back, Sacagawea reaches out from the rocking boat and catches floating journals, instruments, and medicine bottles before the current carries them away; the men watch as she saves most of the light articles.

pages.text: West to the Pacific As the expedition approached the Rockies, Sacagawea recognized the area where she’d been kidnapped. The Shoshone couldn’t be far away. Lewis and three others went ahead to meet them, while Clark and the rest of the group caught up a few days later. Lewis was welcomed into the Shoshone village as a guest of the chief. While Sacagawea was interpreting for Lewis and Clark during negotiations with the chief for horses, she suddenly hugged him and cried. She had recognized the chief as her brother. During that meeting, he traded twenty- nine horses for tobacco, knives, beads, and clothing. The expedition left the Shoshone village on September 1, 1805. Sacagawea left her people to travel with the Corps to the Pacific Ocean.
pages.brief: In a Shoshone village near the Rockies, Sacagawea hugs and cries with the chief, her brother, while Lewis and Clark negotiate for horses; twenty-nine horses are traded for tobacco, knives, beads, and clothing before the expedition leaves on September 1, 1805.

pages.text: Crossing the rugged Rocky Mountains was by far the hardest part of the trip. They had no trail and struggled with snow, getting lost, and finding enough to eat. As they crossed the various ranges of the Rockies, they realized that there was no Northwest Passage connecting North America’s waterways from east to west. The expedition was in the mountains for three weeks before they could see to the other side. Planning to again travel by water, they needed canoes as well as food. Sacagawea’s people had told them about another group of Native people—the Nez Perce (NEZ PURS). They lived just west of the Rockies and would be able to help. The Nez Perce fed the group, helped them build canoes, and gave them directions. The Corps reached the mouth of the Columbia River on November 7, 1805. Here, the river rose and fell with the tides and began to taste salty. They knew the Pacific Ocean was close. Although relieved, they were facing terrible weather and needed a place to spend the winter. Lewis and Clark took a vote about where to build a fort. Everyone in the group voted, including Sacagawea and York, an enslaved Black man claimed as property by Clark.
pages.brief: The Corps struggles through snowy, rugged Rocky Mountain passes with no trail; later, near the mouth of the Columbia River, the group gathers around a fire to vote on where to build a fort, with Sacagawea and York among those voting.

pages.text: Sacagawea recommended staying in an area that had wapato roots, which could provide a food supply. Lewis and Clark took her suggestion and built Fort Clatsop there (near present-day Astoria, Oregon). The Rockies would be too snowy and harsh for travel until spring. They spent the winter making maps and notes of the area. Many Helping Hands Though Sacagawea was the most famous Native person to help Lewis and Clark, she was far from the only one. Historians have noted that without nearly constant help from Native people along the way, the Corps of Discovery never would have succeeded. The Mandans gave them enough corn and buffalo meat to make it through the bitterly cold North Dakota winter. The Hidatsas told them about landmarks on the route that would assure the explorers they were on the right track. The Shoshone and Salish traded horses that allowed the Corps to cross the Bitterroot Mountains. The Nez Perce gave them salmon and camas roots as gifts to help them recover from nearly starving after crossing the mountains. The Native people of the Columbia Plateau provided much-needed food on the expedition’s way out and back. The Chinook and the Clatsop people along the Pacific Coast also gave food and information to help them make their way home. pages.brief: Sacagawea points to wapato roots in a marshy area near the Pacific coast, recommending the spot to Lewis and Clark; men build Fort Clatsop from logs while rain falls, and inside the fort they draw maps and write notes through the winter.

pages.text: The Return Trip After winter ended, the expedition left Fort Clatsop and began their return trip up the Columbia River. On the way, they bought horses from the Nez Perce for crossing the Rockies. At one point, Lewis and Clark separated. Sacagawea, Jean Baptiste, and Charbonneau accompanied Clark’s group by land. On their way to the Yellowstone River, back in Shoshone lands, Clark accepted Sacagawea’s suggestion of which route to take. “The Indian woman who has been of great service to me as a pilot through this country recommends a gap in the mountain more south, which I shall cross,” Clark wrote. After reuniting with Lewis’s party, the expedition traveled to the Mandan village. Lewis and Clark parted ways with Sacagawea at the Mandan village on August 17, 1806. Clark offered to take Jean Baptiste back with him to St. Louis and arrange for him to get an education. Sacagawea said he was too young but that he could go in a year. After leaving, Clark wrote a letter to Charbonneau thanking him for Sacagawea’s service. For such a long and dangerous journey, Clark wrote, she deserved a greater reward than they could offer her when they parted.
pages.brief: On the return trip, Sacagawea guides Clark’s group toward a gap in the mountains; at the Mandan village on August 17, 1806, Clark offers to take young Jean Baptiste to St. Louis for school, and Sacagawea says he is too young but may go in a year.

pages.text: After the Expedition Lewis and Clark were heroes back in Washington, D.C. Congress gave each member of the party extra pay as well as land. When Charbonneau heard about the rewards, he took Sacagawea and Jean Baptiste, now four, to St. Louis, where Clark lived, in the fall of 1809. Jean Baptiste stayed in St. Louis with Clark. Charbonneau and Sacagawea left after two years to join another expedition in present-day South Dakota. Sacagawea gave birth to a daughter, Lisette, in August 1812. Four months later, at about age twenty-five, Sacagawea died of a fever. The following summer, the fort’s clerk took Lisette to join Clark and Jean Baptiste in St. Louis. Clark became the legal guardian of both children. The Lost Children William Clark’s adoption of Sacagawea’s children seems to have been motivated by genuine respect for their mother. However, white control of Native children eventually became a tool used to force Native people to abandon their culture. By the late 1800s, government-backed boarding schools across the country were forcibly separating Native children from their parents. The children were forbidden to speak their own language, practice their religion, or wear traditional clothing or hairstyles. The children were also forced to use Anglo American names. When the children returned home as adults, they often struggled to reconnect with their families and communities.
