books.title: Believe It or Not?
books.art_why: Forests, ships, fields, statues, tombstones and researchers all exist in the real world today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Was this young king’s tomb protected by a curse? Can anyone explain the mysterious losses of ships and planes? Introduction If you heard that hairy giants live in our wilderness or that extraterrestrials make strange designs in wheat fields, would you believe it? What if a friend told you an ancient curse causes people to die or that something in a part of the Atlantic Ocean makes ships disappear? How would you know if these stories were true? After reading this book, you’ll have evidence about these four unsolved mysteries. You can decide whether or not you think they’re real. Who or what has made such intricate designs on acres of fields?
pages.brief: A dark wheat field marked with a huge, intricate pattern of flattened circles; behind it a shadowy forest, a stone tomb entrance and a stormy Atlantic horizon with a small ship and a light plane. The scene gathers the four puzzles the reader is about to weigh.

pages.text: In remote areas of the Pacific Northwest, Native Americans have told stories about gigantic, mysterious, apelike creatures for hundreds of years. The Salish peoples of Canada called them Sasquatch, which means “wild man of the woods.” English speakers most often use the name Bigfoot. Others who have reported encounters with this creature include railway and forest workers, hikers, travelers, and people who live in remote areas. Most of them have never heard the Native American stories. KEY represents one Bigfoot sighting UNITED STATES Bigfoot.
pages.brief: Dense remote forest in the Pacific Northwest, tall conifers, mist and moss. A huge hairy apelike figure stands half-hidden among the trunks, seen from a distance by a hiker with a backpack and by a railway worker in a hard hat on the trail below.

pages.text: A Bigfoot is reported to be as tall as 8 feet (2.4 m) and covered with hair. Based on the depth of its tremendous footprints, its weight is estimated to be between 350 and 800 pounds (160–360 kg). People who see one frequently report hearing high-pitched screams and smelling a foul odor. Cryptozoologists (scientists who study animals that may or may not exist) and a few other people have spent a lot of time and money to find out whether Bigfoot really exists. After following up on thousands of eyewitness reports, they have not yet found proof. Grizzly Bigfoot Human Bigfoot is believed to be smaller than a grizzly bear but taller than the average human.
pages.brief: Side-by-side scale scene in a forest clearing: a towering hairy Bigfoot figure, an average adult human and a grizzly bear, the creature taller than the person but shorter than the bear. A deep enormous footprint is pressed into soft mud in the foreground.

pages.text: In 1924, a lumberjack went into the mountains alone to prospect for gold. During the third night of his trip, he was carried off in his sleeping bag by something huge and smelly. Later, it dropped him in a clearing, where four other apelike creatures surrounded him. They seemed to be a family. He escaped, badly shaken but unharmed, after nearly a week. This is just one report of a Bigfoot encounter. Roger Patterson took this picture in 1967. Is it a Bigfoot, a bear, or a human in a gorilla suit? In the vast forests and glaciers of the northwestern United States, nature quickly gets rid of dead bodies. However, scientists believe that if Bigfoot does exist, someone should be able to find a dead body, a skeleton, or fossil remains, yet nothing has ever been found. In 1977, a Bigfoot sighting in northern Washington turned out to be a hoax that was planned by three young men. This makes some people think that other reports must have been faked as well. Do you think the Bigfoot sightings are real or a hoax?
pages.brief: Night in the mountains: a huge, smelly apelike creature carries a lumberjack in his sleeping bag, then drops him in a clearing where four other apelike creatures surround him like a family. A lone hairy figure strides between distant trees in daylight.

pages.text: Crop Circles Strange circles of flattened plants in fields were reported as early as 1590. Farmers thought they were made by wind. In the 1980s, the number of circles increased, and they changed to more intricate designs. Many crop circles are very large. This one consisted of 149 circles and appeared near Stonehenge within 20 minutes in broad daylight. Most crop circles form mysteriously at night, but a few people report having seen them being formed by spaceships or whirlwinds. Sometimes lights are seen in the sky, and humming or music is heard. Sometimes radiation can be detected inside the circles. The crops inside circles are not crushed. They are bent at the lowest node on the stalk. Often these bent crops grow better than the plants outside the circles. Experiments suggest that microwave beams might cause the circles, but it’s not clear where they would come from. Some people think they are messages from outer space. In areas where many circles are found, some people watch the fields at night for signs of activity. They say that complicated circle patterns can appear in just a few minutes.
pages.brief: Aerial view of a vast wheat field beside Stonehenge's standing stones, holding a huge intricate pattern of 149 flattened circles. In the foreground, watchers sit silently at the field edge at night, looking up at a glowing light and a whirlwind above the crop.

pages.text: Many crop circles are made by humans for a variety of reasons. Some people just want to prove that it can be done, while others want to play tricks. In 1991, Englishmen Doug Bower and David Chorley claimed they had made every crop circle since 1978. Some people accepted the explanation of their hoax, while others doubted they had the skill and strength to create huge patterns at night without being seen. Doug retracted his confession seven years later. Some people suggest that the circles are created by tornadoes. Crop circle designs are controlled and intricate, though, while tornadoes destroy a wide area. Another weather theory is based on a type of whirlwind called a plasma vortex. A plasma vortex can create the lights and sounds reported by eyewitnesses. It can hover in one place or move as if it’s under remote control, which could make it look like a UFO. Some researchers have suggested that the military is developing a high-energy weapon powered by microwaves. In this scenario, crop circles are produced by tests of this top-secret weapon. Do you think crop circles are real or a hoax?
pages.brief: Two men working in a dark field at night, pressing planks and ropes into flattened crop to make a large circle, while others look on. Beside them a glowing plasma vortex hovers above a field, and a tornado twists in the distance over damaged crops.

pages.text: The Curse of the Mummy In 1922, with the help of Egyptian workers, Howard Carter discovered the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun, known today as King Tut. The tomb was filled with incredibly valuable treasures. Newspapers circulated stories of a curse painted on a tomb wall that said, “They who enter this sacred tomb shall swift be visited by wings of death.” Carter’s search for the tomb was funded by Lord Carnarvon. When Lord Carnarvon died in 1923, newspapers said that he was killed by a pharaoh’s curse. The newspapers reported that twenty-six people involved with finding the tomb died in the first ten years. Many of these deaths were thought to involve suspicious circumstances. This mystery has been used as the theme for many movies, books, and games. Howard Carter with Lord Carnarvon (left, inset photo), who funded the search for King Tut’s tomb in an area of Egypt called the Valley of the Kings (left)
pages.brief: Inside a torchlit Egyptian tomb in the Valley of the Kings, Howard Carter and Egyptian workers gaze at golden treasures, a sarcophagus and carved walls. Lord Carnarvon stands beside him, and outside the sunlit desert valley of tombs stretches away.

pages.text: In the early 1900s, reporters sometimes invented facts to make stories more exciting. Lord Carnarvon had actually been sick for twenty years before he died. The timing of his death might have been a coincidence. Research shows that only six people involved with finding the tomb died in the first ten years. Howard Carter worked on the tomb for at least ten years, and he lived for seventeen years after the discovery. The curse that was reportedly written in the tomb was not there at all. King Tut’s tomb was filled with valuable treasures. Dead bodies might produce bacteria that could cause illness and death. Could this have contributed to Lord Carnarvon’s death? Early people who robbed tombs might have become sick in this way. This might have been how stories of a curse started. Early Egyptians believed that kings should be buried with riches to use in their next life. These Egyptians may have started legends of danger to keep people away from the tombs. Do you think the curse of the mummy is real or a hoax?
pages.brief: Researchers at a table compare old newspaper clippings, notes and a calendar, while an older Howard Carter studies treasures inside a torchlit tomb. In a dim ancient corridor, robbers carrying gold clutch their heads and cough as dust rises from a burial chamber.

pages.text: CANADA UNITED STATES BERMUDA MEXICO PUERTO RICO Some people include a larger area when describing strange events in the Atlantic Ocean. Bermuda Triangle Strange things have been happening to ships and planes in the Atlantic Ocean between Florida, Bermuda, and Puerto Rico. In 1965, Vincent Gaddis wrote a book about these strange occurrences called Invisible Horizons. He was the first to call the area the Bermuda Triangle. He also called it the Triangle of Death. Numerous planes and ships disappear in this area. Crews vanish from ships, dense fogs suddenly appear, and compasses and navigation equipment stop working. On a clear day in 1945, while a group of planes was on a routine training mission, all of them lost their bearings and disappeared. The rescue airship that went to look for them also disappeared.
pages.brief: Wide view of the Atlantic between Florida, Bermuda and Puerto Rico: a group of 1945 training planes banking into cloud, a rescue airship following, thick fog rolling over dark water, and a ship's compass spinning uselessly on a deck.

pages.text: The USS Cyclops disappeared in 1918 with 306 people on board and is one of the earliest incidents linked to the Bermuda Triangle. In 1881, the merchant ship Ellen Austin discovered a ghost ship floating without a crew. A crew boarded to steer the ship to port, but a thick fog surrounded both ships. When the ghost ship was found the next day, the second crew had disappeared as well. The USS Cyclops disappeared in 1918. This is one of the earliest incidents linked to the Bermuda Triangle. In 1966, Captain Donald Henry’s tug, the Good News, was towing a cargo barge from Puerto Rico to Florida. When a dense fog suddenly swirled around the barge, the Good News lost the use of all of its instruments and partially lost power. For five minutes, the ship struggled in a tug-of-war with the fog bank; it finally managed to pull itself and the barge free.
pages.brief: Three ships on a grey sea: the big collier USS Cyclops steaming into a squall in 1918, the crewless Ellen Austin ghost ship drifting with sails loose, and Captain Donald Henry's tug Good News towing a barge as dense fog swirls around them.

pages.text: People claim that a mysterious power causes the many losses of ships and crews in the Bermuda Triangle. Some people think that UFOs capture humans and take them away. Others say the unexplained losses are a result of the severe weather common in the area. Any vessel that is destroyed would sink without a trace. After being rescued, some of the missing crews tell stories of being forced to leave their storm-damaged ships. Some insist that nothing unusual is going on in the area. They suggest that some of the losses blamed on the Bermuda Triangle actually happened several hundred miles away. Sometimes vessels that have been reported lost appeared later. Do you think the Bermuda Triangle is real or a hoax? In the vast ocean, violent weather could destroy a ship and not leave any evidence.
pages.brief: Storm over open ocean: violent waves and driving rain breaking a ship apart so no wreckage survives, a storm-damaged crew being helped after rescue, and high above the water a glowing disc of light hovering silently over the swell.

pages.text: Rapa Nui (also known as Easter Island) How were the moai statues carved and moved? Stonehenge Why and how were these structures built? Conclusion Mysteries will always exist. Some people will think they are nonsense, and others will claim they are real. Now that you’ve read evidence about four of them, it’s time to consider what you’ve read and determine what you believe. You can use the Internet and the library to find more information. (Just remember that some sources are more reliable than others!) What do you think about these mysteries, and what others can you find?
pages.brief: The giant stone moai statues of Rapa Nui standing on a grassy hillside above the sea, and the ring of standing stones at Stonehenge under a wide sky. In the foreground a young reader sits with a laptop and library books, thinking.

books.title: Eight Billion and Counting
books.art_why: No photographs exist of Rapa Nui’s past or ancient civilizations, so drawings fit.

pages.text: A Giant Mystery When a group of people settled Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in the Pacific Ocean, they cleared trees for homes and fields. With plenty of fish, wildlife, and crops, the population grew. They carved moai (MO-eye)—huge human figures of stone—and raised them along the coast. Then, around the year 1680, the carving stopped and the population dropped. What happened? One theory is that the Rapa Nui used up many of their resources as their population grew too large. Resources are natural things in our environment that help us live: food, clean water, energy. At one time, the island was able to provide a small population with food, water, and wood for building. During this time, the people may have used the trunks of trees like wheels to move the huge stones. Eventually though, the population grew too large for everyone to get what they needed. The forests were all gone. Many of the people died because they’d used up their resources. Many people today think the eight billion humans on Earth are using up the planet’s resources in much the same way. Will we meet the same end as the people of Rapa Nui?
pages.brief: Rapa Nui settlers clear trees for homes and fields while fish, wildlife and crops support a growing population. People carve and raise huge stone moai along the coast. Later the forests are gone, carving stops and the population drops, leaving an island mystery.

pages.text: These giant statues on Rapa Nui were far too heavy to carry. So how were they moved? How Many Are Too Many? If you look around you, Earth may not seem crowded. There are empty houses, fields, and forests. Even New York City, with an average of 29,729 people per square mile, still has room for parks. Overpopulation is not a problem of space. Rather, it is a problem of not having enough resources. Overpopulation means that people have gone beyond their environment’s carrying capacity —the largest number that can live in a place without using up the resources they need in order to survive. Scientists estimate Earth’s carrying capacity at between two and forty billion people. Why such a wide estimate? Because the carrying capacity depends on how many resources each person uses.
pages.brief: Giant stone statues stand on Rapa Nui, far too heavy to carry. Around them appear empty houses, fields and forests, plus New York City with parks among buildings. People consider carrying capacity and how many resources each person uses.

pages.text: A Growing Global Footprint “Global material footprint” is the total amount of raw materials removed to meet human usage. Our footprint is expected to increase faster than population growth, rising from 43 billion metric tons in 1990 to 190 billion by 2060. That’s an increase of 442 percent. 190 billion (estimated) If everyone on Earth lived the way most Americans live, Earth could only support two billion people. That’s because high-income countries like the United States and those in Western Europe use most of the world’s resources. Those living in low-income countries use only a small share. Three-quarters of the world’s people live in middle-income countries where more and more resources are being used. Two of these countries are China (upper-middle) and India (lower- middle), each with more than a billion people. If everyone on Earth used only what we needed to stay alive, our planet could support forty billion people. Other species would be pushed out, however, and life would be hard.
pages.brief: Earth’s material footprint appears as huge piles of raw materials feeding factories and consumers. High-income countries use most resources, low-income countries use a small share, and middle-income countries such as China and India use more and more.

pages.text: A Recent Problem? Experts suspect the kind of collapse that led to the decline of the Rapa Nui has happened to many civilizations. In the Middle East, where farming began about ten thousand years ago, populations soared with more food from irrigating crops. However, irrigation can erode soil or leave enough salt in the soil to kill crops. This land, once known as the Fertile Crescent because it could grow so much food, wore out. Over time, the theory goes, the carrying capacity of the land decreased and the ancient civilizations disappeared. As populations go beyond their carrying capacity, the result can be starvation, the spread of disease, the destruction of the environment, and wars as people fight for scarce resources. If they can, some people leave to find new resources. The Rapa Nui could not leave because their nearest neighbors were thousands of miles across the ocean, and they had no wood left to build canoes. As the European population boomed in the 1800s, people moved to the Americas and Australia. Clearing trees can cause erosion. Too much salt in the soil can kill plants. Here, clearing trees for farming released salt from the soil and ruined it.
pages.brief: Ancient farmers irrigate fields in the Fertile Crescent, where salt and erosion wear out the soil. People leave worn-out land for new resources, while Rapa Nui sits isolated without wood for canoes. Later European migrants move to the Americas and Australia, and cleared trees cause erosion.

pages.text: The Growth Spurt In 1800, one billion people lived on Earth. It took humans 120,000 years to reach that number. By 1927, just 127 years later, we had doubled that number. Thirty-three years later, in 1960, we’d tripled it: three billion people. The year 2022 saw the eight billionth person on the planet—and the population is still growing at more than 200,000 people each day. The population explosion began with the new technology of the Industrial Revolution (1760–1850). New farming practices, manufacturing, and railroads changed the way people lived. More food and better distribution meant that more children survived and people were healthier. More people moved from farms to cities in order to work in factories. At the same time, scientists discovered the causes of many diseases and ways to save thousands of lives. More children survived to adulthood, which meant that more adults were around to have more children. The human population boomed. A baby breathes penicillin vapor. This medicine has saved countless lives.
pages.brief: A baby breathes penicillin vapor while factories, railroads and growing cities show the Industrial Revolution. More food and better distribution help children survive, and crowds grow from one billion to eight billion people. Scientists discover disease causes and save thousands of lives.

pages.text: Technology to the Rescue! The human population might have grown faster than its ability to grow food, but in the 1940s the Green Revolution began. Scientists developed special seeds so farmers could produce more food. They developed chemicals to control insects and plant diseases. Places once unfit for farming could now grow food with chemical fertilizers and irrigation. This new farming technology spread across the globe, allowing even low-income countries to grow more food. It brought a threefold increase in food production. Some people believed that this kind of human invention would allow the population to grow forever. Yet new technology brought new problems. More water was needed for irrigation. Chemicals used for growing crops polluted food and water, and poisoned the environment. Some people realized that we were destroying the planet we depend on for life. Of course, some resources are renewable. They can be replaced. New trees can be planted. The Sun and wind offer huge supplies of energy. Water is constantly renewed through the water cycle.
pages.brief: Farmers use special seeds, chemical fertilizers, irrigation and insect controls, bringing a threefold increase in food production. New problems appear: more water is needed, and chemicals pollute food, water and the environment. Nearby, new trees are planted while the Sun, wind and water cycle offer renewable resources.

pages.text: Only 2.5 percent of Earth’s water is fresh, however. Of that small amount, two-thirds is frozen in glaciers. The amount of available fresh water is less than 1 percent of the water on Earth. Fresh water is not everywhere on the planet, either. One quarter of people, mostly in Africa and parts of Asia, do not have a safe source of drinking water. Seventy percent of available fresh water is used for irrigation. In the United States, underground water in the West is pumped onto fields faster than it can be replaced. The mighty Colorado River stops short of the sea because so much water is taken for irrigation and cities. As water becomes scarce, much of the cropland that feeds the world will become desert. Nearly 40 million people depend on the Colorado River. It now trickles to an end before it can reach the sea.
pages.brief: A glacier holds frozen fresh water while dry fields and thirsty crops show scarce water. People in Africa and parts of Asia lack a safe drinking source. Irrigation takes most fresh water, and the Colorado River trickles to an end before reaching the sea, as cropland turns to desert.

pages.text: Some of Earth’s resources, like coal, copper, and other metals, can’t be renewed. These resources take millions of years to form, so they can’t be replaced once they are used up. China consumes the most coal, by far. The United States consumes the most oil, and more than its share—with less than 5 percent of the world’s people, it uses 20 percent of the world’s oil. An ecosystem is another resource that can’t be renewed. Ecosystems do the work that keeps our planet healthy. Swamps clean water and reduce flooding, grasslands form rich soils, and forests balance the atmosphere. Yet heavy use of wood and farmland is destroying many important ecosystems. Nearly two-thirds of Earth’s tropical rainforests, the most diverse ecosystems, are gone. Thousands of plant and animal species become extinct each year. We cannot bring them back. Our planet is warming, too. Burning fossil fuels such as oil and coal releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, trapping more heat at Earth’s surface and changing ecosystems around the world. Already we have seen melting polar ice caps, spreading deserts, and wilder weather. These trends cannot easily be reversed.
pages.brief: Coal mines and oil wells show nonrenewable resources, with China consuming the most coal and the United States using much oil. Swamps, grasslands and forests support life, while destroyed tropical rainforests, extinct species, melting polar ice, spreading deserts and wilder weather reveal damage from burning fossil fuels.

pages.text: The Good News By 2010, the global population growth rate had slowed from a high of 2.2 percent to 1.1 percent per year. In many high-income countries, population growth has actually stopped or reversed. Their birthrate is now below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman. The replacement rate is the average number of children born per woman that over time will create a stable population. More people are becoming aware that Earth has limited resources. Renewable sources of energy, such as wind and solar power, are being developed. Many countries have passed laws for cleaner air and water as well as protection for ecosystems. In some places forests have increased, although the ecosystems of old forests are often lost, even when new trees are planted. World Population Projections, 1990–2150 Three estimates show future world population. Though all start at 5 billion, note how much the numbers separate later on. Over sixty years, fewer births make a big difference.
pages.brief: Wind turbines and solar panels stand near cleaner water and protected land, while families in high-income countries have fewer children. New trees grow where forests increased, though old forest ecosystems are lost. Three future population estimates separate over time as births decline.

pages.text: An Uncertain Future Despite the good news, the world’s population continues to grow, mostly in low- income countries. The United Nations predicts a population of nearly ten billion by 2050. By most estimates, this is almost twice the number of people who can live on Earth in a sustainable way. But no matter which estimate you believe, everyone now agrees that the human population cannot keep growing forever without destroying the planet. Lowering birthrates is critical. If high-income countries can share Earth’s resources more fairly, it can actually help lower the global birthrate. How might they do this? First, educate women. When women are educated and given control over deciding the size of their family, they tend to have fewer children. Second, make sure that children get better health care, clean water, and good food. Families generally have fewer children if they believe the children they have will survive. Third, governments can provide help for elderly and sick people so that parents will know someone will take care of them when they are old.
pages.brief: Women receive education while families receive health care, and children get clean water and good food. Government workers help elderly and sick people. Crowded low-income communities show continuing growth, while people discuss sharing resources fairly and lowering birthrates for an uncertain future.

pages.text: Enough for Everyone Consider the United States. Because it has gone past its carrying capacity, Americans must bring in resources from other countries to keep up their standard of living. With eight billion people on Earth, we’d need many more planets for everyone to live like most people in the United States. Everyone in the world can have enough to eat, however, if people in high-income countries eat smarter and waste less. For example, grain is the world’s most important source of food. Yet as meat production has boomed for high- and middle-income countries, a third of the grain grown worldwide is used to feed livestock. It takes a lot of grain to create 1 pound (0.45 kg) of meat. Eating less meat means more grain for people in low- income countries and protection of valuable grasslands. While China surpassed the United States for total energy use in 2009, average Americans use more food and far more water than they need to survive. They are the world’s biggest consumers. They could instead be the world’s most efficient consumers if they make intelligent choices about how to live.
pages.brief: American shoppers surround abundant food and water, with grain fed to livestock and some food wasted. Imports bring resources into the United States. Less meat eating could leave more grain for people in low-income countries and protect grasslands, while Americans remain the world’s biggest consumers.

pages.text: How Many Planets Do We Need? If everyone lived like a resident of one of these countries, this is how many planets we’d need. An Island in Space The Rapa Nui left records on carved tablets, but no one can translate the ancient language today. Even so, we can still learn from them. Hopefully, the tale of their little island can teach us to protect our limited resources on Earth, our own little island in space.
pages.brief: Earth appears as a small island in space, surrounded by darkness. Carved Rapa Nui tablets lie nearby, their ancient language untranslated. People look toward the fragile planet and its limited resources, learning from the island’s tale to protect their own little island.

books.title: Groundwater
books.art_why: Groundwater is explained through underground cutaways and aquifer cross-sections, so drawn explanatory art fits the book.

pages.text: When the Water Runs Out Picture getting up one morning, turning on the faucet, and getting nothing but a gurgle. This happened in 2014 in a part of California famous for its fruits and vegetables. Years of drought there meant little rainfall, so to irrigate their crops, farmers pumped huge amounts of groundwater from under the land. The result? Some two thousand dry wells. Even with rain, experts warn that the shortage of groundwater there will not end soon. Unfortunately, California isn’t the only place with a water crisis. Water in the Ground = Groundwater Groundwater fills the spaces and cracks between rocks, sand, and soil underground.
pages.brief: In a California farmhouse kitchen, a person turns on a faucet and gets only a gurgle, with no water. Outside, dry fruit and vegetable fields show years of drought; farmers pump water from underground, and empty wells sit in the dry land. Below the surface, water fills cracks and spaces between rocks, sand and soil.

pages.text: Water We Can Use All water on Earth Freshwater Surface water 0.3% .7% Saltwater 97% Ground ice and permafrost 70% Freshwater 3% What and Where Is Groundwater? Many of us glance at a globe and are fooled into thinking the planet holds plenty of water for all our needs. Most of Earth’s water is in our oceans, however. Its salt content makes it undrinkable and useless for watering crops. Freshwater keeps us alive, yet less than 3 percent of Earth’s water is fresh. Of that small percentage, polar ice caps and glaciers lock up almost 70 percent. The surface water in our rivers, lakes, and ponds makes up just 0.3 percent of our freshwater supply. Scientists estimate that a whopping 99 percent of Earth’s usable water is groundwater. Groundwater is freshwater that flows slowly underground. Most of it is stored beneath land in aquifers —underground layers of rock, gravel, and sand that retain groundwater like huge sponges. Rain and melting snow percolate very slowly into the surface soil and rock to feed the aquifers.
pages.brief: A globe shows oceans, polar ice caps, rivers, lakes and ponds. Below the land, a cutaway shows layers of rock, gravel and sand holding freshwater like a huge sponge; rain and melting snow soak slowly down through soil and rock into the aquifer.

pages.text: Aquifers can reach down thousands of feet and extend for thousands of miles. They feed our rivers, lakes, and wetlands. Their freshwater also irrigates the best farming regions in the world. For more than a century, people have been pumping billions of gallons of water from underground to drink, grow crops, and meet other needs. Even during droughts, communities and farms located above aquifers can draw groundwater to survive and thrive. This water source keeps much of humanity from going hungry and thirsty. The trouble is that groundwater levels are falling fast. Water crises threaten food supplies and peace. People near and far must conserve this life- giving resource. Center-pivot irrigation makes farming possible in many dry regions.
pages.brief: A center-pivot irrigation system sprays water in a wide circle over a dry farm field. Nearby, rivers, lakes and wetlands are fed by underground aquifers; a cutaway shows deep aquifer layers stretching under the land. People pump water from wells for drinking and crops, even during drought.

pages.text: Too Many Straws Research now shows people are pumping groundwater faster than nature can replace it. According to experts, water levels have declined in almost two-thirds of the wells across the United States since 1995. Experts predict that the Ogallala Aquifer, below the Great Plains, could be 70 percent depleted by the year 2060. Ups and (Mostly) Downs: The Ogallala Aquifer The Ogallala (a.k.a. High Plains) Aquifer waters the wheat fields of America—but that water can’t last forever. This map shows state-by- state changes in the water level of the Ogallala Aquifer over a span of about sixty years. In some places, water levels are largely unchanged today; in others, they have crashed. The water level in one Texas well has plunged more than 120 feet (36.6 m).
pages.brief: An overhead view of the Great Plains shows wheat fields above the Ogallala Aquifer; in some areas the underground water sits high, while in others it has dropped away, and one Texas well reaches deep down. Many wells pump water upward from the aquifer.

pages.text: Sonoma Valley in California is famous for its vineyards. Competition for groundwater is causing conflict in some farming areas. In Northern California, for example, winemakers grow acres of grapes, which require large amounts of water. Many of these growers have drilled deep wells to make sure they can get the groundwater they need. Without it, they might go out of business. Many smaller farmers and homeowners nearby, though, blame these vineyards for sucking up too much of the groundwater they all share, while their shallower wells go dry. In many cases, these smaller property owners cannot afford to drill deeper wells for themselves. It’s as if everyone has their straws in the same drink, but some farms and businesses can pay for more and longer straws. This situation raises big questions: Who owns groundwater? How much usage is fair?
pages.brief: In Sonoma Valley, rows of grapevines stretch across sunny vineyards. A winemaker stands by a deep well, while nearby small farmers and homeowners look at their shallow dry wells. Underground, long wells reach deep into shared groundwater like long straws in one drink, while shorter wells sit above the falling water.

pages.text: Water Use Per Capita KEY 373,600 liters 361,300 liters 205,000 liters 83,500 liters 1,341 million 1,225 million A country’s population can impact its overall water use. Regardless of population, though, these countries use different amounts of water per person. Water Fights Halfway around the world, Pakistan’s available water has dropped by almost 75 percent in the last sixty years. Many in Pakistan put the blame on India, their neighbor to the south. They accuse India of building dams that block river water that would normally flow to them. They say this has forced farmers in Pakistan to pump more groundwater. Indian officials say Pakistan has only itself to blame. They say Pakistan has managed its water poorly. These two countries have fought four wars in the past. Today, both face water shortages and increasing competition for freshwater.
pages.brief: A divided landscape shows people in different countries using water at home and on farms. On the other side, a dam blocks a river between India and Pakistan; Pakistani farmers pump groundwater from wells as river water slows. Officials from both countries face each other in dispute.

pages.text: The United Nations predicts such battles over water will only grow worse. If nothing changes, it estimates the world will fall 40 percent short of its water needs by the year 2030. Nearly two billion people worldwide could face severe water shortages, leading to food shortages and famine. In time, shortages like these can even lead to war, experts warn. In some places, lack of water has already forced large numbers of people to leave their homes. In Syria, for example, drought drove rural people into cities. Evidence suggests that this movement, in turn, helped start a civil war in 2011. As a result, many Syrians have died. Two Syrian children stand outside their shelter in a refugee camp. In many places, groundwater is that important—the difference between green farms or dusty fields, a matter of life or death. Without water supplies that people can rely on, violence and great suffering threaten to spread as people fight for water resources.
pages.brief: Two Syrian children stand outside a shelter in a refugee camp, surrounded by dusty ground. In the distance, dry rural fields and a city show families leaving homes after drought. The camp and empty fields suggest the wider threats of water shortage, food scarcity and war that follow.

pages.text: Staying Out of Trouble There is an old saying: “It is easier to stay out of trouble than get out of trouble.” This is true about the world’s supply of groundwater. Dealing with this crisis now will be much easier than dealing with it after aquifers run dry. Addressing the crisis requires us to plan ahead, however. One growing threat to the world’s groundwater supply is climate change. Almost all scientists who study the Earth now agree that it’s getting hotter. Climate change may also mean changes in weather patterns. For example, regions that rely on regular rainy seasons may see those seasons shift. They may see a change in the amount of moisture those seasons deliver. Freshwater may be harder to come by. Ongoing drought in California led to a series of wildfires in 2015. Another huge challenge is population growth. More than seven billion people live on our planet now. That figure is expected to reach eleven billion by the year 2100. All of us will need water to drink and grow our food. We must manage our groundwater now, and we can.
pages.brief: A hot, dry landscape under a bright sun; shifting rain clouds leave some regions drier. In California, wildfires burn across dry hills. Nearby, a growing city and crowded neighborhood show more people needing water, while a farmer looks over thirsty crops.

pages.text: Farming Smarter Our best hope is water conservation —finding ways to use less water and keep more groundwater in the ground. Improving the way we farm is by far the most important action we can take to conserve groundwater. Experts estimate that about 65 percent of the fresh groundwater Americans pump to the surface is used to irrigate crops, yet many forms of irrigation waste water. They spray and sprinkle water on the surface, where much of it is lost to evaporation. More farmers now accept that they cannot keep pumping so much groundwater. They are using new methods to make sure every drop counts. New meters monitor moisture in the soil and turn the irrigation on and off automatically, wasting less water. Many fruit and nut orchards now bury irrigation pipes. Buried pipes deliver water closer to the tree roots and waste less water. Almond trees in bloom.
pages.brief: Farmers stand in an orchard of almond trees in bloom. Buried irrigation pipes deliver water close to the tree roots, and a soil-moisture meter automatically switches sprinklers on and off. In another field, sprinklers spray water into the air, and some moisture rises away as evaporation.

pages.text: The View from Space EUROPE ASIA INDIAN OCEAN AFRICA ATLANTIC OCEAN Aquifers depleting rapidly Aquifers gaining water Since 2002, NASA has been monitoring changes in groundwater from space. Called the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE), its two satellites respond to Earth’s gravity field. They can measure shifts in water volume on and under the planet’s surface. NASA data gathered over a ten-year period (2003–2013) shows trends for Earth’s largest aquifers. About one-third of these aquifers are dangerously depleted. Planting different crops can also help conserve groundwater. In states such as Kansas and Iowa, some farms are switching from corn to other crops because corn requires a lot of water. However, corn crops earn more money, so many farmers don’t want to change. Farmers need new ways to farm. If they do not conserve water voluntarily, empty aquifers will one day force them to.
pages.brief: Two NASA satellites orbit above Earth, measuring the planet's gravity and water below. A view from space shows large aquifers, some shrinking and some gaining water. Below, in Kansas and Iowa, farmers walk between corn and other crops, considering switching to crops that need less water.

pages.text: The Trouble with Toilets 33.1 (125.3 L) 31.7 (120 L) 26.3 (99.6 L) 23.9 (90.5 L) 22.7 (86 L) toilet shower, bath faucet clothes washer dishwasher, leaks, other Did you know that toilets use more water than anything else in your house? They do, according to a 2016 study of water use inside 23,749 homes spread throughout the United States—but not as much as they did in a similar 1999 study. Newer, more efficient toilets help send less water into the sewer. Some families also practice selective flushing. That means they don’t flush the toilet each time they use it. Future Focus Record drought forced California to conserve water. At one point, cities there could fine people five hundred dollars a day if they failed to follow restrictions on washing cars or watering lawns. As a result, water use there dropped. In just six months, people in California went from using as much as 140 gallons (530 L) per person to just 67 gallons (254 L) a day, on average.
pages.brief: Inside a home, a toilet, shower, faucet, clothes washer and dishwasher show where water is used. A person installs a newer, efficient toilet; another chooses not to flush every time. Outside, a California homeowner avoids washing a car and lets a lawn dry under drought restrictions.

pages.text: Nationwide, 57 percent of American households rely on groundwater. In rural areas, that figure is more than 90 percent. Fortunately, small changes in plumbing and water use can save hundreds of gallons in the average American home each week. By installing low-flush toilets and taking shorter showers, we can use less groundwater. In addition, property owners can save water by replacing thirsty grass lawns with yards that need less water. The motto in California for letting lawns die is pretty catchy: “Brown is the New Green.” Saving our groundwater isn’t easy. People need to drink. Farmers need to irrigate crops to grow our food. Still, we can be smarter about how we use this resource, both now and far into the future. In the dry summer of 2014, some Los Angeles homeowners swapped grass for plants that can thrive on less water.
pages.brief: In a dry Los Angeles yard, homeowners replace a grassy lawn with low-water plants. Nearby, a person installs a low-flush toilet and takes a shorter shower. In a rural area, a household uses a well for groundwater, while a neighborhood shows both thirsty grass and plants that thrive with less water.

books.title: Spain
books.art_why: Spain is a modern country whose cities, palaces, festivals and working people can all be photographed today.

pages.text: Map of Spain BAY OF BISCAY FRANCE ATLANTIC OCEAN Balearic Islands (Spain) SPAIN PORTUGAL Canary Islands (Spain) MOROCCO Where Is It? Spain is a country located in southwestern Europe on the Iberian Peninsula. It lies south of the Pyrenees (PEER-uh-neez) mountains and stretches all the way to the Strait of Gibraltar— a body of water that separates Spain from the continent of Africa. France borders Spain to the northeast, and Portugal borders it to the west. The Balearic Islands off Spain’s eastern coast form an archipelago in the Mediterranean Sea. It is a Spanish province known for its beautiful beaches and rich holiday traditions. The Canary Islands off the western coast of Morocco are a Spanish region and also a popular beach destination.
pages.brief: A map view of southwestern Europe: the Iberian Peninsula, with Spain stretching from the Pyrenees mountains down to the Strait of Gibraltar. Portugal sits to the west and France to the northeast. The Balearic Islands lie in the Mediterranean off the east coast, and the Canary Islands sit off the coast of Morocco.

pages.text: The capital and largest city in Spain is Madrid. Its population is roughly 3.3 million, with about 6.5 million people living in its surrounding area. Madrid sits on a raised plateau about 640 meters (2,100 ft.) above sea level. The Royal Palace in Madrid is one of the grandest buildings in all of Europe. King Alfonso XIII—the last monarch to live in the palace—fled the country in 1931. After the king left, the state took control of the Royal Palace, and no member of the monarchy has lived there since. The Spanish royal family now lives in a much smaller palace outside Madrid. Spain’s government—known as a constitutional monarchy—has a prime minister. It also has a lawmaking group called parliament, whose members are elected by the people. Their king, Felipe VI, is the head of the government. However, only the elected officials can make and pass laws. The Royal Palace was built in the 1700s and boasts 2,800 rooms. Today it is used for state ceremonies and public tours.
pages.brief: The Royal Palace in Madrid, a grand stone building with rows of windows and columns, standing on a raised plateau above the city. Visitors walk through its courtyard on a public tour, and Madrid's rooftops and busy streets spread out beyond, with the parliament building where elected officials meet.

pages.text: Farmers grow more than two hundred types of olives in Spain. Spain overtook Italy in 2014 as the world’s largest producer of olive oil. People The population of Spain is estimated to be fewer than forty-eight million people. The urban population far exceeds that of the rural areas. About three-quarters of the population lives in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, and other smaller cities. Tourism employs about two million people and is very important to Spain’s economy. The auto industry remains one of Spain’s largest employers. Other industries include textiles, food, clothing, shipbuilding, and the making of medical equipment. On top of that, Spain proudly produces and exports more olive oil than any other country in the world.
pages.brief: Farmers harvesting olives in a grove of olive trees on dry Spanish hills, filling crates with the fruit. Nearby, workers assemble cars in a factory, handle cloth and clothing in a workshop, and build ships at a yard, showing the work that employs people across Spain.

pages.text: Spain is a member of the European Union (EU). The EU began in 1951 with the countries of Belgium, Germany, France, Luxembourg, and Italy as members. Its purpose was to have countries work together to solve common issues such as trade, security, and the rights of citizens. Most EU members share a currency called the euro. As of 2022, the EU had twenty-seven member nations. Spain’s official language is Spanish, or Castilian, and most people speak it. Depending on the region, people also speak Basque, Galician, and Catalan languages. Textile workers prepare clothing to be sold in stores (right). People enjoy a sidewalk cafe in Palma, Spain (below).
pages.brief: Textile workers at long tables cutting and preparing clothing to be sold in stores. In a sunny square in Palma, people sit at a sidewalk cafe at outdoor tables, chatting in the afternoon sun, in a country where Spanish, Catalan, Basque and Galician are spoken.

pages.text: Spain’s Landforms ATLANTIC OCEAN Land Spain’s varied landscape ranges from high plateaus in its interior to dry, desert-like regions in the south. Beautiful beaches and mountain ranges around the country create distinct environments. The Meseta Central, a plateau in central Spain, covers about half the country. People mine silver, lead, and copper and raise livestock in the mountains that border the Meseta. The dramatic and rocky Sierra Nevada mountain chain rises over southern Spain, with Mount Mulhacén (moo-lah-THEN) towering over the entire range. The Sierra Nevada is part of the Andalusian (an-duh-LOO-zhuhn) region in the southeast. The Pyrenees mountains lie to the north and form a solid natural border between Spain and France.
pages.brief: The varied land of Spain: the wide, flat Meseta Central plateau covering the middle of the country, dry desert-like ground in the south, and beaches along the coast. The rocky Sierra Nevada rises behind with Mount Mulhacén, its highest peak, and shepherds raise livestock in the mountains that border the plateau.

pages.text: The Pyrenees mountain chain stretches from the eastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea to the coastline of the Atlantic Ocean in the west. The chain extends for 434 kilometers (270 mi.). The western part of the mountain range is a lush, rolling, heavily wooded countryside. In the east, vineyards and orchards are plentiful. The central region includes a rich display of granite peaks, deep canyons, waterfalls, and hundreds of mountain lakes. Several groups of people—the Andorran, Catalan, Béarnese (bair-NEEZ), and Basque—call the Pyrenees mountains their home. Traditionally, they make a living through agriculture and raising livestock. A wide variety of animals also live in these mountains. The brown bear, a species of goat- antelope called the chamois (sham-WAH), and the rare bearded vulture all live in the Pyrenees. Forests of fir, pine, and oak cover the slopes of the Pyrenees mountains.
pages.brief: The Pyrenees mountain chain: rolling wooded hills in the west, vineyards and orchards in the east, then granite peaks, deep canyons, waterfalls and hundreds of mountain lakes. Forests of fir, pine and oak cover the slopes, where a brown bear, a chamois goat-antelope and a rare bearded vulture live.

pages.text: Moors built the Alhambra, a palace and fortress, in Granada, Spain, on a high point overlooking the entire valley. History People from Phoenicia (fi-NEE-shuh) settled southern Spain around 800 bce. Phoenicia is Lebanon, Syria, and Israel today. Phoenicians were skilled artisans and sailors who traded ivory and perfumes for bronze and silver goods. Greek traders from Carthage (now Tunisia) followed around 500 bce and brought with them olive trees and grapes. Then, around 200 bce, the Romans arrived and ruled Spain for about six hundred years. They made roads and bridges that connected towns. They also built aqueducts that carried water from rivers to cities. Germanic people came from the north after the Romans. Then, Muslim settlers known as Moors arrived in 711 ce and ruled until the Catholic era. Moorish buildings can still be seen in Spain today, including monuments such as the Alhambra, a palace in Granada built in the 1300s, and the Great Mosque of Córdoba.
pages.brief: The Alhambra, a Moorish palace and fortress with red stone walls and towers, standing on a high point above Granada and looking out over the whole valley. Further off, a Roman road and an aqueduct carry water toward a town, reminders of the peoples who settled Spain.

pages.text: For many centuries, Spain had been divided into kingdoms. The main ones were Aragon, Castile, and Granada. Two of these kingdoms became one when King Ferdinand II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile married. They were Catholic monarchs who won a war against the Moors for control of Granada. The king and queen set up the Spanish Inquisition, a group that killed people who were not Catholic. The Inquisition also pushed Jewish and Muslim people out of Spain. Ferdinand and Isabella paid explorers such as Christopher Columbus to find new trade routes for Spain to Asia. When Columbus arrived in the New World (islands in the Caribbean Sea), Spain set up colonies there. They brought gold, silver, spices, and enslaved people back to Europe. At the time, much of Spain’s wealth was built on the slave trade with Africa and the Americas. During the 1800s and early 1900s, inequality between the rich and the poor led people to try overthrowing the elected government. When that failed, the Spanish Civil War broke out in 1936 and lasted until 1939. When the war ended, General Francisco Franco took control of the country and ruled as a dictator until his death in 1975. After Franco’s death, King Juan Carlos I became the next king. He then made Adolfo Suárez—who brought democracy to Spain—prime minister.
pages.brief: King Ferdinand II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, the Catholic monarchs, standing together in a stone hall of their kingdom. Beyond the castle, an explorer's sailing ship reaches islands in the Caribbean Sea, carrying the wealth and enslaved people later brought back to Europe.

pages.text: Celebrations Spanish people look forward to local holidays called fiestas, or festivals. These holidays often celebrate local harvests, historical events, or saints. Lively and fun, they include dancing, singing, parades, and fireworks. St. George’s Day, on April 23, is a time for people to give loved ones books and red roses. In July, Pamplona hosts the Festival of San Fermín. During this festival, people try to dodge bulls as they run through the streets of Pamplona. National Day takes place on October 12. This is the date that Spain first arrived in the Americas. For Spanish people, it is also the date that honors Spain as an important country in the world. La Tomatina La Tomatina is a yearly festival held in honor of a patron saint. It is likely the world’s biggest tomato fight. At this festival, ripened tomatoes are brought in by the truckload, and people throw tomatoes at one another—just for fun.
pages.brief: A street in Pamplona during the Festival of San Fermín: people running ahead of charging bulls while crowds watch behind wooden barriers. Beside them, a stall of books and red roses for St. George's Day, and a crowd hurling ripe tomatoes at one another in a giant La Tomatina fight.

pages.text: Spanish people usually eat three meals a day. A Spanish breakfast might be coffee, milk, or hot chocolate, a sweet roll, and sometimes cereal. They eat lunch—the biggest meal of the day—around two in the afternoon. Lunch may include soup, salad, a main course, and dessert. Dinner is a lighter meal. It is served late, anywhere from nine to eleven in the evening. Each region in Spain enjoys its own style of food. Regions near the ocean typically serve seafood. People in central Spain often eat beans, lentils, lamb, and pork. Valencia, known for its rice dishes, is famous for paella—a rice dish that can be made with fish, meat, and vegetables. A delicious and popular soup called gazpacho comes from the Andalusian region of Spain. Made with tomatoes and other vegetables, the soup is often served cold in the summer as a refreshing meal. Tapas Tapas are finger foods that can be eaten cold or hot and are usually served on small plates. People serve shrimp and squid along the Spanish coasts, while people serve sausages inland. Food.
pages.brief: A Spanish table: a wide pan of paella made with rice, fish, meat and vegetables, small plates of hot and cold tapas with shrimp, squid and sausages, and a bowl of cold tomato gazpacho. A family sits down together to a late dinner in the evening.

pages.text: Antoni Gaudí designed this remarkable church, which stands in Barcelona, Spain. Construction began in 1882 and it still continues. Conclusion Many Spanish people are proud of their culture. Although many identify with the town or region they’re from, their celebrations and festivals bring them together as a nation. Some regions still try to preserve their own traditions, but the country has been unified for many years. Spain is one of the most lively cultural centers in the European Union. It boasts an amazing heritage due in part to the arrival of people from many different parts of the world who have brought celebrations, food, and architecture to Spanish culture. Spain’s history is long and complex, and its culture and past actions have impacted many parts of the world. Spain’s beauty and the warmth of its people help make our world a more interesting place to live in.
pages.brief: The Sagrada Família church in Barcelona, designed by Antoni Gaudí: tall spires and richly carved stone facades rising above the street, with cranes and scaffolding still around it because construction that began in 1882 continues. People on the pavement stop and look up at the building.

pages.brief: A wide view of Spain: the capital city of Madrid with its streets and rooftops, and farmland, hills and coastline stretching beyond, with Spanish people going about their daily lives. Coins of the euro, the country's currency, rest beside a map of the nation.

books.title: Mysterious Shipwrecks
books.art_why: These wrecks and sinkings happened mostly in the 1700s and 1800s, long before any camera could record them, and the book is about ships and events, not one famous person, so cartoon does not fit.

pages.text: Mysterious Shipwrecks.
pages.brief: A broken wooden sailing ship lies half-sunk in a dark, restless sea, its mast snapped and its hull tilted, waves breaking across the deck. Heavy grey storm clouds press down and no land is in sight. The scene is still and eerie, hinting at a mystery nobody has ever solved.

pages.text: Marine Mysteries, Lost and Found The United Nations estimates the world’s coastlines and seafloors are littered with more than three million shipwrecks. Marine archaeologists study some wrecks that date back hundreds, even thousands, of years. Treasure hunters search for other wrecks because of the riches rumored to have sunk with them. In some cases, however, ships have simply disappeared without a trace. No clues are left behind that might suggest their fate. A wreck at the bottom of the Red Sea in Jordan Every shipwreck holds some kind of mystery. What was the ship carrying? Where did its wreck end up? What happened to the people on board? The mystery that seizes people’s curiosity the most, however, is this: what really sent the ship to its doom? Stories of shipwrecks are often full of danger, death, sunken treasure, and schemes. Clues can help us solve mysteries. In most cases, however, the clues of a ship’s fate remain hidden for years— and sometimes forever.
pages.brief: Underwater in the Red Sea off Jordan, the scattered timbers of an old shipwreck rest on a sandy seafloor in blue-green water. Two marine archaeologists in diving gear hover above the broken hull, measuring and sketching it, while sunlight ripples down through the surface toward them.

pages.text: The Richest Wreck In 1708, a British warship sent a Spanish galleon to the bottom of the sea. On it were gold and emeralds meant to fund Spain’s war against Great Britain. The wreck’s location remained a mystery—until recently. It was found in 2015 off the coast of Colombia. Spain and Colombia have long disagreed about who owns the wreck and its treasures. The goods are estimated to be worth as much as $17 billion. That makes it one of the most valuable shipwrecks in the world. Mystery of Antiquity In 1900, divers found a shipwreck near a Greek island. The partially buried wreck lay 55 meters (180 ft.) beneath the sea’s surface. No one knew how it got there. But Greek archaeologists soon realized the more interesting question was when it got there. As divers brought artifacts to the surface, researchers learned the ship was more than two thousand years old. It was loaded with amazing art and luxury goods. One of these items has been described as the earliest known computer. The device used gears to figure out the exact positions of the stars and planets. More than 120 years after its discovery, research teams are still studying the wreck. A piece of the world’s oldest computer.
pages.brief: On the seabed off Colombia, gold coins and green emeralds lie scattered among the broken timbers of a Spanish galleon. Nearby a diver lifts a corroded bronze object set with gear wheels, no bigger than a shoebox, that once showed the positions of the stars and planets.

pages.text: Long Lost Victory HMS Victory was launched in 1737, armed with 110 cannons. It was the finest ship in Great Britain’s impressive navy. In early October 1744, the Victory was leading its fleet back to Britain. They were caught in a fierce storm in the English Channel, and the Victory became separated from the other ships. It disappeared along with some 1,150 people. That night, locals on nearby islands heard the booming of cannons—a maritime cry for help. Unfortunately, the seas were far too dangerous for any attempt at rescue. Days later, wreckage from the vessel washed up on the shores of the islands. However, the ship’s hull and decking were nowhere to be found. HMS Victory sails through turbulent seas in a painting by Thomas Butterworth. In 2008, a marine salvage company located the ship’s remains. The salvage company and British government worked together to respectfully retrieve valuables from the wreck. Today, the world’s oldest naval ship still in commission bears the name of HMS Victory.
pages.brief: HMS Victory, a towering warship with rows of cannons along its sides, heels over in a violent storm in the English Channel, sails torn and sailors clinging to the rigging. On a rocky island shore, frightened locals stand listening to the boom of its distress guns.

pages.text: The Fraidy-Cat of Empress of Ireland Emmy was considered the ship’s cat on the Empress of Ireland. The day before the ship sailed from Canada, Emmy fled the vessel two times. Her behavior was viewed as a bad sign. The next day, the Empress of Ireland struck another ship and sank in just fourteen minutes. More than one thousand people died, making it the deadliest wreck in Canadian history. Ghost Ship: Mary Celeste Some lost ships experience a fate even more mysterious than sinking to the bottom of the sea. On November 7, 1872, the cargo ship Mary Celeste set sail from New York, bound for Italy. The 30.1-meter (100 ft.) vessel had a crew of seven, plus the captain and his family. Mary Celeste One month later, a British ship spotted a vessel drifting in the Atlantic Ocean. It was the Mary Celeste, but a boarding party found no one on the ship. The navigational equipment and a lifeboat were missing, but there were no signs of violence. All cargo and gear were left behind. The last entry in the captain’s log held no clues about a possible problem. The captain, his family, and the crew were never seen again. The lack of answers has led to many imagined accounts of the mystery. They usually feature treachery, murder, and even sea monsters.
pages.brief: A grey cat leaps from a ship's gangplank onto a Canadian dockside, fleeing the Empress of Ireland before it sails. Far out in the Atlantic, the Mary Celeste drifts alone with sails half-set, while two sailors from a British ship row across in a small boat to board her.

pages.text: A painting of HMS Erebus stuck in the ice by François Etienne Musin The Long Hunt for HMS Erebus and HMS Terror In 1845, the British navy mounted the Franklin Expedition to search for a shortcut for shipping between Europe and Asia. The expedition included 129 people on two ships—HMS Terror and HMS Erebus. On July 26, 1845, two whaling ships spotted Terror and Erebus in Canada’s Baffin Bay. Then two years passed with no word from the expedition’s commander. Officials and the public feared for the safety of the explorers.
pages.brief: Two British navy ships, HMS Terror and HMS Erebus, sit among white icebergs in Canada's Baffin Bay, masts and rigging dark against a pale sky. In the distance two whaling ships watch them pass in July 1845, before the long silence begins.

pages.text: Search and rescue ships eventually discovered abandoned gear, graves, and notes left behind by desperate crew members on uninhabited islands. The two ships had been trapped in pack ice in September 1846, and the commander of the expedition died the following June. For two years, the sailors—sick and dying—waited for the ice to release their ships. Finally, in April 1848, the survivors attempted a desperate hike southward to reach the Canadian mainland. In 1855, local Inuit told investigators about a group of Europeans who had starved to death along the coast. Evidence showed that the group had resorted to cannibalism to try to survive. In 2014, a ship equipped with sonar found the wreck of the Erebus. It was well preserved in 12 meters (40 ft.) of Arctic waters. Its partner ship, also well preserved, was found in September 2016 about 72 kilometers (45 mi.) away. A diver explores the remains of the Erebus.
pages.brief: A diver in a drysuit swims above the well-preserved wreck of HMS Erebus, its decking and fittings still in place in cold, dim Arctic water, ice overhead. On a nearby uninhabited island lie abandoned gear, a grave and a scribbled note left by desperate crewmen.

pages.text: Terror on the Rocks: SS Valencia The SS Valencia was one of the most terrifying shipwrecks of all. In January 1906, the passenger steamer was on its way to Seattle with 173 people on board. Near midnight on January 22, its iron hull ran aground near Vancouver Island. Pounding waves trapped the ship. The crew lowered lifeboats, but most boats flipped, or capsized, in the churning seas. People were tossed into freezing water, where they drowned. High winds and waves hampered rescue efforts. About thirty-six hours after the stranding, witnesses onshore watched in horror as a huge wave swept over the upper deck, where dozens of passengers were holding on for their lives. In total, only 37 out of 136 passengers survived. A Valencia lifeboat escapes the violent seas. It bears some of the few survivors of the wreck.
pages.brief: The iron steamer SS Valencia lies aground on rocks near Vancouver Island in wild black seas. A huge wave curls over the upper deck, where passengers cling to the railing, while a lifeboat packed with survivors is tossed away from the doomed ship.

pages.text: Valencia leaves San Francisco eight years before the ship’s tragic sinking. How, why, and where were not the mysteries of the Valencia wreck. Investigations concluded that the captain and crew had made bad decisions that endangered the ship and its passengers. Most of the mysteries came later and inspired supernatural tales. In 1910, for example, newspapers reported that sailors had seen a ghostly Valencia sailing near the site of the wreck. A rumor also spread that a lifeboat filled with skeletons had been found in a nearby cave, though the story was never confirmed. Then in 1933—twenty-seven years after the disaster—one of Valencia ’s lifeboats was discovered in a nearby bay. Its nameplate is now displayed in the Maritime Museum of British Columbia.
pages.brief: A pale, ghostly steamer with dim lights glides over dark water near the site of the Valencia wreck, its outline faint and unreal. In a quiet bay nearby, an old wooden lifeboat with a nameplate rests among the rocks at low tide.

pages.text: The disappearance of USS Cyclops, pictured above, remains the largest loss of life in U.S. naval history in an event not directly related to combat. Gone Without a Trace: USS Cyclops USS Cyclops was a huge U.S. Navy supply ship. While serving during World War I, the Cyclops crew picked up a heavy load of ore in Brazil. While there, Captain W. Worley reported to his superiors that one of the engines needed repairs and was not operational. He was told to get it fixed once he reached the United States. On February 22, 1918, the ship left Brazil for Baltimore with 309 crew members. Cyclops disappeared somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. Not a single piece of wreckage has ever been found. At the time, people wondered if a German submarine had sunk the ship. Some naval officials wondered if Captain Worley, who had been born in Germany, might have secretly handed the ship over to the enemy, though there was no proof of that.
pages.brief: USS Cyclops, a long navy supply ship with tall funnels and deep ore holds, lies at a Brazilian port while cranes swing heavy loads of ore aboard. Crew members line the rail. Soon the ship will sail for Baltimore and vanish into the Atlantic with all 309 hands.

pages.text: Some ships have been sunk on purpose in the Bermuda Triangle. They are used to create artificial reefs, which help sea life in the area. Another theory notes that the ship disappeared in the Bermuda Triangle. This area in the Atlantic Ocean has a reputation for swallowing ships. Most naval experts, though, believe that in addition to lacking full engine power, the ship was overloaded and unstable. They think it may have been caught in a violent storm that occurred on March 10, which could have capsized the ship. The Bermuda Triangle The Bermuda Triangle is an area of the Atlantic Ocean. Its corners are near Bermuda, Puerto Rico, and the tip of Florida. According to legend, a high number of unexplained disappearances of ships and aircraft occur there. As a result, there are rumors of supernatural powers sinking or snatching ships. However, researchers have determined that ships are no more likely to disappear there than in other busy shipping areas. Bermuda United United ATLANTIC OCEAN States States Florida Bermuda Triangle Caribbean Caribbean Islands Islands Puerto Rico.
pages.brief: The supply ship USS Cyclops is caught in a violent storm in the Atlantic, listing heavily as huge waves break over its long deck and dark clouds close in. The grey sea between Bermuda, Puerto Rico and the tip of Florida stretches around it, empty and threatening.

pages.text: There and Gone: SS Edmund Fitzgerald On November 9, 1975, SS Edmund Fitzgerald, a huge freighter, left Superior, Wisconsin, fully loaded with iron ore. A storm was forecast, but the captain was not concerned. On the afternoon of November 10, the U.S. Coast Guard warned all ships to seek shelter. The Edmund Fitzgerald headed for Whitefish Bay, Wisconsin. At about 7:00 p.m., the captain reported the ship was taking on water but radioed, “We are holding our own.” Moments later, the ship no longer appeared on radar. No lifeboats were launched. None of the twenty- nine crew members were found. Days later, the Coast Guard located the wreck on the lake floor. The ship had been snapped in half. Investigators suspect a series of three rogue waves may have sunk the ship so quickly that there was no time even to make a distress call. Rogue Waves Researchers suspect “rogue waves” for some unexplained shipping disasters. What makes these waves so dangerous is their unpredictability, size, and power. A rogue wave comes out of nowhere and is much bigger than the waves around it. It is created by a powerful combination of strong water currents and high winds, usually far out at sea. The sudden jump in wave size can flip large freighters.
pages.brief: The huge freighter SS Edmund Fitzgerald pushes through Lake Superior at dusk, fully loaded with iron ore, its long deck awash as a single enormous rogue wave rises far above the water around it. Through the gloom the ship's lights are barely visible.

pages.text: The Slave Wrecks Project Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, as many as one thousand ships carrying enslaved people were lost at sea. Most of those shipwrecks remain undiscovered and undocumented today. Organizations such as the Slave Wrecks Project, founded in 2008, are working to find those lost ships and the historical information they contain. In 2014, the Slave Wrecks Project made its first major recovery. It found a sunken ship near the coast of Cape Town, South Africa. The Sea Keeps Many Secrets Sailing the seas has always involved an element of danger. The oceans stretch vast distances, and the weather can suddenly turn foul. Also, reefs and rocks often hide along coastlines. Modern equipment makes shipping safer than ever. Even so, dozens of shipwrecks still claim the lives of about two thousand people every year. Working on a ship remains one of the world’s most dangerous jobs. Sailors entrust their lives to their knowledge, skills, and the ships they serve on. Still, sometimes, their fate is a matter of luck. Every shipwreck leaves behind mysteries. Some of these mysteries can be explored and eventually explained, and older wrecks may provide us with a glimpse into the past. Much of the time, though, the sea’s secrets are never revealed.
pages.brief: Divers in the sea off Cape Town, South Africa, hover over the sunken timbers of a ship that once carried enslaved people, recording and photographing what remains of her. Far above, a small support boat waits in the swell on the surface.

books.title: 1849: The California Gold Rush
books.art_why: An 1848-1850s event, so period illustration is used rather than cartoon, and it is not about one named famous person.

pages.text: 1849: The California Gold Rush.
pages.brief: An opening view of the California gold country: a wide river winding between dry brown hills, willows along the bank, and a small wooden sawmill with a water ditch running from the river, morning light shining on the water.

pages.text: Keeping a Secret On the morning of January 24, 1848, James Marshall went to inspect the ditch that carried water from the American River through the new sawmill his crew was building in California. The crew had deepened the section of the ditch that ran out of the mill to make the water flow more quickly. At the end of the ditch, about six inches under the water, he spotted something shiny. Marshall collected several pieces and showed his crew. They tested the pieces. It was gold! Marshall showed the gold to the owner of the mill, John Sutter, who controlled forty-eight thousand acres of land in California he called “New Switzerland” after his home country. Sutter bought the land from the Mexican government, but it actually belonged to the Indigenous Nisenan people. Sutter had taken more than land. Sutter’s deal with the Mexican government required that he not harm any of the Nisenan people in the area. Nevertheless, he trained many Native people to become part of his own private army and kidnapped and enslaved other Native people to work the land. Sutter tried to get everyone to keep the secret that gold had been discovered. He wanted to keep the riches for himself.
pages.brief: James Marshall kneels beside the mill ditch, reaching into six inches of shallow water where shiny gold pieces glint; behind him his crew of workmen lean in to look at the pieces they are testing, and the wooden frame of the new sawmill stands beside the American River.

pages.text: Territory Lost to the U.S. in the Mexican-American War Land that today makes up the states of California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming were included in the treaty. These lands were home to many Native peoples, but Mexico had claimed ownership, then gave them to the U.S. after the war. United States Sutter’s Mill San Francisco PACIFIC OCEAN Mexico Six days after Marshall found the gold, Mexico signed the treaty that ended the Mexican-American War. The treaty gave California to the United States. Neither side knew that gold had just been discovered there. Sam Brannan, who ran a store near Sutter’s Mill, soon let out the secret. Brannan wanted to cash in when he heard the news, but he wasn’t interested in mining. Instead, he bought all the shovels in the nearby city of San Francisco. Then he filled a bottle with gold dust and ran through the streets yelling about the great discovery. The city of 850 people almost emptied after Brannan sold them each the tools they needed to find gold—picks, axes, pans, and shovels—at very expensive prices.
pages.brief: Sam Brannan runs through the streets of small San Francisco holding up a bottle of gold dust and shouting, while people pour out of doorways; his store stands with shelves of picks, axes, pans and shovels waiting to be sold at high prices.

pages.text: Panning Unlike gold in most places, California’s gold wasn’t locked deep under the ground. Erosion had long ago washed the metal down the mountains and into rivers. Miners used a technique called placer mining that allowed them to sift gold out of the riverbed using a shallow, flat pan. Placer mining works because gold is much heavier than gravel. Prospectors stood in rivers and shoveled gravel into their pan. They removed large rocks, then carefully swirled the pan. The dirt and gravel spilled over the edges with the water. The shiny flakes of gold stayed at the bottom of the pan. Each day, most miners only found gold that would be worth between $10 and $15 today. Word Wise The term prospector means a person who moves to a spot with the prospect, or possibility, of finding gold and becoming rich.
pages.brief: Two prospectors stand knee-deep in a clear river, one shoveling gravel into a shallow flat pan, the other swirling it so dirt and water spill over the rim while shiny flakes of gold settle at the bottom; rocks and gravel lie on the riverbed around them.

pages.text: The Forty-Niners Rumors soon swirled in the eastern states about gold out West. A California official sent a report about the gold to Washington, D.C.—along with a sample. In December 1848, the president told Congress about the discovery. It was true! A gold miner shovels gravel in California in 1852. Gold fever—the greed and contagious excitement brought on by the discovery of gold— took hold of many people. At the time, many workers earned less than a dollar a day. For them, it was the opportunity of a lifetime. In 1849, around ninety thousand people—called forty-niners — joined the Gold Rush. Around 10 percent, or nine thousand, were women. The forty-niners came from across the United States as well as from Mexico, Central and South America, Asia, Australia, and New Zealand. Black people were among the forty-niners as well. Around 200 to 300 were enslaved and had been forced by their enslavers to go to California. Free Black people also traveled west in hopes of finding gold. By 1852, around 2,000 Black people lived in California, which was about 1 percent of the population.
pages.brief: A gold miner in California in 1852 shovels gravel beside a river in a wide hat, rough shirt and boots; other miners work the banks behind him and a rough camp of tents sits in the background as crowds of forty-niners arrive.

pages.text: The trip to the gold mines could take months—and was not cheap. People had to pay for transportation and supplies to last until they arrived in California. Many forty-niners left behind jobs and families. They planned to make a fortune quickly and return home. Others were ready for whatever adventure they found. People from California, Oregon, and Mexico were the first to show up at the rivers near Sutter’s Mill. Locals only had to travel short distances with their pack animals. It took longer for immigrants to arrive by boat from faraway countries and for people to cross the United States. At that time, it was easier to get to California from China than from the East Coast. The Routes the Forty-Niners Took NORTH AMERICA ATLANTIC OCEAN Panama PACIFIC OCEAN SOUTH AMERICA Cape Horn.
