pages.brief: Prospectors from California, Oregon and Mexico reach the rivers near Sutter's Mill with loaded pack animals and mules; further off, travelers step off a boat after a long sea voyage, and a group crosses a jungle track carrying supplies on their backs.

pages.text: By Ship About half of the forty-niners decided to travel by ship to avoid crossing the lands of Native peoples. It took ships between five and eight months to sail from the East Coast, around the tip of South America, and back up to California. The cheapest ticket was $75—about $2,300 in today’s money. Lodging was a tiny bunk in the bottom of the ship. Passengers ate dried meat and hard biscuits filled with weevils, and drank water. They suffered as a result of shipwrecks, seasickness, and disease. Many reported that the worst things were crowding and boredom. Posters like this one advertised ships that would carry forty-niners from New York City to San Francisco. Some passengers decided to save time by taking a shortcut through Panama. They could canoe and hike across 60 miles (97 km) of jungle, then catch another ship. These forty-niners faced an extreme environment with hazards they were unfamiliar with, including bad weather and wild animals. Many fell ill. If they made it across, there was still a risk that they would have to wait weeks or months to catch a ship on the other side.
pages.brief: Below deck on a crowded sailing ship, passengers lie in tiny wooden bunks packed close together, eating dried meat and hard biscuits and drinking water; a few sit on deck looking seasick while the ship rolls, and travelers with packs push through thick Panama jungle.

pages.text: A drawing from around 1900 shows people traveling together in a group of wagons called a train. By Wagon It took about the same amount of time to get to California by wagon. Much of the land between forty-niners on the East Coast and California still belonged to Native peoples. Settlers moving out West often hunted without permission, stole from Native peoples, and attacked them. Native peoples thus viewed them with hostility. Most people left from Saint Louis, Missouri, the westernmost U.S. city at the time. Wagons followed the California Trail for 2,100 miles (3,380 km) across the flat prairie. A wagon could travel about 15 miles (24 km) in a day—if it didn’t break down, there wasn’t much rain, and the oxen stayed healthy. The forty-niners had to get the wagons across rivers, up mountains, down cliffs, and across deserts.
pages.brief: A long train of covered wagons drawn by oxen rolls across flat open prairie, families walking beside them; the line of wagons stretches toward distant mountains, with a river crossing ahead and dust rising from the wheels.

pages.text: They were pounded by rain, wind, and snow. In addition to bad weather, other dangers facing forty-niners came from disease, starvation, and accidents. For those who made it to California, life did not get easier. Prospectors lived in mining camps made of tents and rough shelters, and worked twelve hours a day. Many fell ill, often due to poor conditions and diet. Despite these challenges, it was difficult to give up—the next pan of gravel might be worth a fortune!
pages.brief: A mining camp of canvas tents and rough brush shelters beside a muddy river; prospectors in soaked clothes work long hours at the water through rain and wind, while others huddle inside a tent, some looking thin and ill, with snow on the hills behind.

pages.text: Equal Opportunity? For Native peoples, the Gold Rush was disastrous. It opened the gateway to the West. Throngs of adventurers and settlers poured into Native lands. Many different groups of Native peoples lived in California. As forty-niners moved out West, violent attacks forced Native peoples off much of their land. Thousands were killed, and thousands more died of disease. Once California became a state in 1850, the U.S. government took control of the land, including areas with gold. Soon, fear and hatred led to the killing of thousands of Native peoples. New laws allowed settlers to arrest Native people for minor wrongdoings. The government then forced them to pay their fines by working on ranches. Around three hundred thousand Native peoples lived in California before the Gold Rush. More than one hundred thousand were dead only twenty years later. Good Prospects, Bad Endings Several of the men involved in the original discovery of gold ended up with nothing to show for it. John Sutter lost his golden property when the United States would not recognize his land grant from Mexico. Sutter, along with Sam Brannan and James Marshall, eventually lost their fortunes.
pages.brief: Groups of Native people in California move away from their homelands as crowds of armed settlers and prospectors pour into their lands, carrying their belongings with them; in a separate scene John Sutter, Sam Brannan and James Marshall stand with nothing left.

pages.text: As the hills filled with prospectors, white miners began to oppose other groups hunting for gold, especially Chinese miners. White prospectors sometimes violently forced miners from outside the United States to leave the mines. Almost three thousand Chinese people came to California in 1851. A terrible crop season in China made that number rise to more than twenty thousand the next year. California taxed miners from outside the United States to prospect. Some U.S. miners wanted to make it so difficult for them to mine that they would leave. Chinese miners search for gold in California around 1850. One in every five miners who came to California in 1849 died within six months. Even those who found gold often lost it to robbers, gambling, or paying high prices for everyday goods. Some early prospectors were successful. Most of the riches from gold went to large companies. They were able to mine with high-pressure jets of water or dig deep mines.
pages.brief: Chinese miners search for gold in a California river around 1850, working pans and a wooden rocker; nearby a group of white prospectors stands over them, ordering them to leave the claim, their shovels and picks resting against the bank.

pages.text: Prices Gone Wild Forty-niners could get what they wanted—for a steep price. Here’s what some items cost in 1849 San Francisco and in 2021 dollars (adjusted for inflation): Entrepreneurs made a fortune by selling to the miners. Sam Brannan became one of the first millionaires in the United States. Levi Strauss sold pants tough enough to handle the work—blue jeans. Women, especially, had many more opportunities in the West. They started businesses cooking, running boarding houses, and washing clothes for the prospectors. Mary Ellen Pleasant Mary Ellen Pleasant was a Black American businesswoman who worked as part of the Underground Railroad. Women weren’t accepted as important prospectors during the Gold Rush. Some people say that Pleasant worked as a cook and a housekeeper just to get close to wealthy people to secretly hear what they were talking about. Pleasant became a millionaire buying and selling buildings and businesses during the Gold Rush. Mary Ellen Pleasant.
pages.brief: A busy San Francisco storefront in 1849: miners crowd the counter paying steep prices for picks, pans and tough blue jeans; women cook, wash clothes and run a boarding house nearby; Mary Ellen Pleasant, a Black businesswoman, stands before the buildings she buys and sells.

pages.text: San Francisco in 1851 (top) and today (bottom) The Golden State The biggest winners of the Gold Rush were white settlers, the U.S. government, and wealthy investors. The Gold Rush was devastating to Native peoples, however. Around three hundred thousand settlers, mostly white, swarmed California. In the 1860s, the country began to connect the East and West by building the transcontinental railway, causing further destruction to Native lands. The Gold Rush changed the western United States forever. Today, California has more people than any other state. It has a huge economy —larger than that of most countries. Nearly two centuries after the Gold Rush, California still lives up to its nickname: the Golden State.
pages.brief: Two views of San Francisco: in 1851, low wooden buildings, tents and crowded ships along the waterfront; today, a tall modern skyline of glass towers stretching along the bay, with hills rising behind the city.

books.title: Water Cities
books.art_why: The book shows modern real places that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Water Cities.
pages.brief: A wide aerial view of a city built on water, with canals threading between buildings and small boats moving along them. Bridges connect islands, and water surrounds the whole settlement, suggesting many places where people live close to water.

pages.text: The Grand Canal is the main waterway of Venice. Living Near Water People from across the globe come to Venice, Italy, to see the famous city of canals and bridges built on more than a hundred islands. Although Venice is the world’s best-known water city, it is definitely not the only one. Water cities are places that are built on or near a body of water. Water cities range from tiny communities to huge urban areas. They are located near—or in—oceans, seas, bays, lakes, and rivers on every continent except Antarctica. They exist for many reasons, and each one has a fascinating story to tell.
pages.brief: A wide view of Venice’s Grand Canal, with boats on the water and stone bridges linking buildings across more than a hundred small islands. Visitors stand along the canal to look at the famous waterway. In the distance, other kinds of water cities sit beside oceans, seas, bays, lakes, and rivers.

pages.text: Europe Amsterdam, Netherlands Amsterdam is another European city that is famous for its canals. It is the capital of the Netherlands, a country with roughly one-third of its land below sea level. People have reclaimed about one-sixth of the land from lakes and the North Sea by pumping out water. Amsterdam itself is about 2 meters (6.6 ft.) below sea level. The city was founded in the late twelfth century as a fishing village. It became an important seaport in the seventeenth century and is now one of Europe’s largest seaports. EUROPE Amsterdam.
pages.brief: An aerial view of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, showing its famous canals curving through the city beside narrow buildings. Boats travel the waterways, and bridges cross the canals. The surrounding land lies low, with some areas below sea level, reflecting how water shapes the city.

pages.text: Amsterdam was surrounded by a moat from 1480 to 1585. Its population surged in the 1600s as the city grew. Workers drained swamps and built three more canals around the downtown area. The four waterways were used for transportation, defense, and water management. Besides the main canals, Amsterdam has 161 others, totaling over 100 kilometers (62 mi.) in length, that divide the city into close to 100 small islands joined by over 1,200 bridges. Although the canals were the city’s main transportation routes for centuries, they are now mainly used by smaller boats. However, they are still an important part of the city’s character. Reine, Norway A tiny Norwegian fishing village more than 100 kilometers (62 mi.) above the Arctic Circle has earned the nickname “The Most Beautiful Place in the World.” Located along the coast of one of the Lofoten Islands, Reine offers fishing, kayaking, skiing, whale watching, hiking, and gorgeous beaches. It’s also a perfect place for dramatic views of the northern lights.
pages.brief: A split view: on one side, Amsterdam’s many canals divide the city into small islands linked by bridges, with small boats on the water; on the other, the tiny Norwegian fishing village of Reine sits on a Lofoten Island coast beneath dramatic mountains, with fishing boats and a view of the northern lights.

pages.text: Singapore is one of the world’s busiest port cities. Singapore Singapore is the world’s only island city-state— an island that is both a city and an independent country. It is made up of sixty-three islands. Singapore depends on goods from other places since it has few natural resources of its own. The country must import almost everything it needs. Singapore’s land area has increased by almost 25 percent since the 1960s. Unlike Amsterdam, which has reclaimed land by removing seawater, Singapore has added land by dumping rocks and sand into the water. A project begun in 2016 will use Amsterdam’s methods to increase its land area. ASIA Singapore Asia.
pages.brief: A busy port city on Singapore’s coast, with cargo ships and cranes along the water and tall buildings behind. The city-state spreads across many islands. Nearby, workers dump rocks and sand into the sea to add new land, extending the shoreline.

pages.text: Dubai, United Arab Emirates Dubai is a modern city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The city is the site of many construction projects. One of Dubai’s largest construction projects is Palm Islands—three artificial islands shaped like palm trees. The islands are being built along the coast by piling up huge amounts of sand and rock. They are adding hundreds of miles of coastline to the city as well as homes for many thousands of people. Construction began in 2001, and the first one was completed in late 2016. A curved seawall around the island protects it from strong waves and storms. Palm Jumeirah is one of the largest artificial islands in the world. ASIA Dubai INDIAN OCEAN.
pages.brief: An aerial view of Dubai’s coast in the United Arab Emirates, showing a large artificial island shaped like a palm tree surrounded by a curved seawall. Construction equipment and piles of sand and rock sit along the shoreline, and buildings and homes cover the island and mainland nearby. The sea stretches beyond.

pages.text: The village of Ganvié is sometimes called the Venice of Africa. Ganvié, Benin In startling contrast to the modern cities of Singapore and Dubai is Ganvié (GAWN-vye), the largest stilt village in Africa. The village is located in Lake Nokoué (NOHK-we) in the country of Benin. Ganvié has about twenty thousand residents and three thousand buildings. Only the school and a cemetery are located on land. Ganvié began during the seventeenth century, at a time when humans in West Africa were being captured and sold as slaves by Europeans. During that period, a powerful tribe called the Fon also captured and sold people from other tribes into slavery. The Fons’ religion forbade them from pursuing people who lived on water. Another tribe, the Tofinu, escaped to Lake Nokoué to avoid capture. They founded the stilt village and set up a way of life that continues to this day. Their success is reflected in the name of their village, which means “we survived.” Ganvié AFRICA Africa.
pages.brief: A large stilt village stands over Lake Nokoué in Benin, with thousands of wooden buildings raised on poles above the water. Residents move in canoes between homes. On the shore, a school and a cemetery sit on dry land. The scene shows the community founded by the Tofinu, whose village name reflects survival.

pages.text: Villagers mainly make their living by fishing. They keep and breed fish using underwater fences. They also keep chickens and goats on patches of grass that grow in the water. People travel in long, narrow canoes called pirogues. Fadiouth (Shell Island), Senegal The residents of Fadiouth (fad-YOOT), Senegal, live on an island made up entirely of clamshells. For over three centuries, they have been eating clams and recycling the shells to make not only buildings and streets but also the land itself. The shells are held in place by the roots of trees and reeds.
pages.brief: In Ganvié, villagers fish from long, narrow pirogues and tend underwater fences for keeping and breeding fish. Chickens and goats stand on patches of grass growing in the water. Nearby, on Fadiouth in Senegal, an island made entirely of clamshells rises from the water, with shell-built streets and buildings held together by tree and reed roots.

pages.text: The Uru people make reed canoes for transportation. South America Uros Floating Village, Peru Like the people of Ganvié Lake Village, the residents of Uros, a floating village in Peru, moved to water for safety. The Uru people escaped to Lake Titicaca over five hundred years ago. At that time, the Inca and Colla peoples took over their land. Approximately two thousand Uru now live on about seventy floating islands made of reeds. The islands, which are 1.2 to 2.4 meters (4–8 ft.) thick, break down from the bottom. New reeds must always be added on top. The Uru people also use the reeds to make canoes, homes, and furniture. They make their living from fishing and selling crafts. Even though the Uru live by traditional ways, they have some modern conveniences. Uros has its own radio station, and some residents have solar panels and motorboats. Uros SOUTH AMERICA.
pages.brief: On Lake Titicaca in Peru, about seventy floating islands made of reeds support Uru homes and families. People travel in reed canoes and use reeds to build houses and furniture. Some homes have solar panels, and a motorboat sits near a small radio station, showing traditional life alongside modern conveniences.

pages.text: NORTH AMERICA Mexcaltitán Mexcaltitán sits on a 400-meter (1,300 ft.) sandbar off Mexico’s coast. North America Mexcaltitán, Mexico The Aztec people ruled large areas of Mesoamerica between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. According to legend, they came from a mythical island in a lagoon, and their gods told them to seek out a new homeland. After searching for two hundred years, they founded Tenochtitlán, their capital city. After the Spanish conquest in 1521, Tenochtitlán became known as Mexico City.
pages.brief: A small island town sits on a low sandbar off Mexico’s coast, surrounded by shallow lagoon water. In the background, an Aztec scene shows people searching for a new homeland and founding their capital, Tenochtitlán, which later became Mexico City after the Spanish conquest in 1521.

pages.text: Mexcaltitán (mes-kahl-tee-TAHN) is a small human-made island near the Pacific coast of Mexico. Some historians think Aztec civilization began there. Records show that the early Aztecs used small canoes like those used by Mexcaltitán’s residents. In addition, a map from 1579 shows the mythical island and Mexcaltitán to be in the same place. Mexcaltitán, which is about 350 meters (1,150 ft.) by 40 meters (130 ft.), is now home to about eight hundred people. They live in houses made of adobe, brick, and cement. Many make their living by catching shrimp for local restaurants. This water town is sometimes called the Mexican Venice. In summer, during the rainy season, boats are the only way to travel through the streets. Children have fun playing “water soccer” on the island’s only soccer field, which is underwater. Locals boat and swim in the streets during the flood season in Mexcaltitán.
pages.brief: The small human-made island of Mexcaltitán near Mexico’s Pacific coast is flooded in the rainy season. Streets turn into waterways where locals travel by boat and swim. Children play soccer in water on the island’s only field. Houses of adobe, brick, and cement line the flooded lanes, and residents catch shrimp for local restaurants.

pages.text: Auckland is New Zealand’s largest city. Oceania Auckland, New Zealand This modern city of 1.5 million people is on the North Island of New Zealand in the South Pacific Ocean. Auckland is located between two large harbors on an isthmus less than 2 kilometers (1.2 mi.) wide at its narrowest point. The harbors open to the Pacific Ocean to the east and the Tasman Sea to the west. Auckland’s nickname is the “City of Sails.” About one-sixth of Aucklanders own a boat, and the city has hosted the America’s Cup yacht race twice. The city has thousands of beaches. Water- related activities include kayaking, parasailing, swimming, surfing, fishing, diving, and beach horseback riding.
pages.brief: Auckland, New Zealand, sits between two large harbors on a narrow isthmus, with the Pacific Ocean to the east and the Tasman Sea to the west. Sailboats fill the harbor near the city skyline. Along nearby beaches, people kayak, swim, surf, fish, dive, parasail, and ride horses on the sand.

pages.text: California Italy Aircraft carrier People and Water Many kinds of water cities exist besides the ones you’ve just read about. For instance, Italy has a tiny fishing town made up of brightly colored homes built on steep, rocky cliffs. Northern California has a floating community made up of different kinds of houseboats. Members of the military may spend months living on aircraft carriers. Water represents different things to different people. For residents of water cities, it may mean recreation, work, safety, or a way of life. It may also mean a connection to nature or the rest of the world. Earth’s water cities are proof that people can make a home for themselves just about anywhere.
pages.brief: Three scenes show different water cities: a tiny Italian fishing town with brightly colored homes on steep rocky cliffs; a Northern California floating community of varied houseboats; and an aircraft carrier at sea where military members live for months. Water surrounds each place, showing recreation, work, safety, and a way of life.

books.title: The Story of Plastic
books.art_why: The book mixes historic invention and environmental scenes, so drawn illustrations fit best.

pages.text: The Story of Plastic.
pages.brief: A clean, simple opening scene of a plastic bottle and a plastic pen resting on a plain table in soft light, presented as everyday objects that introduce the material discussed in the book; no people are visible.

pages.text: of of of.
pages.brief: A simple divider illustration of a smooth plastic sheet curving gently across a plain background, with a few soft shadows, suggesting the material before the next section begins; no people or objects other than the plastic sheet are shown.

pages.text: The Convenience of Plastic The Convenience of Plastic In 2016, people around the world bought more than 480 billion plastic drinking bottles. That figure equals almost 70 bottles for each person on Earth. Every minute, more than a million plastic bottles are sold around the world. Disposable bottles are just one example of how we use plastic. This amazing material is everywhere. It’s lightweight and inexpensive, strong yet flexible, and can be molded into almost any shape for a million different purposes. Plastic products are all around us. Your computer keyboard? Your pen? Your candy bar wrapper? These and many other products are made of some type of plastic. We live in an age of plastic. This material is a modern-day wonder. It is also cause for growing concern as we consider what to do with all our plastic trash.
pages.brief: A busy modern scene shows people around the world buying and using plastic drinking bottles, with shelves of bottles and a huge stack representing billions; nearby, a computer keyboard, pen, and candy wrapper sit on a desk, and a full trash bin hints at concern.

pages.text: A Short History of Plastic A Short History of Plastic Not that long ago, plastic didn’t exist. In the 1850s, British inventor Alexander Parkes became the first maker of plastic. He called it Parkesine and saw it as a means for waterproofing cloth. American John Wesley Hyatt bought the patent for Parkesine and conducted experiments to improve upon it. In 1869, he came up with a new kind of plastic and named it celluloid. It proved to be a good replacement for elephant ivory, animal horn, and tortoise shell. Combs, false teeth, piano keys, and billiard balls were all manufactured from this amazing new material. Celluloid was also used to make photographic and cinematic film.
pages.brief: In an 1850s workshop, British inventor Alexander Parkes treats cloth with Parkesine to make it waterproof; nearby, American John Wesley Hyatt experiments and later shows celluloid combs, false teeth, piano keys, billiard balls, and film.

pages.text: In 1907, Belgian American chemist Leo Baekeland accidentally invented the first completely synthetic plastic. Called Bakelite, the material could be formed into most any shape and then cooled into a hard, stiff form. It was the forerunner of such materials as plexiglass, polyester, nylon, and vinyl. Bakelite was used to make telephones, radios, kitchenware, car parts, and thousands of other products. The word plastic itself, though, did not become popular until the 1930s. It comes from the Greek word plassein, which means “to mold or shape.” Plastic can be molded and shaped into almost anything, and chemists and material engineers are still finding new forms and uses for it. Do You Know? Leo Baekeland was trying to create a new chemical for coating furniture when he accidentally created Bakelite. Like Baekeland, many scientists have created important substances by accident. Charles Goodyear reportedly created weatherproof rubber after accidentally leaving a chemical mixture on a hot stove. Chemist Stephanie Kwolek came up with Kevlar, used in bulletproof vests, while working to develop a strong, lightweight fiber for tires.
pages.brief: In a 1907 chemistry laboratory, Leo Baekeland accidentally creates Bakelite, then shapes it and cools it into hard objects; finished telephones, radios, kitchenware, and car parts surround him, while chemists experiment with rubber and Kevlar fiber.

pages.text: Cotton, wood, and latex from rubber trees are all natural polymers. Miracle Material Miracle Material Plastic is special because of its atomic structure. Atoms link together to form molecules—the tiny building blocks of all matter. Plastic is a polymer—a substance made of large molecules that are linked in repeating units. These molecules bond very strongly in long chains, making them difficult to break and therefore very durable. Cellulose, a material that forms the cell walls of plants, is a type of natural polymer. Most plastics today, though, are made from synthetic polymers that don’t occur in nature. Scientists are able to create these polymers using oil, natural gas, or chemicals that can be made from them. The chemicals are loaded with carbon atoms that form strong bonds with other atoms.
pages.brief: A close-up illustration shows atoms linking into long molecular chains, with strong bonds making a durable plastic polymer; beside it, cotton, wood, and latex from rubber trees appear as natural polymers, while oil and natural gas feed synthetic plastic production.

pages.text: There are two types of plastics— thermosets and thermoplastics. Thermosets are hard and brittle, and can withstand heat. Once they are shaped and cooled, they cannot be remelted. Examples of thermoset plastic include bathroom tiles, countertops, and baking dishes. Thermoset countertop tiles are strong and heat resistant. Thermoplastics can stretch and can also be melted, reformed, and recycled fairly easily. Milk jugs, plastic storage containers, and most toys are examples of this kind of plastic. Thermoplastics make up more than 90 percent of plastic products we know and use. Plastic storage containers are light and strong.
pages.brief: A split scene shows hard thermoset plastic as bathroom tiles, a countertop, and a baking dish that withstand heat; on the other side, thermoplastic milk jugs, storage containers, and toys are shown being melted, stretched, reformed, and recycled, with the containers looking light and strong.

pages.text: The Case for Plastic The Case for Plastic In the past century, plastic became the shape- shifting wonder of manufacturers’ dreams. Wood, metal, stone, glass, and ceramics can be fragile and difficult to work with. Plastic, on the other hand, can be molded with great precision to meet the needs and wishes of businesses and consumers. Plastic is easy to make and transform, and has come to represent convenience. It is the plastic bottle we drink from, the toothbrush we use to clean our teeth, and the disposable plates we picnic on and toss away. Plastic has also proven its value in other ways we may not notice.
pages.brief: Manufacturers shape plastic with precision as wood, metal, stone, glass, and ceramics sit nearby looking fragile; a person drinks from a plastic bottle, brushes teeth with a plastic toothbrush, and picnics with disposable plates that are tossed away, showing plastic's convenience.

pages.text: One example of plastic’s benefits is energy savings. Builders use plastics to insulate homes, schools, and office buildings. Insulation saves energy by keeping heat in on cold days and keeping heat out when the thermometer climbs. Plastic is also lighter than glass or any other material that might be used for packaging. The lighter weight saves fuel when shipping goods. In a similar way, plastic parts have helped reduce the weight of cars, trucks, aircraft, and other forms of transport. The less a vehicle weighs, the less fuel it needs to move. In turn, lower manufacturing and shipping costs save money for shoppers. Most plastic products can also be mass-produced more efficiently and cheaply than products made from other materials, again reducing costs for consumers. Plastic packaging also reduces food waste by keeping meat, bread, and vegetables fresh for longer periods. Plastic has proven to be good business for manufacturers, retailers, and customers.
pages.brief: Builders install plastic insulation in a home, school, and office building while a thermometer shows heat kept in and out; lightweight plastic packaging sits beside glass, and lighter car, truck, and aircraft parts suggest fuel savings, with fresh meat, bread, and vegetables wrapped to reduce waste.

pages.text: Any visit to a hospital or doctor’s office demonstrates plastic’s value to health care. Operating rooms are packed with plastic equipment, from monitors to tubes to surgical instruments. Plastic is easy to clean and resists contamination. Cheap, disposable supplies like syringes, examination gloves, and patient gowns reduce costs as well as the chances of infection. Cheap to make, lightweight, durable, versatile —these are the big reasons we have found so many uses for plastic in our lives. Disposable plastic medical supplies help keep doctors and patients safe in hospitals but create a large amount of plastic trash.
pages.brief: In a hospital operating room, doctors and nurses work among plastic monitors, tubes, and surgical instruments; nearby, disposable syringes, examination gloves, and patient gowns are shown as cheap, clean supplies that reduce infection, while a bin of used plastic medical trash stands beside them.

pages.text: An Ocean of Plastic An Ocean of Plastic Each year, more than 9 million metric tons of plastic goes into the ocean. 1 That’s more than one truckload of garbage every minute. 2 That amount is doubling every 11 years. 3 Larger pieces of plastic can harm fish and wildlife when they eat it, choke on it, or become entangled in it. Larger pieces of plastic can harm fish and wildlife when they eat it, choke on it, or become entangled in it. million million million million Plastic doesn’t go away Plastic doesn’t go away! Plastic doesn’t go away Plastic doesn’t go away! Tiny pieces of plastic also make their way up the food chain into people. The average seafood eater takes in 11,000 pieces of plastic each year. 4 Plastic doesn’t go away! It just gets smaller over time. A single plastic bottle can break down into more than 10,000 tiny pieces of plastic. These tiny pieces of plastic are eaten by shellfish and other sea life. It just gets smaller over time. pieces of plastic each year. 4 The Problem with Plastic The Problem with Plastic Plastic has proven to be a miracle material, but more and more its drawbacks are there for all of us to see. A glance into a full dumpster reveals the problem—plastic trash. Plastic is turning into an environmental disaster. A plastic bottle of water can be a cool, refreshing drink, but it comes at a price. More than four hundred years from now, that plastic bottle will likely still be on Earth, perhaps buried in a landfill or lying on the seafloor.
pages.brief: A wide ocean scene shows floating plastic bottles and bags, with fish and seabirds tangled in larger pieces and tiny plastic bits drifting toward shellfish; on shore, a full dumpster overflows, and one plastic water bottle lies on the seafloor, unchanged.

pages.text: Plastic’s durability presents huge environmental challenges. Most food, wood, paper, and other plant materials break down over time and can be reused by nature. Plastic is different, though. Because most plastic is made from petrochemicals, natural forces cannot break it down easily, if at all. Over time, a plastic object may break into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, but it never completely disappears. The low cost of making plastic also adds to the problem. It is cheaper to make new plastic bottles and other products than to reuse or recycle them. Many communities in the United States have recycling programs, but less than 10 percent of plastic is recycled, while another 15 percent is burned for energy. More than 75 percent of plastic is trucked to landfills or ends up dumped in the ocean. Plastic trash is not just ugly; biologists have proven that plastic is harming and killing wildlife. Dead whales have washed ashore with their guts stuffed with plastic bags they have mistakenly swallowed, thinking they were jellyfish or other food. Many seabirds are dying after swallowing plastic bits, and researchers are finding microplastics in fish, oysters, and other seafood we eat.
pages.brief: A landfill and ocean edge show plastic trash persisting while food, wood, and paper break down nearby; a dead whale lies ashore with plastic bags inside it, seabirds swallow plastic bits, and researchers examine fish, oysters, and seafood for microplastics.

pages.text: As the plastic piles up, more people are taking action to help solve these problems. Communities are banning disposable plastic bags in their stores. Some countries are experimenting with charging customers a small deposit on each plastic drink bottle; they then get that money back when the container is returned. Norway’s “Deposit Return Scheme” has resulted in 96 percent of that country’s plastic bottles being recycled instead of becoming garbage. In some cases, kids are leading the way in tackling plastic pollution. Milo Cress was nine years old when he started the Be Straw Free campaign in 2011. He urged restaurants and their customers to stop using plastic straws. The organization estimates that Americans use half a billion straws every day, and straws are among the most common forms of plastic trash. Plastic drinking straws can often be replaced with paper or metal straws, which are less harmful to the environment. Still, plastic pollution remains a big problem in search of an answer.
pages.brief: A nine-year-old boy, Milo Cress, stands in a restaurant holding paper and metal straws while restaurant staff and customers set aside plastic straws; nearby, community shoppers use reusable bags and a bottle deposit return machine shows bottles being collected for recycling.

pages.text: Inventing a New Future for Plastic Inventing a New Future for Plastic Plastic is here to stay for many, many reasons. Plastic products make our daily lives easier, more affordable, and more convenient. Chemical engineers and inventors used their creative genius and worked hard to create a material that has so many good uses. Now, similar minds need to embrace the challenge of creating new forms of plastic that do less harm to the environment. In the meantime, we all can take action to be more mindful of our plastic habits. We need no special talents or knowledge to reduce our use of plastic, reuse it when possible, and recycle it at every opportunity— while still enjoying its benefits. Biodegradable Plastic? Plastic makers are working to create biodegradable plastics. These plastics are designed to break down naturally from exposure to weather or by means of chemicals released by microorganisms. However, materials engineers and chemists have yet to produce plastics that break down under normal environmental conditions. A fork made from a special corn-based plastic breaks down in as little as forty-five days.
pages.brief: Chemical engineers and inventors work in a bright laboratory, designing new less harmful plastics; beside them, a corn-based plastic fork breaks down in soil over forty-five days, while families sort and recycle everyday plastic items, showing people reducing and reusing plastic in daily life.

books.title: Taiga
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing; ice-age and late-1800s scenes cannot be photographed as events.

pages.text: This forested biome is mostly uninhabited. A Carpet of Green If you look down on Earth from a satellite high above the North Pole, you’ll see the Arctic Ocean. The first ring of land surrounding the North Pole is the treeless tundra region. Beyond the tundra lies a wider ring of deep green that is mostly empty of roads and cities. This region is home to an amazing number of trees as well as some of Earth’s hardiest animals. It remains nearly untouched by modern life. This region is the taiga. Sources disagree on the meaning of the Russian word taiga. Some say it means “forest-covered mountain,” while others believe it means “swampy, moist forest” or “coniferous forests.” In North America, the taiga is often referred to as the boreal forest. Boreal, which means “northern,” comes from Boreas, the Greek god of the north wind.
pages.brief: A satellite view high above the North Pole shows the Arctic Ocean surrounded by a ring of treeless tundra and then a wider deep-green ring of taiga. The taiga stretches across northern land with no roads or cities visible, full of trees and hardy animals.

pages.text: Winter in the taiga can last for the majority of the year. The Taiga Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Deserts, grasslands, rainforests, and oceans are examples of biomes. So is the taiga. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. Two important ones are latitude—how far a location is from the equator—and elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. Climate, land, and water are also important building blocks of biomes, as are plants and animals. The taiga is located in cold regions of the Northern Hemisphere. This biome’s main plants are conifers —trees that produce seeds in cones instead of flowers.
pages.brief: A cold taiga biome in winter stretches beneath a pale sky, with snow covering the ground for most of the year. Conifer trees stand among the snowy landscape, their seeds growing in cones rather than flowers.

pages.text: Earth’s Taiga Regions EUROPE ASIA NORTH AMERICA AFRICA SOUTH AMERICA AUSTRALIA ANTARCTICA The Russian taiga measures about 5,800 kilometers (3,600 mi.) from east to west. The taiga—Earth’s largest land biome—occurs in a wide band across northern regions of North America, Europe, and Asia. In North America, much of Canada and Alaska are taiga. In Europe, the taiga occurs in small patches in the Highlands of Scotland. It then stretches from Norway, Sweden, and Finland all across Russia to the Pacific Ocean. It also extends into parts of China and Mongolia. About one-sixth of Earth’s land is taiga. To the north is the tundra, where almost no trees grow. The border between the two biomes is known as the tree line. Just south of the taiga, some parts of the world have temperate forests, while others have grasslands.
pages.brief: A view of Earth shows a wide green band of taiga across northern North America, Europe, and Asia. North of the band lies the treeless tundra and the tree line; south of it lie temperate forests and grasslands.

pages.text: Climate and Soil The climate in the taiga is typically cold, although it varies from place to place. Because of the taiga’s location far north of the equator, sunlight strikes the land at a low angle. As a result, this region receives less heat energy than places nearer the equator. Snow cover also contributes to the cold by reflecting sunlight instead of absorbing it. A third factor is the taiga’s long winter nights, which allow more heat to escape into Earth’s atmosphere. Winters in the taiga are long, cold, and windy. Temperatures are usually below −10°C (14°F) in January, the coldest month. In eastern Siberia, winter temperatures have dropped as low as −50°C (−58°F). Accumulated snow generally lasts all winter—five months or more in the southern taiga and up to eight months in the northern taiga. Glaciers and Land Bridges Much of the taiga was covered with glaciers during the last ice age, which ended just under twelve thousand years ago. With so much of Earth’s water frozen, sea levels remained lower. As a result, many of today’s islands, such as the British Isles, were connected to the mainland above water. A land bridge between the far eastern part of Russia and parts of Alaska and Canada allowed many animal species to move to North America.
pages.brief: A cold taiga landscape under low-angle sunlight, with snow reflecting light and a long winter night sky above. In the distance, a glacier covers part of the land; a low land bridge connects far eastern Russia with Alaska and Canada.

pages.text: Skies are deep purple during a foggy thunderstorm in the Canadian taiga. July, the warmest month, ranges between 15 and 20°C (59–68°F) and may even reach 25°C (77°F) during the hottest time of the day. Frequent thunderstorms with lightning and low rainfall can cause forest fires during warmer months. Fires can be useful because they remove old and sick trees and make room for new ones to grow. Annual precipitation in the taiga is highest in eastern North America and northern Europe, which have many lakes, streams, and wetlands. These areas may receive over 100 centimeters (39 in.) of precipitation each year.
pages.brief: A foggy thunderstorm darkens the Canadian taiga with a deep purple sky. Lightning flashes above a conifer forest, and a small fire burns among the trees after low rainfall in July, the warm summer month.

pages.text: Soils in the taiga are generally cold, shallow, rocky, and nutrient poor. This limits the types of plants that can grow in many places. In warmer areas of the taiga, soils contain more nutrients because organic matter breaks down more quickly. In many parts of Canada, glaciers have scraped the land, leaving the soil too thin for mature forests to grow. Spruce and tamarack trees, along with mosses and other plants, grow in boggy areas. Permafrost—permanently frozen ground— or else solid rock lies just below the surface soil in many areas. Neither one allows soil to drain well. For this reason, the taiga has many shallow bogs. Climate change is creating more bogs as the permafrost melts. Permafrost in the Taiga Areas of the taiga with below-freezing average annual temperatures may contain permafrost. Many species of trees are unable to grow in these areas, but some, including tamarack and black spruce, can still thrive if the layer of surface soil above the frozen ground is deep enough. Permafrost is common in northern Canada and the Asian portion of Russia. It tends to occur in areas that receive less sunlight, such as the north side of mountain slopes.
pages.brief: A shallow, rocky taiga soil lies under mosses, spruce, and tamarack trees in a boggy area. Solid rock and permafrost sit just below the surface, preventing drainage; patches of shallow bog spread where the frozen ground melts.

pages.text: Taiga Plants Plants in the taiga must survive a short growing season as well as cold temperatures, permafrost, and nutrient- poor soil. As a result, fewer species grow there than in biomes at lower latitudes. The main plants are conifers, including pine, fir, and spruce. Many of these trees are evergreens, which keep their leaves year-round. But tamarack, another common conifer, is deciduous, dropping its leaves in winter. Some flower-bearing deciduous trees, such as poplar and birch, also grow in the taiga, although they’re less widespread. Scotch pine is one of the most common trees found in the taiga. Much of the ground cover is mosses, lichens, and mushrooms, which have shallow roots. They don’t require much sunlight or water, and they can bear the cold. Some grasses, ferns, and other low plants also grow in the taiga. Calypso orchids grow in damp areas of the taiga during summer.
pages.brief: A summer taiga scene shows Scotch pine, fir, spruce, and tamarack trees mixed with birch and poplar. On the damp ground grow mosses, lichens, mushrooms, grasses, ferns, and Calypso orchids, while shallow roots take in little sunlight and water.

pages.text: Plants have several important adaptations for surviving in the taiga. Keeping their leaves all year helps evergreen trees conserve energy and nutrients. Growing new leaves in spring would require more sunlight and soil nutrients, both of which are in short supply. Scotch pine needles conserve water (top). A Norway spruce withstands heavy snowfall (bottom). Many cone-bearing trees in the taiga, such as pines, have needlelike leaves with a waxy coating. This leaf design allows trees to conserve water, which may be scarce due to low rainfall or because it’s frozen. Needles also protect trees from freezing since they don’t contain much sap. Dark-green leaves increase heat absorption and help trees take in the Sun’s energy for use in photosynthesis. Many trees are cone shaped, with branches that shed snow quickly so the snow’s weight doesn’t break them.
pages.brief: Close up, Scotch pine needles with a waxy coating conserve water, while a Norway spruce with cone-shaped branches sheds heavy snowfall. Dark-green needles absorb heat and help the tree take in the Sun’s energy; the needles contain little sap, protecting the tree from freezing.

pages.text: Taiga Animals The cold climate and restricted types of plants limit the kinds of animals that can live in the taiga. Animals there are hardy and well adapted to the challenging conditions. Mammals tend to grow thick fur for insulation, and larger species often have long legs and large feet to navigate in deep snow. moose The biome’s large herbivores include deer, elk, moose, and caribou (also known as reindeer). Predators include black and grizzly bears, wolves, wolverines, lynxes, and weasel-like martens, as well as Siberian tigers in eastern Russia. Squirrels, snowshoe hares, and lemmings are among the smaller mammals. Birds of prey, including eagles, hawks, and owls, hunt them from trees. pine marten lynx.
pages.brief: In deep snow, a moose, caribou, deer, and elk stand among conifers while a lynx and pine marten watch nearby. A black bear, grizzly bear, wolf, wolverine, and Siberian tiger hunt in the taiga; squirrels, hares, and lemmings hide, and eagles, hawks, and owls hunt from trees.

pages.text: Enormous numbers of insects breed in bogs, lakes, and ponds in the summer. Waterfowl and many other kinds of birds migrate to the taiga to take advantage of this plentiful food source and raise their young. These birds migrate south to warmer regions during the long, cold winters. Woodpeckers, ravens, loons, and chickadees are year-round residents. The taiga is a challenging biome for reptiles and amphibians, which can’t regulate their body temperature internally. In spring and summer, some parts of the taiga are warm enough for these animals. They cope with the cold by hibernating in winter, either on land or, in the case of turtles and some frogs, at the bottom of lakes and ponds. Frozen Frogs Wood frogs survive the taiga’s cold with the help of an unusual adaptation: their blood and body tissues freeze while they hibernate. In this frozen state, their breathing and heartbeat stop, blood ceases to flow, and ice crystals form under their skin. Special proteins and sugars protect their cells from damage. These frogs can tolerate more than half of their body freezing.
pages.brief: A summer taiga pond teems with insects. Waterfowl and migrating birds gather to feed and raise young, while woodpeckers, ravens, loons, and chickadees stay year-round. Turtles and frogs hibernate at the pond bottom, and a wood frog lies partly frozen with ice crystals under its skin.

pages.text: People in the Taiga People have lived in the taiga for thousands of years. More than six hundred traditional communities live there today. Their livelihoods include reindeer herding, fishing, hunting, and crafts. Many of these people are working to preserve both the forests and their traditional way of life. This woman is a tribal elder of the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi in Quebec. Her tribe is one of the most active native groups working to protect the taiga in Canada. Because the taiga is forested, trees are a key natural resource, and logging is widespread. Mining, oil and gas exploration, and road construction are other industrial activities in this biome. People also travel to the taiga to enjoy boating, fishing, hiking, skiing, snowmobiling, dogsledding, and relaxing in cozy cabins. Most of the taiga is fairly unpopulated. The two largest cities are Toronto, Canada, and Moscow, Russia.
pages.brief: A Cree First Nation elder woman from Waswanipi, Quebec, stands in the taiga forest. Around her, people herd reindeer, fish, hunt, and make crafts; logging, mining, oil and gas work, and road construction continue nearby. Boats, hikers, skiers, snowmobiles, dogsleds, and cozy cabins show recreation in the mostly unpopulated biome.

pages.text: One of the world’s largest taiga areas lies in Russia. Where Conifers Rule The taiga stretches nearly 13 million square kilometers (about 5 million sq. mi.) across Earth’s northern lands. Conifers reign supreme in this cold region. Siberia, in Russia, includes vast areas of taiga. Russian playwright Anton Chekhov traveled to the Siberian taiga on horseback in the late 1800s. He was so struck by the endless expanse of green conifers that he wondered if he’d ever get out. Although it’s certainly possible to leave the taiga, those fortunate enough to experience this land won’t soon forget it.
pages.brief: A vast Siberian taiga in Russia stretches out as an endless expanse of green conifers. In the late 1800s, Anton Chekhov travels on horseback through the forest, surrounded by cone-bearing trees in every direction, with no end to the green wilderness in sight.

books.title: Lakes
books.art_why: Lakes are real places today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Healing Waters Being near water is healing. Recent scientific research confirms what people have likely known since the dawn of time. Water soothes us, calms our busy minds, inspires creativity, and gives rise to a sense of wonder. While all kinds of water can be healing, lakes and ponds have a character all their own. They generally have still water, which is quite different from wild ocean waves or the rush of a flowing river. If you’ve ever marveled at a landscape perfectly mirrored in a lake, you’ve experienced the calming power of lakes. Morning fog rises from a lake in Vermont’s Green Mountain National Forest.
pages.brief: Morning fog drifts over a still lake in Vermont’s Green Mountain National Forest. The water mirrors the forested mountains and sky. Soft mist hovers above the surface, and trees line the shore in a quiet, calm scene.

pages.text: The Lake Biome Different types of environments cover Earth’s surface. These regions and the communities of plants and animals that live there are called biomes. Deserts, rainforests, and rivers are examples of biomes. So are lakes. Many factors play a part in creating Earth’s biomes. For land biomes, which cover more than one-fourth of the planet’s surface, two important factors are latitude—how far north or south of the equator a location is—and elevation, or height above sea level. Both help determine how warm or cool a place is. For water biomes, which cover nearly three- fourths of Earth’s surface, one of the most important factors is whether they contain salt water or fresh water. In this book, you’ll learn about lakes and ponds, most of which contain fresh water. These bodies of water are completely surrounded by land. They have standing water rather than a fast-moving current. Lake or Pond? There is no exact difference between a lake and a pond. However, ponds are usually smaller and shallower than lakes, waves tend to be smaller, and sunlight is more likely to reach all the way to the bottom. The temperature of ponds is generally more uniform. Water lilies on a pond.
pages.brief: A pond surface is dotted with water lilies and their flat green leaves. The water is still and shallow enough for sunlight to reach the bottom. The pond is completely surrounded by land, with plants growing in and around it.

pages.text: Lakes Around the World Lakes exist on every continent and within every land biome. Earth’s millions of lakes vary greatly in size and depth. The largest is the Caspian Sea, a saltwater lake. (Long ago, it was named a sea because it is huge and salty, but scientists generally consider it a lake.) The largest freshwater lake is Lake Superior, one of the Great Lakes, which are on the border between Canada and the United States. Although we often think of lakes as calm, large lakes such as the Great Lakes have strong currents and possess some of the characteristics of an ocean. Notable Lakes Around the World NORTH NORTH AMERICA AMERICA EUROPE EUROPE ASIA ASIA AFRICA AFRICA SOUTH SOUTH AMERICA AMERICA These are just a few of Earth’s best-known lakes.
pages.brief: A broad saltwater lake, the Caspian Sea, lies surrounded by land, while Lake Superior, a huge freshwater lake, sits on the Canada–United States border. Lakes of many sizes and depths appear across continents and land biomes.

pages.text: Formed in 1991, Lake Pinatubo, in the Philippines, is one of the world’s youngest crater lakes. At 2,000 feet, it is also the country’s deepest lake. How Lakes Form Lakes often form when low areas of land, called basins, fill with water. Lake basins can form in many different ways. The Great Lakes, along with many other lakes in the Northern Hemisphere, formed around fourteen thousand years ago at the end of the last ice age. Huge glaciers moved slowly, carving out basins and eroding the land. As they moved, they ground up the rock and sediment beneath them, creating tiny pieces called glacial flour. Water from melting glaciers later filled the basins. Volcanoes can also cause lake basins to form. After a volcano stops erupting, rain or melted snow can fill its crater. Water can also fill a caldera, a large depression formed when the top of a volcano collapses during a violent eruption.
pages.brief: A crater lake fills a volcanic depression in the Philippines, deep and still. In another scene, huge glaciers slowly carve basins into the land, grinding rock into tiny pieces called glacial flour. Melting glacier water later fills the basins.

pages.text: Plitvice (PLEET-veet-suh) Lakes National Park, in Croatia, has sixteen solution lakes connected by waterfalls. Some lakes form as a result of water dissolving certain types of underground rocks. Rocks made of limestone or salt are most likely to dissolve. Once they do, the ground above them lacks support, so it caves in and forms a lake. Rocks that dissolve are called soluble, which means “able to be dissolved,” and the lakes they form are called solution lakes. The movement of huge pieces of Earth’s crust deep underground can also create lake basins. Deep cracks called faults can form when these pieces move. Lake Baikal, in southern Russia, formed in this way. It is Earth’s deepest lake, with an estimated depth of 1,637 meters (5,369 ft.).
pages.brief: Water cascades between sixteen connected lakes in Plitvice Lakes National Park in Croatia. Limestone rock dissolves underground, causing the ground above to cave in and form solution lakes. In southern Russia, deep faults create a basin for Lake Baikal, Earth’s deepest lake.

pages.text: Several types of lakes don’t begin as a basin that fills with water. Oxbow lakes, for example, are formed by river currents. Some rivers flow in a winding path. Erosion is greater on the outside of the bends, where the current is faster, than on the inside. Sediment builds up on the inside because water moves more slowly. Over time, those sediments cause a loop to close off and the river to follow a new path. The water that remains in the closed-off loop forms an oxbow lake. Landslides and mudslides can also form lakes. Rocks, soil, and mud that slide down a hill or valley can pile up, causing a stream’s flow to become blocked. Lakes that form in this manner are usually temporary. Small streams can also get blocked by beaver dams. People create artificial lakes, or reservoirs, when they build hydroelectric dams on rivers. Lakes are not permanent, even though they may seem to be, given our life span. Most lakes that exist today are less than twenty thousand years old. Lakes eventually turn into wetlands and later disappear completely. A few ancient lakes formed as a result of movement in Earth’s crust. The oldest, Lake Baikal, is at least twenty- five million years old.
pages.brief: A winding river bends across land, with sediment building up on the inside of a loop. The loop closes off to form an oxbow lake. Elsewhere, a landslide blocks a stream, a beaver dam stops water, and a hydroelectric dam creates a reservoir.

pages.text: Salt Lakes Scientists consider lakes to be either open or closed. Most water in open lakes leaves by flowing into a river or another body of water. The water in most closed lakes only leaves by evaporating. These lakes are salty, or saline, because when water evaporates, salt is left behind. Saline lakes are often surrounded by salt flats—areas where all the lake water has evaporated, leaving behind a thick layer of salt on the ground. Freshwater lakes contain very little salt—just 0.05 percent (5 parts per thousand [ppt]) or less. The amount of salt in ocean water is about 3.5 percent (35 ppt). The salt content in saline lakes can be greater than 30 percent (300 ppt), although it varies a great deal. The largest saline lake in the Western Hemisphere is Great Salt Lake, in Utah. Its salinity ranges between 6 and 30 percent (60–300 ppt). The Dead Sea, a saline lake in the Middle East, has a salt content of 33.7 percent (337 ppt). One of the saltiest lakes on Earth is Don Juan Pond, which is located in Antarctica. Its salinity can be as great as 44 percent (440 ppt). Because of the high salt content, the pond doesn’t freeze unless the surrounding temperature drops below –50 degrees Celsius (–58°F).
pages.brief: A saline lake lies in a dry landscape, surrounded by white salt flats where water has evaporated. Great Salt Lake in Utah and the Dead Sea in the Middle East hold very salty water. In Antarctica, Don Juan Pond stays liquid in extreme cold.

pages.text: Lake Zones and Organisms Sunlight often reaches all the way down to the bottom of shallow lakes and ponds. In contrast, deep lakes and ponds have zones that differ with regard to light, wind, and temperature. The littoral zone is the part of a lake closest to the shore. It has the shallowest, warmest water. Both the water and the soil beneath it receive plenty of sunlight, which allows plants and algae to live there. Some plants, such as cattails and reeds, are rooted and stick out above the surface of the water. Other rooted plants, including pondweed, grow completely underwater. Perhaps the best-known plants in the littoral zone are rooted plants with floating leaves, such as water lilies. Other plants, such as duckweed, float freely on the water. Many animals make their homes in littoral zone plants. These include insects, frogs, crayfish, snails, sponges, worms, and small fish. Many also lay eggs on the plants. A great blue heron hunts for fish in the littoral zone.
pages.brief: A great blue heron stands in shallow water at the edge of a lake, hunting for fish among cattails, reeds, pondweed, and floating water lilies. Sunlight reaches the bottom. Insects, frogs, crayfish, snails, sponges, worms, and small fish live among the plants.

pages.text: Lake Zones littoral zone littoral zone limnetic zone profundal zone benthic zone The limnetic zone is the open water near the surface in the middle of a lake. Like the littoral zone, it receives plentiful sunlight and supports plant growth. Microscopic organisms known as phytoplankton and zooplankton live here, along with many fish. The water contains a lot of oxygen. The profundal zone, located below the limnetic zone, is colder. Because of its depth, it doesn’t receive sunlight. Fewer fish live here because oxygen levels are low during certain seasons. The benthic zone is the sediment at the bottom of a lake. Most of this zone is cold and dark. Worms, clams, and other animals live here and are food for certain kinds of fish. Dead organic matter from other zones falls to the benthic zone, where it is broken down by bacteria.
pages.brief: A view into a lake shows four zones: the shallow littoral zone near shore, the sunlit limnetic zone in open water, the cold dark profundal zone below, and the benthic zone of sediment at the bottom. Plankton and fish swim in the sunlit water.

pages.text: Lakes support many animals that aren’t strictly aquatic. Frogs, salamanders, turtles, muskrats, otters, beavers, alligators, loons, ducks, geese, herons, and others require both land and water habitats. Lakes also provide food for visiting animals, such as moose, raccoons, and migrating birds. In addition, ponds are breeding grounds for many different kinds of organisms, and lake plants offer hidden places to raise babies. In winter, lakes and ponds freeze from top to bottom. Because most never freeze solid, many organisms are able to survive winter in deep water. Each year, hundreds of thousands of flamingos gather on Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru in Kenya, East Africa, to feed on algae and raise chicks.
pages.brief: Flamingos gather by the thousands on Lakes Bogoria and Nakuru in Kenya, feeding on algae and raising chicks. Around other lakes, frogs, salamanders, turtles, muskrats, otters, beavers, alligators, loons, ducks, geese, and herons live near the water. A moose and raccoons visit for food.

pages.text: People and Lakes Lakes and ponds have been important to people since ancient times. Ships have crossed large lakes for travel and trade. Farmers have used the water in lakes and ponds to irrigate their crops. Today, lakes supply much of our drinking water as well as water to cool power plants, steel mills, and chemical plants. Reservoirs store water that can be used in case of drought. Lakes also provide plentiful opportunities for recreation. Fishing, boating, swimming, and water-skiing bring thousands of people to lakes each year. Camping, hiking, photography, and watching wildlife are also popular, as are ice- skating and ice fishing in winter. A mother fishes with her daughter in Wyoming’s Bighorn Mountains.
pages.brief: A mother and daughter fish together beside a lake in Wyoming’s Bighorn Mountains. People also boat, swim, water-ski, camp, hike, take photographs, watch wildlife, ice-skate, and ice-fish on lakes. Farms use lake water, and reservoirs store water for droughts.

pages.text: The last light of day is reflected in Maligne (muh-LEEN) Lake, the longest and deepest lake in the Canadian Rockies. Peace and Beauty When we think about how lakes form, we are reminded that our planet is constantly changing. Yet the glassy surface of a secluded lake shows us that nature can also be serene. Lakes invite us to take comfort in the beauty of wild places. They also call on us to slow down and pay attention to our surroundings. The American writer Henry David Thoreau was so inspired by that call that he left his regular life in Concord, Massachusetts, to live alone at Walden Pond for two years. During that time, he lived simply, while studying nature and writing about it. In his words, “A lake is the landscape’s most beautiful and expressive feature. It is earth’s eye; looking into which the beholder measures the depth of his own nature.”
pages.brief: The last daylight reflects on Maligne Lake in the Canadian Rockies, the longest and deepest lake there. Its glassy surface is serene. At Walden Pond, Henry David Thoreau lives alone for two years, studying nature and writing about the lake’s beauty and depth.

books.title: Ukraine
books.art_why: The book covers ancient ruins, medieval castles, and historical events from before photography.

pages.text: Ukraine Ukrainian children wear national costumes during Lviv City Day celebrations in honor of the 762nd anniversary of Lviv’s founding. Connections.
pages.brief: Ukrainian children wear national costumes during Lviv City Day celebrations in honor of the 762nd anniversary of Lviv’s founding. They are gathered in the city for the festive event, representing their culture and connection to the community.

pages.text: Welcome to Ukraine Ukraine became an independent country in 1991, making it one of the youngest countries in the world. Yet it has a long and fascinating history. Because of its rich soil, one of the world’s first civilizations to practice agriculture developed there more than five thousand years ago. Some of the castles and cities you can visit in Ukraine today have been standing for more than one thousand years. Due to its location, various empires fought to control it for centuries. Today, the cultural influence of these empires can be seen in Ukraine’s art, cuisine, and architecture. From delicious food to medieval castles and lively music festivals, there is so much to see and experience in Ukraine! A group of people wear traditional Ukrainian clothing during a march in the city of Kyiv.
pages.brief: A group of people in traditional Ukrainian clothing march through Kyiv. The scene reflects Ukraine’s long history, from early agriculture on rich soil to castles and cities standing for over a thousand years, and the art, cuisine, and architecture shaped by various empires.

pages.text: A large portion of Ukraine’s land is used for farming. The Land Ukraine is the largest country that is located entirely in Europe. (Russia is larger, but it spans Europe and Asia.) It’s twice the size of Italy but slightly smaller than the state of Texas. Ukraine shares borders with seven countries: Belarus, Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Russia, and Slovakia. The country is also bordered by the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in the south. The Dnieper (NEE-pur), Ukraine’s longest river, runs through the middle of the country, from Belarus in the north to the Black Sea. To the south of Ukraine is the Crimean Peninsula, which is connected to the mainland by an 8-kilometer (5 mi.) strip of land.
pages.brief: A broad landscape of Ukrainian farmland shows flat fields stretching across the country. The Dnieper River runs through the middle from north to south, while the Black Sea and Sea of Azov lie to the south near the Crimean Peninsula, which connects to the mainland by a narrow strip of land.

pages.text: Ukraine is the world’s biggest producer of sunflower oil, a popular oil for cooking. Besides the Carpathian Mountains in the west and the Crimean Mountains on the peninsula, most of Ukraine is flat. Summers are often warm and humid, while winters are cold and dry. The fertile soil and mild weather of the country’s plains make the land ideal for growing wheat. Because of this, Ukraine is sometimes referred to as the “breadbasket of Europe.” Wheat, corn, sunflowers, potatoes, and sugar beets are some of the main crops grown there. Synevir Lake is a popular destination for visitors.
pages.brief: Synevir Lake lies in a calm natural setting, a popular destination for visitors. Around it, Ukraine’s mostly flat plains and fertile fields are ideal for growing wheat, corn, sunflowers, potatoes, and sugar beets, with the Carpathian Mountains in the west and the Crimean Mountains on the peninsula.

pages.text: The People Although Ukraine is twice the size of Italy, it has about seventeen million fewer people. More than two-thirds of the country’s population lives in cities. Kyiv (KI-yeev), the capital of Ukraine, is the largest city. Nearly three million people live there. Most people in the country are native Ukrainians, with Russians making up the next largest group. Ukrainians are part of an ethnic group called Slavs—people primarily from central and eastern Europe who speak a Slavic language. Kyiv is one of the oldest cities in Eastern Europe. It was founded in 482 ce— more than 1,500 years ago.
pages.brief: A view of Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital and largest city, which is home to nearly three million people. The city is one of Eastern Europe’s oldest, founded in 482 CE. Most people in Ukraine are native Ukrainians, with Russians as the next largest group, and Ukrainians belong to the Slavic ethnic group.

pages.text: Elementary school students in Ukraine practice their reading skills. Most people in Ukraine speak Ukrainian. Many other languages are spoken as well, including Russian, Polish, and Yiddish (a language spoken by some Jewish people in Europe). Today, Ukrainian is the official language of the country, but that wasn’t always the case. In fact, at various times throughout the country’s history, the language was banned in schools, churches, theaters, and other public institutions. For a while, it was even against the law to publish books in Ukrainian or give babies Ukrainian names. Ukrainian became the country’s official language once again in 1989.
pages.brief: Elementary school students in Ukraine practice their reading skills together in a classroom. Most people in Ukraine speak Ukrainian, the country’s official language, though Russian, Polish, and Yiddish are also spoken. Ukrainian became official again in 1989 after periods when it was banned in schools and public life.

pages.text: History Humans have lived in Ukraine since prehistoric times. In the 8th century bce—around 2,750 years ago—groups of people from what is now Iran settled in the plains. In the following centuries, Greeks established colonies along the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov. Around the same time, Slavs were migrating from their homeland north of the Carpathian Mountains to settle throughout the region. They built settlements that later developed into important centers for business and politics. Kyiv grew out of one of these early settlements. By the 11th century ce, the Slavs had joined with Viking invaders from Scandinavia and formed a powerful kingdom called Kyivan Rus. It was the largest empire in Europe at the time. The empire’s reign ended when the Mongols arrived from central Asia and attacked the kingdom in the 1200s. Lithuania then took control of most of Ukraine in the 1300s. These are the ruins of the ancient city of Tauric Chersonese, built around 422 bce.
pages.brief: The ruins of the ancient city of Tauric Chersonese stand on the landscape. Built around 422 BCE, the city was founded as Greek colonies spread along the Black Sea. The scene traces Ukraine’s early history, from prehistoric people and Slavic settlements to the powerful kingdom of Kyivan Rus and later invasions.

pages.text: The Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle is thought to have been built in the 13th or 14th century. In the late 1500s, Poland invaded Ukraine. The Polish forced most Ukrainians to become serfs— farmers who were obligated to work on land they didn’t own. Serfs had little wealth or power. Angry over their situation, the serfs rebelled in the 1600s. They formed a military force called the Cossacks and asked for Russia’s help in defeating the Polish. The Cossacks won independence from Poland, but by the late 1700s, Russia had gained control of nearly all of Ukraine. It was during this time that use of the Ukrainian language was prohibited. By 1922, Ukraine was part of the Soviet Union, the largest country to ever exist. It included what are now the separate countries of Lithuania, Belarus, Russia, and Moldova, among many others. The Soviet Union broke apart in 1991, and Ukraine declared its independence. That year, the country elected its first president, Leonid Kravchuk.
pages.brief: The Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle stands as a large stone fortress, thought to have been built in the 13th or 14th century. The scene follows Ukraine’s history through Polish rule, Cossack rebellion, Russian control, the Soviet Union, and the 1991 declaration of independence.

pages.text: The Chernobyl Disaster In April 1986, explosions at a nuclear power station in Chernobyl (chair-NOH-bil) released radioactive material into the air. Radioactive materials give off a form of energy called radiation, which can be dangerous to living creatures in high amounts. Wind carried the radioactive material as far west as France and Italy, exposing hundreds of thousands of people and millions of acres of land to harmful radiation. Following the accident, thousands of people were forced to leave their homes. The government made it illegal to come within 30 kilometers (18 mi.) of the nuclear power station because the land, water, and air had become radioactive. The radiation had also caused deformities—misshapen or abnormal body parts—in animals born near the site. To this day, no people live there because the land and animals are still radioactive. Landmarks Ukraine has many incredible landmarks, both natural and human-made. It has more than forty- five national parks, including the Carpathian National Nature Park, which was established in 1980 to protect the landscapes of the Carpathian Mountains. Mount Hoverla (hoh-VAIR-lah), the tallest mountain in Ukraine, is there. Another popular park is the Oleshky Sands National Nature Park in southern Ukraine, which contains 1,620 square kilometers (625 sq. mi.) of sand dunes. That’s twice the size of Kyiv! The Sun rises on a misty morning in the Carpathian Mountains.
pages.brief: The sun rises on a misty morning in the Carpathian Mountains. The scene also recalls the Chernobyl disaster, when explosions released radioactive material in 1986, forcing thousands from their homes. It notes Ukraine’s many national parks, including Carpathian National Nature Park, Mount Hoverla, and Oleshky Sands.

pages.text: Ukraine is home to many castles, palaces, monasteries, and cathedrals. One popular destination for visitors is the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra (peh-CHAIRSK LAHV-rah), also known as the Kiev Monastery of the Caves. The monastery is one of Ukraine’s seven World Heritage Sites— places considered important to world history. It was founded in 1051 ce. Beneath it lies caves and catacombs—underground burial sites—which contain important religious relics, as well as the bodies of monks mummified and preserved in glass coffins. Khotyn Fortress Another important Ukrainian landmark is the Khotyn (HOH-tin) fortress located in Khotyn, one of the oldest towns in Ukraine. The structure, originally made of wood, was probably built in the early 11th century, though different rulers have added to it over time. It’s one of the oldest preserved fortifications—structures built to defend an area against attacks—in Eastern Europe. This is probably because a wall nearly 6 meters (20 ft.) thick and over 40 meters (130 ft.) high was added to it in the 1400s, making it strong enough to withstand cannon fire. The fortress is one of more than five thousand fortifications in Ukraine.
pages.brief: Khotyn Fortress stands as a large stone fortification in one of Ukraine’s oldest towns. Its defenses were strengthened in the 1400s with a wall nearly 6 meters thick and over 40 meters high. Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, a monastery founded in 1051, has caves and catacombs beneath it.

pages.text: Ukraine’s Tunnel of Love One of the most popular places to visit in Ukraine is the Tunnel of Love, a 4-kilometer (2.5 mi.) natural tunnel that surrounds a train track in the city of Klevan. Trees were planted on either side of the tracks in the 1940s to hide trains heading to an army base. Over time, the trees’ branches formed arches across the tracks. Today, the tunnel’s beauty draws visitors from all over the world. Celebrations Ukraine has many celebrations throughout the year. One of the most important is Independence Day on August 24. This holiday marks the day Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. It is celebrated in cities throughout the country with concerts, festivals, and parades.
pages.brief: The Tunnel of Love is a 4-kilometer natural tunnel around a train track in Klevan. Trees planted in the 1940s grew branches into arches over the rails, and visitors come from around the world to see it. Independence Day on August 24 is celebrated with concerts, festivals, and parades.

pages.text: Like many countries, Ukraine also has holidays to celebrate the seasons. One is Ivan Kupala Day, which marks the beginning of summer. There are many traditions associated with this holiday, including dancing around a bonfire, making wildflower wreaths, and bathing in lakes. Masliana is a week-long holiday celebrating the end of winter and the arrival of spring. Many traditional dishes eaten during this week are made with cheese and butter. Two of the most popular dishes are varenyky (vah-REH-nih-kih), or dumplings, and pancakes. Long ago, people believed that the more fun they had during this holiday, the more successful the following year would be, so it is often celebrated with lots of music, entertainment, and food.
pages.brief: People celebrate Ivan Kupala Day by dancing around a bonfire, making wildflower wreaths, and bathing in lakes. Another holiday, Masliana, marks the end of winter with music, entertainment, and food such as varenyky dumplings and pancakes made with cheese and butter.

pages.text: Conclusion Ukraine is home to incredible landscapes, beautiful architecture, and vibrant cities that attract millions of visitors each year. The country has a long, sometimes difficult history, because it was ruled by many different empires and rulers for centuries before finally gaining its independence. But throughout Ukraine’s history, its people maintained their language and culture. Even today, annual celebrations keep centuries-old traditions alive. From stunning national parks to joyful festivals, the country of Ukraine has a lot to offer. A woman holds Ukraine’s national flag.
pages.brief: A woman holds Ukraine’s national flag. Ukraine has incredible landscapes, beautiful architecture, and vibrant cities, along with a long and sometimes difficult history. Despite centuries of rule by different empires, its people maintained their language and culture, and annual celebrations keep old traditions alive.

books.title: Ships of Discovery
books.art_why: The book follows boats from ancient Egypt, Polynesia and the Vikings through the Age of Discovery, all before photographs could exist, so pictures must be drawn.

pages.text: Introduction People often settle along rivers, lakes, and seas where they can find fresh water, nutrient-rich soil, and bountiful fishing. Long ago, people who lived near large bodies of water were curious about what might exist beyond the horizon. They also speculated that traveling over water might be easier than traveling over land.
