They noticed that particular materials, such as wood, reeds, or skins full of air, were buoyant. These thoughts led to the construction of the first simple boat. As boats and ships became more practical, people were able to travel farther from home. Advancing technology created new types of boats that were able to carry more cargo and were often safer, faster, and more comfortable. Boats became important tools for commerce, exploration, and defense. Let’s examine how boats were used to explore the world and how they have changed over time.
pages.brief: On a calm shore beside a river mouth, a group of early people gather reeds and logs and tie the bundles into a small floating raft. One person wades out and pushes it into the water. Behind them sits a settlement, with fishing gear and fresh water nearby.

pages.text: Early Years The oldest record of sea travel comes from Egypt. People might have been sailing the seas before them, but the Egyptians were the first to leave us records of their journeys. More than 6,000 years ago, the Egyptians took to the water and carved images of themselves doing so in stone. Since the mighty Nile River dictated much of ancient Egyptian life, it’s not surprising that Egyptians mastered the art of traveling by water. Originally, they built simple boats by carving out the trunks of trees, but the Egyptians were not the only people to make boats from trees. Far away in the Americas, Indigenous peoples were also building dugout canoes by hollowing out tree trunks. These were sturdy boats, but they couldn’t carry much.
pages.brief: Beside the wide Nile River, Egyptian workers carve pictures of boats into a stone wall, while others hollow out a tree trunk with tools to make a dugout canoe. Far away in the Americas, Indigenous people shape their own dugout canoe from a fallen tree trunk on a forest riverbank.

pages.text: Over time, people wanted to transport larger cargoes over waterways. It became necessary to construct boats that could carry many people for long voyages. They also needed to be able to carry food, animals, and other items to trade. Canoes carved from a single oak tree and steered with a pole were adequate boats for crossing a lake or going down a river, but they didn’t work well for carrying bulky objects. Imagine trying to row a narrow canoe across a wide lake with six sheep crammed around you. The space just wasn’t sufficient. Humans have always strived to perfect and upgrade their inventions, so it was natural that ancient people searched for methods to build bigger, faster, and safer boats. People realized that they needed better boats if they were going to explore places far from their homeland.
pages.brief: A narrow canoe cut from a single oak tree floats on a wide lake. Six sheep are crammed in around one person, who pushes a long pole into the water to steer. The boat sits low and crowded, with almost no room for the animals.

pages.text: The next evolution in boat building was the use of wooden beams to make a frame. The frame was covered with wooden planks or bark from trees. Some cultures even used animal skins stretched over the frame to create a hull, the outer shell of a boat. These boats were bigger than previous designs, but were also more streamlined and able to hold more cargo. People also developed paddles and oars to move in deep water, where poles could not reach the bottom. The Egyptians were the first people to cover wooden frames with long, flat pieces of wood to create hulls. Some of their boats measured as much as 21.3 meters (70 ft) long. The Egyptians were also the first to use sails to harness the power of the wind. The use of sails eliminated or reduced the need for people to row the boats. Some boats used both rowers and sails.
pages.brief: Boat builders stretch bark and animal skins over a frame of wooden beams to form a hull. Nearby, a long Egyptian boat with a wooden hull and a square sail moves down the river, some crew pulling oars while the sail catches the wind above them.

pages.text: Soon, the Greeks, Phoenicians, and other peoples around the Mediterranean Sea were building large boats powered by sails. About 3,000 years ago, sailing ships were built with two masts, each one holding a sail. The addition of a second mast made a ship much easier to steer and also made it much faster. Five hundred years later, the Greeks developed a ship with four sails. This ship was safe enough to leave the Mediterranean Sea and travel down the west coast of Africa. Some of the fastest ships at the time were built for battle. These warships often had as many as three levels of rowers on each side of the ship. Arranging the rowers above each other on separate tiers provided a great deal of power in a small amount of space. Greek ships with three tiers of rowers were called triremes. These larger ships allowed people to travel to and explore distant places, and it was during this period that exploration and trade moved beyond the Mediterranean Sea. Although ocean travel still had its dangers, it had become safe enough that some brave explorers and traders dared to risk it.
pages.brief: A Greek trireme cuts across the Mediterranean, its hull lined with three tiers of rowers stacked one above another, oars sweeping the water. Above, two masts carry sails. Another sailing ship with four sails travels down the west coast of Africa, far from home waters.

pages.text: The Polynesians In the South Pacific, groups of Pacific Island peoples were building boats that could sail in the open ocean. Over 3,500 years ago, these people were traveling east, well beyond the archipelago of islands where they lived. They also explored areas off the Asian mainland. More than a thousand years ago, these people made journeys of thousands of miles in open boats. These Polynesian sailors built a type of boat that was an early version of the modern catamaran. They took two canoes and connected them using large wooden poles. A deck was then built to span the poles. These boats usually measured about 15 to 18 meters (50–60 ft) long. The central deck held masts for sails and had enough space for several people and their supplies for the duration of a lengthy voyage. Polynesian catamaran.
pages.brief: In the South Pacific, Polynesian builders lash two long canoes together with large wooden poles and lay a deck across them. Sails rise from masts on the central deck, and people stow supplies for a long open-ocean voyage of thousands of miles.

pages.text: PACIFIC OCEAN ASIA Hawaiian Islands Easter Island AUSTRALIA New Zealand Routes of Polynesian expansion These early boats provided safe travel from one island to another. The Polynesians settled many new islands they discovered. By 1000 ce, they lived on nearly every habitable island they could find in the Pacific Ocean. Their new homes included Hawai ‘ i, New Zealand, and Rapa Nui (Easter Island). The Polynesians were accomplished sailors. They became so familiar with the ocean that they could determine their location by the size and shape of the waves. They also knew how to navigate using the stars. They could easily travel great distances by going from island to island. The Polynesians grew to accept sea travel as a way of life.
pages.brief: A Polynesian navigator stands on the deck of a double canoe at night, studying the stars above the ocean and reading the size and shape of the waves. In the distance a green island rises from the sea, one of the many new homes found across the Pacific.

pages.text: The Vikings More than 1,300 years ago, another group of people in another part of the world began to build larger boats. These people were the Vikings. They lived in the northern part of Europe. The Vikings were well known as warriors and conquerors. They were accustomed to traveling over water. By the year 700 ce, they were sailing boats that were superior to any others on the ocean. The boats they built, called knarrs (kuh-NARS), were used primarily for trading. These boats were up to 16.5 meters (54 ft) long and 4.5 meters (15 ft) wide. Because they were flat bottomed, the knarr boats could carry extremely heavy loads, and they were wide enough to carry a large amount of cargo. They were also very stable and could travel safely across the open ocean. At that time, most sailors did not like to lose sight of the coast, but the Vikings were fearless. They used a wooden dial called a sun compass to help them navigate and conquer new lands. They were the first Europeans to visit North America.
pages.brief: Viking sailors load heavy cargo into a wide, flat-bottomed knarr on a northern European shore, the boat broad enough to carry barrels and bundles. One sailor holds up a wooden sun compass, while out on the open ocean the sturdy ship sails on toward land in North America.

pages.text: The Vikings also built warships known as longships. It often was difficult to tell if a longship was coming or going because they looked the same in the front and in the back. Because of the design of their longships, Viking attackers could easily change direction. Longships were able to travel as fast as 15 knots. (A knot is a way to measure speed on water. One knot is a little faster than one mile per hour.) Some of the larger longships carried as many as 200 warriors. The combination of large, speedy, easy-to-handle ships and a fierce fighting spirit made the Vikings tough to defeat. The Vikings ruled the ocean for nearly three centuries, but they did not improve on the design of the longship, and other nations eventually developed mightier ships.
pages.brief: A long, narrow Viking longship speeds across the water, its front and back shaped alike so it looks the same coming or going. Rowers pull hard at the oars and a sail fills above them. Two hundred warriors crowd the deck with their shields.

pages.text: Age of Discovery Until the 1400s, most sea explorers remained close to their home waters, but with the coming of the Age of Discovery, things changed dramatically. Every European sailing nation wanted to find new lands. The race was on, and the Americas were the prize. Shipbuilders searched for ways to build faster and safer ships. In the 1400s and 1500s, sea explorers used small, swift, sturdy ships known as caravels. These ships had three masts to hold sails. This design made the ships faster and easier to steer. Caravels had square sails on the fore and main masts, and a triangular-shaped sail, called a lateen, on the mast at the rear of the ship.
pages.brief: In a busy 1400s shipyard, shipbuilders finish a small, swift caravel with three masts. Square sails hang on the fore and main masts, and a triangular lateen sail slants from the mast at the rear. The tidy ship waits at the quayside for a voyage of exploration.

pages.text: Consider the Conquered What impact did these discoveries have on the people already living in these places? Too often, the impact was a tragic one. Christopher Columbus, Hernan Cortes, and other Europeans who led these expeditions often exploited both the land and people they encountered. Their motive was usually financial gain. Before long, ships would also be used to carry people across oceans and enslave them far from their homes. Christopher Columbus sailed three of these ships. Santa Maria was the largest at 27.4 meters (90 ft) long and 9.1 meters (30 ft) wide. Compared to modern ocean liners and cargo ships, these ships were tiny—they didn’t even have cabins where the crew could sleep at night. Sailors just had to lie down on the deck or in the hold. But even though caravels were quite small, the famous explorer Ferdinand Magellan set out to sail five of these ships around the world with a crew of 260 sailors. Almost three years after they began the trip, Magellan’s crew returned. Only one of the ships and eighteen of the sailors made it around the world. The other ships were lost at sea, and the other sailors died. Magellan was not one of the survivors. He was killed somewhere in the Philippine Islands.
pages.brief: A small wooden caravel with no cabins crosses open ocean, sailors lying down on the deck and in the hold to sleep. Three such ships sail together under Christopher Columbus, tiny on the vast water, while Magellan's fleet of five ships sets out with 260 sailors aboard.

pages.text: The Chinese While Europeans were sailing the world, the Chinese had also taken to the sea in another part of the world. By the 1400s, they were skilled sailors. Chinese people had long since invented the magnetic compass. They also invented the rudder a thousand years before Westerners. They used rectangular sails reinforced with strips of bamboo called battens. The battens made the sails sturdier and easier to furl and unfurl, and sailors could even climb them like ladders! From 1405 to 1443, the most famous Chinese explorer, Zheng He, traveled on seven long voyages with a fleet of sixty-two treasure ships. The Chinese called these ships junks. Inside the hull, the ship was divided into many sections, partitioned off with watertight walls or bulkheads to minimize potential damage. If the hull were breached, the leak could only flood a small section of the ship, rather than sinking the entire ship. Zheng He’s junks were much larger than European ships. His largest ship was so big that it could have held all three of Columbus’s ships on its deck. This massive ship was 121 meters (400 ft) long and 45.7 meters (150 ft) wide.
pages.brief: Chinese shipwrights finish a huge junk, its hull divided inside by watertight bulkheads, its rectangular sails stiffened with strips of bamboo battens. Zheng He's fleet of sixty-two treasure ships sets out, his largest ship, 121 metres long, dwarfing everything else on the water.

pages.text: In addition to the sixty-two main trading ships, more than a hundred smaller support boats were in the fleet. The Chinese sailed all the way to Africa to trade as well as to show the might of the Chinese empire to the rest of the world. Zheng He even carried a giraffe home to the emperor. War with their Asian neighbors caused the Chinese to turn their attention away from exploration, however. The emperor made ocean voyages illegal and had all the treasure ships destroyed.
pages.brief: Zheng He's great treasure ships, surrounded by more than a hundred smaller support boats, arrive at an African port where people gather to trade. Aboard one ship a tall giraffe stands in a pen, a gift being carried home to the Chinese emperor before he orders the voyages stopped.

pages.text: Later Years As sea exploration continued, the Spanish led the way. By the 1500s, European shipbuilding had experienced vast improvements. The newest ships, called galleons, were larger, faster, and more comfortable. It took two thousand oak trees to build one galleon. These vessels were as long as 42.7 meters (140 ft), but were still small compared to the Chinese ships. Many of them had nice, comfortable living quarters, at least for the officers. Galleons were dual-purpose ships that served as both trading vessels and warships. Because of their great size, these warships were capable of mounting many cannons, making them dangerous in battle. In the late 1700s, the British captain James Cook began some of the greatest explorations of his time. On his first ship, Endeavour, Cook sailed around the world.
pages.brief: In a Spanish shipyard, shipwrights raise the hull of a galleon built from two thousand oak trees, with comfortable quarters for the officers and rows of cannon along the sides. Far away, Captain James Cook's ship Endeavour sails out of port to begin a voyage around the world.

pages.text: While many previous explorers sailed to make war or find treasure, Cook was interested in knowledge and science. He brought three scientists with him when he traveled, one astronomer (a scientist who studies the night sky) and two naturalists (scientists who study plants and animals). He also took many artists to document their discoveries. Cook observed the stars as he sailed, and whenever he came to a new land, he learned as much as he could about its plants and animals. His work broadened the European understanding of the world. Cook kept his crew healthy by making them eat foods such as limes and cabbages. Until Cook’s time, up to one-half of the crew on a long voyage would die of scurvy or other diseases. Cook knew his success as an explorer depended on keeping his crew in good health. Soon, all British sailors knew that they needed to eat vitamin C to survive. In the late 1770s, Cook visited Hawai ‘ i three times. On his last trip, in 1779, a fight broke out between the Hawaiians and Cook’s crew. Cook was killed.
pages.brief: On the deck of the Endeavour, Captain Cook watches the night sky with an astronomer, while two naturalists examine plants and animals brought from a new shore and artists sketch what they find. Below deck, sailors eat limes and cabbages to stay healthy on the long voyage.

pages.text: Conclusion By the mid-1800s, sailors had explored and mapped most of the world’s coastlines. Very fast sailing vessels called clipper ships carried people across oceans in a matter of days. One clipper, Sir Lancelot, set a record by sailing from Australia to England in three months. Some of these ships had as many as thirty-five sails, and they could travel even in light breezes. By the 1870s, however, the steam engine largely replaced wind power. The Industrial Revolution swung into full gear, and machines became more significant to everyone. Bigger and faster ships than had ever been imagined suddenly became possible. Today, steam power is outdated, and ships run on different types of engines. Some submarines and aircraft carriers even run on nuclear power! Cruise ships carry thousands of people at a time like floating cities. When we look at some of the ships used by early explorers to sail across oceans, we have to admire the ingenuity of the people who designed those ships of discovery. While the impacts of sea exploration weren’t positive for everyone, setting sail into the unknown helped create the world we know today.
pages.brief: A clipper ship with thirty-five sails races across the ocean in a light breeze, carrying people from Australia to England in three months. Nearby, a modern cruise ship carrying thousands of people, a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier and a submarine show how far ships have come.

books.title: Seeing the Evidence: Forensic Scientists at Work
books.art_why: Real-world forensic science and labs exist today, and this is not a biography of a named famous person.

pages.text: Seeing the Evidence: Forensic Scientists at Work.
pages.brief: A forensic scientist in a clean crime laboratory lifts a small trace sample with tweezers under bright light, while another investigator photographs a surface nearby. The room is calm and orderly, showing science being used carefully at work.

pages.text: Introduction A man walked quickly across a field into an old mill, a building where wheat was crushed to make flour. Inside the building, he killed someone and then hurried away without being seen. Later, when police questioned the man, he insisted that he was innocent. This suspect might have gotten away with the crime if only he had wiped trace evidence off his shoes. Trace evidence is dust, hairs, threads, and other tiny bits of material found on or near a suspect or victim of a crime. When a detective named Edmond Locard used a microscope to study the man’s shoes, he noticed something no one else had seen: traces of flour on the heels and soles. This trace evidence matched the flour found at the mill where the victim was killed. This placed the man at the scene of the crime and helped to convict him of murder. Traces of flour could be seen on the suspect’s shoes with a microscope.
pages.brief: A man in dark clothing hurries away from an old flour mill across a field. Later, detective Edmond Locard leans over a microscope in a lab, studying the suspect’s shoes; tiny traces of flour are visible on the heels and soles, linking the man to the mill.

pages.text: The flour mill killer was caught by forensic science, the use of science to solve crimes and convict criminals in courts of law. Detectives began to use science to solve crimes around 1900. Before then, police used eyewitnesses and informers to solve crimes. Today, crime scene investigators (CSIs) are an important part of many criminal cases. Locard’s Exchange Principle Investigators work in a crime lab, a room filled with scientific equipment. They use the equipment to help discover and study forensic evidence. The world’s first crime lab was set up in 1910 in Lyons, France. It was created by police detective Edmond Locard. He was the same detective who solved the flour mill case. Locard stated a guiding principle that today’s forensic scientists still follow. He called it the Exchange Principle: “Objects or surfaces that come into contact always exchange trace evidence.” In other words, everyone who enters a crime scene takes away something from the scene and leaves something of themselves behind.
pages.brief: Inside an early crime laboratory in Lyons, France, Edmond Locard stands among scientific equipment with other investigators. He gestures toward surfaces and trace samples, illustrating how contact exchanges tiny evidence. The room is filled with microscopes and tools used to discover and study forensic evidence.

pages.text: Case File #1 The Crime The scene of the crime is a remote stretch of railroad track in southern Oregon. The year is 1923. A Union Pacific freight train has been robbed. The bandits killed the engineer and two other train workers, and then used a homemade dynamite bomb to blow open the mail car. Back then mail often held valuable stock and bond certificates and sometimes cash or gold. When police searched the scene, the only piece of evidence they found was a pair of stained overalls that one of the bandits had left behind. Stop and Think! What could someone discover about you from examining your clothing?
pages.brief: On a remote stretch of railroad track in southern Oregon in 1923, a Union Pacific freight train stands damaged after a robbery. Near the tracks, police search the scene and find a pair of stained overalls left behind by one of the bandits. The mail car shows damage from a homemade dynamite bomb.

pages.text: Case Fact! The bandits stole a detonator from a construction site. They actually used too much dynamite and blew up any money that may have been in the mail car. The explosion also killed the Railway Post Office clerk. The explosion was so loud and destructive that the bandits ran from the scene without having robbed anyone of anything. Two men investigate dynamite and other explosive materials in 1924. How the Case Was Solved The police asked for help from Edward Heinrich, head of the Berkeley, California, forensic science laboratory. Heinrich was famous for being able to discover a great deal from very little evidence. Heinrich told the police to be on the lookout for a left-handed lumberjack in his early twenties weighing about 166 pounds (75 kg) and standing 5 feet 10 inches (1.8 m) tall. He also said the lumberjack had light brown hair, rolled his own cigarettes, and was unusually neat about his appearance.
pages.brief: Two investigators in 1924 examine dynamite and explosive materials beside a damaged railway car, with debris from a powerful blast around them. Nearby, a construction site suggests where a detonator was stolen. The scene is tense and smoky, showing the destructive force that stopped the robbery.

pages.text: How could Heinrich have discovered all that from a pair of overalls? Heinrich explained: the fact that the left pocket was more worn than the right meant the owner was left-handed. What stained the overalls was sap from trees that grow in southern Oregon forests where lumberjacks work. The overalls’ size told Heinrich the lumberjack’s height and weight, and he could estimate the owner’s age from a light brown hair caught on a button. Tobacco shreds in a pocket and nail clippings caught in a seam told him the rest. And one more thing, Heinrich said, showing police a piece of paper he had found rolled up at the bottom corner of a pocket. The paper was bleached clean from many washings, but when treated with iodine, words began to appear. It was a receipt from a post office, made out to a man from Eugene, Oregon. Police went to the man’s house and learned that he was missing, along with his two brothers. Neighbors’ descriptions of the man matched Heinrich’s description exactly. When police tracked down the brothers several years later, they confessed to the robbery and murders and were sent to prison. The railroad robbers’ case was just one of some two thousand cases that Heinrich solved during his career as a forensic investigator.
pages.brief: Forensic investigator Edward Heinrich holds a pair of worn overalls in a laboratory, pointing to the more-worn left pocket. On a table lie a button with a light brown hair, tobacco shreds, nail clippings, and a washed paper receipt being treated with iodine. The details reveal a left-handed lumberjack from Eugene, Oregon.

pages.text: Case File #2 Place: Anyplace, U.S.A. Date: anytime after 1950 Crime: a series of burglaries Evidence: dirty dishes The Crime Police thought that a series of burglaries had been committed by the same gang of thieves. When detectives finally located and raided their apartment, it was empty. The entire place had been wiped clean, except that the thieves had forgotten to run the dishwasher. How the Case Was Solved How could the police discover their identities? The secret was on the thieves’ hands. Look closely at the tips of your fingers and thumbs, and you will see raised ridges of skin running in patterns of curving lines: your fingerprints. Each of your fingerprints is different from the other nine, and each one is unique. No one else on Earth has fingerprints like yours, and no one ever will. In 1896, an Englishman named Edward Henry discovered a system to classify fingerprints. In 1901, he became a police commissioner and used his system to identify criminals.
pages.brief: Police detectives stand in a cleaned-out apartment after a raid, finding a dishwasher still holding dirty dishes. In the foreground, a close view shows fingertips with raised ridges in curved patterns. The empty rooms and forgotten dishes suggest thieves who wiped everything clean but left fingerprints behind.

pages.text: Classifying Fingerprints Edward Henry based his system on features that every fingerprint shares. Every print has ridges (the raised lines) and furrows (the low spots between ridges). Prints also have arches, loops, and whorls. Arches are either tented (pointed at the top) or plain (rounded). Loops are either radial (running toward the thumb) or ulnar (running toward the little finger). Whorls are circular. Henry added smaller features—known as forks, dots, islands, hooks, and bridges—to his system. The type, number, and position of these features make each fingerprint unique. Henry’s basic system is still used today. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has more than seventy million fingerprints in its database— the largest worldwide. Prints found at crime scenes can be compared quickly with all the prints in the databases. When a match turns up, police have a piece of evidence that places a person at the scene of a crime. Criminals are careful not to leave their fingerprints behind. In this case, CSIs got fingerprints from the dishes in the dishwasher and matched them to prints in the database.
pages.brief: A fingerprint examiner compares a print from a dish in a crime lab. Large images of arches, loops, and whorls show ridge patterns, with small features like forks, dots, islands, hooks, and bridges marked. Nearby, a computer database of fingerprints suggests millions of prints being searched for a match.

pages.text: What Is DNA? DNA is the part of each of your body’s cells that carries instructions that tell your body how to live and grow. About 98 percent of these instructions are the same in all people. The 2 percent that are different make your DNA unique, just like your fingerprints. Scientists can make microscopic X-ray pictures of unique DNA, known as DNA profiles. Just like fingerprint databases, police have developed computer databases of DNA profiles. DNA can be collected from almost any cell in your body, including cells in your hair, saliva, blood, sweat, and tears. DNA technology is so advanced that even a single skin cell could produce a DNA profile. Profiles can also be created using animal DNA. A database of cat DNA was started in Great Britain in 2013 to help establish that a cat hair found on a victim came from a particular suspect’s cat.
pages.brief: A scientist in a laboratory studies a microscopic X-ray image of a DNA profile on a screen. Nearby, samples of hair, saliva, blood, sweat, and tears are laid out as possible sources of cells. A cat hair sample suggests animal DNA can also be profiled and compared in a database.

pages.text: Case File #3 The Crime Not all evidence is tangible, or something that can be picked up, examined, and taken to the crime lab for testing. In many cases, the evidence comes in digital form. Emails, web searches, and GPS tracking information can all be used as evidence in court. One winter evening, Rito Llamas-Juarez and his family members answered an ad in an app where people connect to buy and sell their belongings. Llamas-Juarez found a listing advertising two cell phones for $500. His family contacted the person selling the phones, who used the name “Sports.” They arranged to meet in a parking lot. Three men approached Llamas-Juarez and his family members. One of the men shot and killed Llamas-Juarez, before fleeing the scene. Stop and Think! How could a digital trail help lead investigators to the suspect?
pages.brief: On a winter evening in a parking lot, Rito Llamas-Juarez and his family meet three men after arranging a cell phone sale through an app. One man raises a gun while the others stand nearby. A phone screen in the foreground shows a listing for two cell phones, hinting at the digital trail left behind.

pages.text: How the Case Was Solved Crime scene investigators searched the scene and discovered a smoked cigarette. They also found a cell phone box from the botched sale in Llamas-Juarez’s car. Investigators searched the phone Llamas-Juarez’s family used to arrange the sale. Police obtained a warrant to make the app used in the sale reveal the name of the owner of the Sports account. It was connected to a social media account that belonged to Larry Thomas. Once investigators had a suspect, they obtained a warrant to search his home. They discovered ammunition that was an exact match for the type used in the murder. Investigators swabbed Thomas for his DNA, and it matched the DNA found on the cigarette. They also matched the fingerprints discovered on the box to Thomas. In addition to physical evidence, investigators had digital evidence. They searched Thomas’s cell phone and found the password connected to the Sports account. Further, Thomas had emails from other potential buyers. Other key pieces of evidence included a photo of Thomas posing with the type of gun used in the shooting. Thanks in a large part to forensic digital investigators, Thomas was found guilty of his crimes.
pages.brief: Crime scene investigators collect a smoked cigarette and a cell phone box from the car. In a lab, a detective compares DNA and fingerprints from the cigarette and box to a suspect named Larry Thomas. On a table, ammunition, a cell phone, emails, and a photo of a man posing with a gun show the digital and physical evidence.

pages.text: DNA Profiling Scientists use DNA to make a DNA profile for a specific, but unknown, suspect. Then they try to find a match— although it might take years. Police have a database where they can search DNA profiles of people involved in other crimes. People can also voluntarily upload their DNA to genealogy websites to find out information about their ancestors and locate unknown family members. Some genealogy websites allow law enforcement to upload crime scene DNA to search for matches. This new field of forensic science is called investigative genetic genealogy. Matches aren’t always exact, but rather allow investigators to close in on families with ties to the DNA sample. Investigators trace family trees connected to the DNA, and use clues such as age, gender, and known locations to determine their suspect. To confirm their suspicions, investigators need a DNA sample, often obtained from unknowing suspects in the form of a used straw or coffee cup from a suspect’s trash. DNA is not only used to convict suspects, but also to free wrongly convicted suspects. Investigators are now finding out that many convicted criminals, some serving lengthy or even life sentences, are not the real perpetrators. Many people are working hard to use DNA to free wrongly convicted people. A forensic scientist bags evidence at a crime scene.
pages.brief: A forensic scientist kneels at a crime scene and bags evidence while a laboratory screen nearby shows a DNA profile and a family tree. A used straw and coffee cup sit on a table as possible sources of a suspect’s DNA. The scene suggests investigators tracing family connections to solve a case.

pages.text: Conclusion Each of the cases in this book explores a different kind of forensic evidence. There are other kinds of forensic evidence, too—footprints, shoe prints, palm prints, lip prints, bite marks, paint chips, tire tread marks, the markings on a bullet, and more. Any of these can link suspects to the scene of a crime or can show who is innocent. Together, the law enforcement officers and scientists who gather and study forensic evidence use virtually all of the sciences, from anthropology to zoology, in their work. Whatever science they specialize in, they all have one thing in common—they use their knowledge to see what goes unnoticed by the rest of us. bullet tire tracks.
pages.brief: In a crime laboratory, forensic scientists examine a variety of evidence laid out on tables: a shoe print, a bullet, tire tracks, paint chips, and other trace materials. Officers and scientists work together, using different sciences to link suspects to a crime scene or show who is innocent.
